author: Rishika Pardikar
title: African Arguments Interview with Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah Ahead of COP31
content:
The 31st climate talks (COP31) began in Antalya,

Türkiye

on 9 November

.

The African Group of Negotiators (AGN), an alliance of all of the 54 countries from the continent, had submitted three agenda proposals to the UNFCCC for the conference. One concerned a demand to triple adaptation finance, the other related to trade-related climate measures like carbon border taxes and the last one was about financing arrangements under the Green Climate Fund (GCF), a climate fund established under the UNFCCC to assist developing countries in mitigation and adaptation. None of the three proposals made it into the final agenda adopted for COP31. However, the COP31 presidents said negotiation tracks concerned with trade-related climate measures and the GCF will take the respective matters under consideration during negotiations in the following days. If the proposals by AGN were accepted, all three themes would have been negotiated as separate agenda items in their own right. 


Nevertheless, the fact that AGN made three submissions shows that the bloc seeks to assert its voice on the global stage.


After the agenda was adopted Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the AGN from Ghana, said in the plenary ‘Africa comes to Antalya with one clear message: implementation depends on means of implementation. Our continent contributes the least to this crisis and is among the most exposed to its impacts.’ It was in this spirit, the chair added, that AGN had proposed three agenda items and also that it participated actively in the negotiations on the agenda and supported the conclusions that were reached. 


With COP32 scheduled to be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, African Arguments interviewed Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah about AGN’s priorities for COP31 and the outcomes it hopes to secure to build momentum towards the next climate summit:


AA: What are AGN’s priorities for COP31? 


Firstly, thank you for the interview. We all need to be speaking to each other in this precious space.


Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement, we have been able to set up a number of structures for implementation. There are methodologies and structures for the implementation of Article 6 [on carbon markets]. Countries have submitted their NDCs [Nationally Determined Contributions] and NAPs [National Adaptation Plans]. Over 80 developing countries have submitted NAPs–this is more than half the number of total developing countries. Even on Article 13 on enhanced transparency framework, we have a solid framework to make sure reporting on climate action is taken care of. So, the groundwork for implementation has been laid. The question now is whether we implement it and how we implement it. Our focus for COP31 and COP32 is to actually bring the issue of implementation to reality. And here, we need to talk about finance, technology and capacity. We are coming to COP31 believing we can make progress on the finance work programme and on the goal to triple adaptation finance. We also come to COP with an understanding that trade-related issues impede our development, especially on climate-related measures [like carbon border taxes]. This COP is mainly about support for implementation. Ambition goes not only with NDC targets and creating awareness but also financial support. Because temperature goals can only be met if developing countries have resources to meet their mitigation targets and other long-term strategies.  


AA: AGN was the first group that brought the Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) to worldwide attention in 2013 with a submission to the UNFCCC that linked global adaptation efforts and costs to temperatures. Then in 2015, GGA was incorporated into the Paris Agreement, as a result of a collective push by the G77+China bloc. Now, more than a decade into this process, do you see progress? What have been the major successes and roadblocks? 


When we first submitted the GGA proposal [in 2013], it sounded strange to a lot of stakeholders, especially developed country parties. I remember it very well because I was a part of the process. The initiative and the understanding from our side, as Africa, was to give visibility to adaptation within the global climate negotiations and provide space for the mobilisation of resources to address adaptation activities across countries. I would say that we have seen success because nobody believed GGA would be adopted as part of the Paris Agreement. But now have a whole Article 7 that focuses on adaptation. Through …

author: Mebratu Kelecha
title: Who can make peace hold?
content:
On October 4, Ethiopian government forces and their Tigrayan allies entered Mekelle

 after fighters loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) withdrew from the city. Twelve days later, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed

announced a new caretaker administration

, promising to restore public services, help displaced families return, and prepare elections. From Addis Ababa, this appeared to mark the beginning of a political reset. But the situation in Tigray was far less settled. Armed factions continued to contest authority,

hundreds of thousands of people remained displaced

, and the

territorial disputes

 that had helped fuel the last war were unresolved. Mekelle had changed hands. Whether Ethiopia had moved any closer to peace was another question.

The five-member caretaker administration has six months to begin rebuilding Tigray’s public institutions, and its officials will operate under federal oversight

. Yet the military retreat that preceded its appointment did not end armed resistance.

Some former combatants have sought to return to civilian life; other commanders have vowed to keep fighting

. The

TPLF has also joined an opposition alliance with Amhara and Oromo armed groups

, even as Ethiopia’s relations with its former wartime ally

Eritrea have deteriorated into a border crisis

. This is the government’s dilemma: It must restore everyday order while the alliances, territorial claims, and chains of command that determine that order remain contested.

To understand the danger, it helps to recall how Ethiopia reached this point.

For nearly three decades, the TPLF was the most influential party

 in a ruling coalition that governed a formally federal state through an unusually centralized political system. Abiy’s rise in 2018 disrupted that arrangement. His rapprochement with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki ended two decades of hostility, but the growing confrontation between Addis Ababa and Tigray culminated in war in November 2020.

Eritrean troops and Amhara forces joined the federal campaign against the TPLF

. Their common enemy concealed sharply different visions of the peace that would follow.

The African Union–brokered

Pretoria agreement of November 2022

 ended the main phase of the fighting. It was not an empty ceasefire. The federal government and the TPLF

pledged to protect civilians, restore services, allow humanitarian access and establish a transitional administration

; disarmament and political dialogue were also envisaged. A

subsequent agreement in Nairobi

 linked the surrender of Tigrayan heavy weapons to the withdrawal of foreign and nonfederal forces. That sequencing mattered: One side could scarcely be expected to disarm confidently while forces it feared remained in place.

The agreement’s weakness lay less in what it promised than in who could deliver.

Eritrea was not a signatory

.

Amhara armed groups that had helped prosecute the war

 did not necessarily answer to federal negotiators. The TPLF, meanwhile, could sign for Tigray without ensuring that its own leadership and fighters would remain united. Pretoria brought a terrible war to a halt, but it could not freeze the balance of power among those expected to implement it. Peace required not only consent at the negotiating table but authority over armed men, budgets and territory.

Western Tigray illustrates why these distinctions are more than diplomatic technicalities. The area, claimed by Amhara actors as Welkait, changed hands during the war. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International

documented mass expulsions and abuses against Tigrayan civilians

. In April 2026, Human Rights Watch reported that Tigrayan residents

continued to face restrictions on identity documents, movement, work and access to land

. For displaced families, territorial settlement means the possibility of returning home. For authorities entrenched since the war, it may entail surrendering offices, property, and economic advantage. A boundary left unresolved does not stand still when those controlling it can determine who is allowed to live there.

Disarmament poses a similarly concrete problem. A

United Nations–supported reintegration program began in 2024

, and former fighters have continued to register. But registration is not reintegration. A man who hands over his weapon without secure work, protection or confidence in the local authorities may be available to the next recruiter. Nor is reintegration solely a Tigrayan …

author: Fraser Needham
title: ISC minister says she was not expecting Kinew’s comments about abolishing the Indian Act
content:
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty says she was as surprised as anyone when Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew raised the idea of abolishing the Indian Act last month and was hoping for more information on what role the province would play.

“I think it’s interesting to see somebody who’s a provincial premier wanting to frame up that space,” she said. “Clearly, in his role he would have to indicate his responsibility in the provincial seat and how you would serve those off-reserve community members.

“I think that’s the initiative I was hoping to see as a minister coming out of that space because you have to increase the responsibility, the partnership, the role of the provincial government in the path beyond the Indian Act.”

The idea of getting rid of the Indian Act was raised by Kinew during a press conference at the First Nations First Ministers meeting in Ottawa on Oct. 26.

“What you saw was a spontaneous moment where premier Kinew wanted to speak about status. Wanted to speak about the Indian Act.”

The Indian Act, passed in 1876, continues to govern matters of Indian status, First Nations governance, and reserve lands. The federal government has tried, and failed, to abolish it a number of times in the past 50 years.

At a later press conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he was open to the idea as long as it was co-developed with First Nations and has tasked some of his ministers to look into the issue.

He said he was directing Gull-Masty to chart a path with First Nations on amending or abolishing the act.

Conservative MP Billy Morin says the 2026 federal budget is disappointing on a number of levels.

“This might be the most overrated Prime Minister (Mark Carney) I’ve seen in quite some time,” the MP for Edmonton Northwest said. “Even more overrated than his predecessor (Justin Trudeau). This guy’s apparently a banker, a guy who knows how to do finances.

“He’s running deficits bigger than Trudeau. Bigger deficits than Trudeau and he takes great pride in that?”

The budget projects deficits of well over $50 billion over each of the next five years.

The 2023/24 deficit, the last budget under Trudeau, came in at $61.9 billion and the 2026/27 deficit is projected to be $62.3 billion.

Morin is the Indigenous Services critic for the Conservatives.

The president of the Manitoba Métis Federation says leaving Métis people out of the 2026 federal budget is not a mistake the Carney government can afford to make.

“It shouldn’t be something that we need to worry about whether it’s a budget or not,” David Chartrand said. “It should be automatic. It’s part of the fiduciary responsibility and constitutional responsibility of Canada,” he said.

The 2026 budget makes roughly $50 billion over ten years in investments in Indigenous priorities but makes no mention of Métis-specific investments.

Some have expressed fears the government is returning to a non-distinctions-based funding model that largely focuses on First Nations people.

Chartrand said the government collects billions of dollars in taxes from Métis people every year and it needs to invest that money back in their communities.

Fraser spent the last 20 years working in both print and radio in Saskatchewan – mostly in the northern part of the province. Before joining APTN’s Ottawa bureau, he was news director for the Missinipi Broadcasting Corporation working out of their Prince Albert office. He holds a bachelor of arts degree in political science from Carleton University and a diploma of journalism from Algonquin College.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Nunavik’s new sex-education curriculum takes shape
content:
Nunavik’s sexuality education pilot project will initially cover four subjects, including healthy relationships, pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections and contraception.


Kativik Ilisarniliriniq — Nunavik’s school board — and the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services

rolled out the curriculum

 this month in Kuujjuaq and Umiujaq.


The program is intended for students from kindergarten to Grade 11 (Secondary V), with lessons adapted to their ages and stages of development.


At a Nov. 4 parent information session in Kuujjuaq, school commissioner Eva Kauki-Gordon said age appropriateness had been her main concern but after reviewing the material, she was satisfied that lessons would differ between grade levels.


Kauki-Gordon said she hopes the program will help young people feel more comfortable discussing their bodies and sexual health.


Growing up, she said, sexuality and puberty were rarely discussed at home. She recalled finding it difficult to speak to her mother about getting her first period.


“I think this would help for them to be more open,” she said of students.


Five parents attended the Kuujjuaq information session. Kauki-Gordon encouraged more families to get involved in their children’s education.


“Be involved in the education that is being given,” she said. “You have [a] responsibility for your child.”


The health board developed the curriculum after consulting health-care professionals, parents, teachers and people of different ages across Nunavik.


Teaching materials or lesson plans won’t be released yet because the content may change based on findings from the pilot project.


“What is covered in kindergarten levels is very surface-level information, compared to other primary grades,” Andreas Schaffhauser-Carpentier, a media liaison with the health board, said in a written response to Nunatsiaq News.


Secondary students will also discuss topics that are more relevant to address after puberty.


The pilot project does not cover every subject planned for what will eventually become the full curriculum. Topics such as body image and a broader understanding of sexuality will be added later. The health board said the wider program will also address consent, bodily autonomy, personal boundaries and sexual abuse prevention.


The final curriculum will include a parental component with cue cards sent home after each module to explain what students learned and suggest ways families can discuss the subjects together.


“Our goal is to give students a range of options and objective information on sexual education,” Schaffhauser-Carpentier said.


The pilot runs next week at Kiluutaq School in Umiujaq, following sessions that were held in the first week of November at Jaanimmarik and Pitakallak schools in Kuujjuaq.


Feedback from the pilot will help the two organizations revise the curriculum before considering a wider rollout across the region’s schools.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: 6- Cuttings will regrow – Sitting-in for Grandmother Cottonwood
content:
On July 27th, 2026 the U.S. government and Fisher industries cut down three ancient cottonwood trees in a small town called Lochiel, Arizona in order to build not just one but two border walls. This area is the habitat of the endangered Mexican Wolf as well as jaguars, bears, foxes and many other bizarre, beautiful bugs and animals. It is also the home of the Tohono O’odham people, important to many indigenous tribes on both sides of the border. When the three grandmother cottonwoods were cut, one brave comrade stood in front of construction equipment, preventing the destruction of the last ancient tree and the construction of the border wall. In that last tree, we began our tree sit. With the support of hundreds of activists, the land owners, nearby towns and tribes, and even the local sheriff department, we halted construction of the walls for 75 days.

For 75 days, activists sat in the remaining cottonwood as ground support grew into a sprawling camp. It was the first tree sit to stop border wall construction and was briefly the first binational tree sit in history, with a sit erecting on the Mexican side for three days in August. During these 75 days, O:shad camp, jaguar in O’odham, held morning ceremony in the easement, the road which enforced the border. Ceremony frequently extended to effectively halt all construction vehicles for the day, or days at a time. People fell in love, they danced in the mud, cooked communal meals, all while defending the land. Utopia felt nearby.

Then, on October 5th, hundreds of border patrol officers, accompanied by turning point usa, invaded O:shad camp. They cut down the grandmother cottonwood and forcibly removed the tree sitter without a proper extraction team, risking her life. Activists on the ground circled the trunk to protect the tree and continue their resistance against the wall. More than 10 activists were arrested and many more brutalized. Though on private property and with no warrant, they ransacked the camp and destroyed our belongings.

Indigenous and non-white activists were singled out and beaten much worse than white comrades. Border Patrol violently pushed, pulled and dragged, but also kneeled on throats, punched eyes, pushed skin into barbed wire. They specifically targeted our medic (who is Indigenous) to be violently dragged, beaten, and arrested. They prevented our media team from capturing what happened, while escorting Turning Point USA to film the day in order to spread their right wing propaganda.

The next day, as Border Patrol expanded their boundaries further into private property to make way for the wall, five more of us were taken, and lawyers were unable to find them in the system while border patrol ignored calls from their lawyers, friends and family.

A day later, my comrade locked herself to a cement truck and stayed in a stress position without food or water for 7 hours while Border Patrol covered her with an emergency blanket despite the hot climate. One officer told her and the other officers that they should drive her to the middle of nowhere where no one would be able to hear her scream. They began to move the vehicle with her still above the tire; we all thought she would be killed. Two comrades who ran towards her, worried for her life, were tackled, brutalized, and arrested – one was sexually assaulted during her arrest. Finally they brought in an expert extractor who took her out of lockdown and she was taken to detention and then federal prison. She is now facing federal assault charges.

The rest of us were shot with pepper balls, tear gassed, leaving us vomiting, injured, bruised and emotionally exhausted. After the tree sitter was removed from the grandmother tree in Lochiel, a comrade reinstated the sit on the mexico side. Cut off from ground support by border patrol, she went over two days without food or water. When mexican firefighters and Fisher construction workers went to pull her out, she free climbed further up the tree. They destroyed her platform and life sustaining materials, leaving her to perch in the cottonwood branches without a platform or supplies. She suffered dehydration and starvation in high heat but still managed to keep a backpack on her, which she filled with clippings of the Abuela tree so that no matter what happened, the trees offspring could be replanted.

The following day the wall continued.

In total 30+ of us have been arrested, and many more brutalized, injured, and traumatized. We are the …

author: Carla Habif
title: How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win
content:
This article

How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On Oct. 25, Brazilians made history by resisting hopelessness and achieving, for the first time since the return to democracy in 1985, a comeback in the runoff of a presidential election. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection by more than 4 million votes after losing the first round to opponent Flávio Bolsonaro by over 2 million votes.


Lula, a former metalworker and union leader who co-founded the left-wing Workers’ Party,

was seeking his fourth term as president. Flávio, by contrast, was the candidate of the far-right Liberal Party and was running as the successor to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally who was

convicted and imprisoned for attempting a coup d’état

.


The first round suggested that Flávio and his party were on track to gain an enormous amount of power. The party won

more seats in Congress than any other


—

 nearly a quarter of the lower house and more than a third of the Senate — which, together with other right-wing parties,

gave the right a majority in both houses

.


Two days after the vote,

Flávio said he would use that majority to “change the Constitution” and “re-democratize” the country. Asked what he meant, he

proposed

 limiting the powers of Supreme Court justices, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and ending presidential reelection, and he left open the possibility of extending the presidential term from four to five years.


“I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”


In addition, whoever won in October would be able to

appoint up to four of the 11 justices of the federal Supreme Court

,

the same court that convicted Jair Bolsonaro. A Flávio victory would have given the far right control over all three branches of government, amid the advance of the far right in Latin America and the United States.


As a result, after the first-round results came in on

the night of Oct. 4, the mood among Lula’s supporters was one of deep discouragement and fear. But this fear quickly turned into forms of popular organizing that were diverse, complementary and consistently nonviolent — and they changed the course of the race. The mobilizations included a large-scale effort by politicians, activists, content creators and ordinary supporters to organize and amplify pro-Lula content on social media, and an equally massive occupation of the country’s streets in peaceful demonstrations.


Students took center stage in the street mobilizations, with thousands turning out for protests such as one

led by the National Union of Students, or UNE, at the Candelária

 church in Rio de Janeiro, and one led by UNE and the University of Brasília’s student council on the Esplanade of Ministries in Brasília. People in the streets and on social media acted together and complemented each other.


Beyond protests and online activism, people organized to make sure that those who had not voted in the first round would go to the polls, including elderly people and those who live far from their polling places. They also got off the internet and talked in person with undecided voters who had not yet made up their minds, a process that had a name: vira voto, or flip the vote.


For Gabriel Rochlin,

a director, actor and teacher who took part in a vira voto group in Rio de Janeiro, this was a way to get out of the social media bubble. “The work of vira voto has a lot to do with breaking through the algorithm,” he said. “The street has this real quality of not having an algorithm that separates people: you’re going to meet people you would never meet on your feed.” He saw the fear engendered by the first round as the turning point: “I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”


From demoralization to esperançar


Given the collective feeling of fear and hopelessness after the first round of voting, the first challenge was to shift the mood of the left. It was on Oct. 5, the day after the results, that popular mobilization began in earnest.

We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.

author: FMF Staff
title: Aisha Wahab’s Victory Shows What Afghan Women Can Achieve. The Taliban Is Denying Afghanistan That Future.
content:
Last week, amid the many historic firsts and important victories in the midterm elections, Afghan American Aisha Wahab won her first full term representing California’s 14th District.

Wahab’s victory is a powerful reminder of what women can accomplish when given the opportunity to lead. Her commitment to public service reflects the talent, determination, and leadership Afghan women bring to their communities and to the world.

At a time when women and girls in Afghanistan are systematically excluded from public life, her achievement is also a reminder of what Afghanistan is losing by denying its women the opportunity to serve, lead, and shape their country’s future.

The contrast could not be more striking.

Wahab’s achievement should not be exceptional. Women’s leadership should be the norm, not the exception. Yet women’s opportunities to lead are still too often denied, obstructed, or dismissed.

Afghan women are just as capable of serving their communities, shaping policy, and holding public office as women anywhere in the world. They have the knowledge, ambition, and commitment. What they need is the opportunity.

The Taliban has made that opportunity impossible for women and girls in Afghanistan. Since returning to power in August 2021, it has barred girls from education beyond the sixth grade, excluded women from universities and most employment, and systematically erased women from public life by issuing over 160 decrees. These restrictions are not simply a collection of discriminatory policies. They are part of a system designed to deny women autonomy, human rights, and participation in society. In other words, it’s a system of gender apartheid.

And Afghanistan is paying the price.

When women are excluded from public service, the country loses leaders who could work for its people. When women are denied education, the country loses future teachers, doctors, scientists, advocates, and policymakers. When women are forced out of the workforce, families, communities, and the national economy suffer. The Taliban’s oppression of women is not only a violation of their rights; it is an assault on Afghanistan’s future.

Aisha Wahab’s victory makes visible what the Taliban seeks to suppress: Afghan women’s capacity to lead, contribute, and shape the world around them.

Her story is a reminder that women’s rights have never been a question of capability or merit. They are a matter of policy, equality and opportunity. The barriers are not a reflection of what women can achieve, but of the systems designed to deny them the chance.

The world must not forget the women and girls of Afghanistan. Their exclusion must not become normalized, and their struggle must not fade from the global agenda. Leaders, governments and institutions must continue to demand an end to the Taliban’s system of gender apartheid and stand for Afghan women’s fundamental rights to education, employment, and full participation in society.

An Afghanistan that excludes its women cannot fulfill its potential. And a world that celebrates women’s achievements while forgetting those denied the chance to achieve is failing them too.

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: smǝlqmíx Youth lead rally against greenlit Copper Mountain Mine expansion: ‘They don’t care that their decision makes us sick’
content:
smǝlqmíx Youth and members of the nmlqitkʷ (Similkameen River) Defenders stand together at a gathering that they led in Keremeos on Nov. 8, where they continued to voice their opposition to the nearby Copper Mountain Mine’s New Ingerbelle Expansion project. From left to right: Chase Dennis, Isaac Dennis, Madeline Terbasket, Meadow Arcand, Kirsten Lindley, and Coven Terbasket.

 Photo by Aaron Hemens


A group of smǝlqmíx (Similkameen) Youth are continuing calls to stop a controversial mine expansion project in their homelands after it was greenlit by the province earlier this year. 


Members of the nmlqitkʷ (Similkameen River) Defenders, a group of syilx smǝlqmíx Youth “fighting for the water,” hosted an event on Sunday in the town of Keremeos, speaking about

their “refusal”

 of the Copper Mountain Mine’s New Ingerbelle expansion.


More than 50 people of all ages and backgrounds were in attendance, with many displaying signs with messages that read “No to the Ingerbelle Mine Expansion.” 


After years of deliberating,

the “B.C.” government greenlit the New Ingerbelle expansion in February

, issuing Mines Act and Environmental Management Act permits. The open pit gold and copper mine is located near “Princeton” in smǝlqmíx territory, which is about an hour northwest of Keremeos.


There have been years-long concerns from syilx communities and advocates about the impact that the expansion of the mine and its already towering tailings dam will have on the Similkameen River,

which some worry

 could have “catastrophic impacts” on the valley. 


The expansion will see the mine’s existing 192-metre tailings dam — roughly equivalent in height to a 58-storey building — increased by an additional 87 metres,

according to the province’s Environmental Assessment Office (EAO)

.


While acknowledging that she was “angry” and “upset” to have to stand up for the water; the land; and all the beings that rely on them, nmlqitkʷ defender Meadow Arcand said on Sunday that the Indigenous Youth “have a responsibility to do this work.”


“What we’re really looking out for is these young ones, the sacred ones that are going to come after us. Like our ancestors did before us, like our Elders did before us, like the old people did before us,” said Arcand.


“We’re standing here so people can’t say that we didn’t.”


She extended this same responsibility to anyone benefitting from Okanagan waters and territories – not just syilx smǝlqmíx people.


“We need people to care about our relationships with all life: with the water, with each other, and with the future generations,” she said.


“What we do here now matters. What our ancestors did matters.”


More than 50 people gathered in Keremeos on Nov. 8 to stand in solidarity with nmlqitkʷ (Similkameen River) Defenders, a group of syilx smǝlqmíx Youth who are opposed to the nearby Copper Mountain Mine’s New Ingerbelle Expansion project.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


‘They don’t care that their decision makes us sick’


Older generations of the smǝlqmíx community also spoke on Sunday, denouncing the mine expansion and sharing their support for the Youth. The organizers left handouts to resources – such as their online

petition

 and

declaration

 – and other information bulletins on what’s happening with mining in their homelands.


They also brought with them the syilx Okanagan Nation’s

siwɬkʷ (Water) Declaration

.


The expansion project is set to see the century-old mining operation revive its old Ingerbelle open pit gold and copper mine site near the Similkameen River. The expansion will extend the mining’s operation until 2047, according to the province.


After the province greenlit the mine’s expansion project in February, leadership at both Upper and Lower Similkameen Indian Bands (USIB, LSIB)

denounced the government’s decision

, saying that “no consent” was given.


y̓ilmixʷm (Chief) kalʔlùpaɋʹn Keith Crow of LSIB told IndigiNews in 2022 that the Similkameen River is the lifeblood of the valley.


“If we lose that, we lose our identity. We lose who we are,” Crow said.


An aerial view of the Similkameen River, flowing through the town of Keremeos in smǝlqmíx homelands in December 2024.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Meanwhile, the mine’s owner Hudbay Minerals

issued a statement

 saying it “proactively engaged” with USIB and LSIB throughout the permitting process, and “finalized refreshed participation agreements” with both communities — “reinforcing the company’s commitment to …

author: Roderick Long
title: C4SS Panelists on the Intellectual Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
There will be a Molinari/C4SS presence at the 10th annual PPE Society meeting, 12-14 November 2026, at the Westin New Orleans (100 Iberville St.).


I’ve organised a panel on “The Intellectual Legacy of Don Lavoie.” We’re in the very first session of the conference: Thursday, 12 November 2026, 9:00-10:30 a.m. (Central time) in River Room II.


The panel features Cory Massimino (C4SS) on “National Economic Planning: What is Right?” and Nathan Goodman (Mercatus; co-authoring with Molly Rovinski and Karla Segovia) on “Immigration Restrictions as Non-Comprehensive Planning.” Zak Woodman was also scheduled to speak at the panel, on “Ratcheting Up State Power: The Knowledge Problem, the Power Problem, and Legibility,” but will probably not be able to make it.


(This is not to be confused with the panel on the same topic at last month’s Mercatus Markets & Society conference, organised by Nathan Goodman and featuring Jason Byas, Akiva Malamet, and again Cory Massimino.)


Jason Byas, currently in his first year as Assistant Professor in Philosophy and Political Economy at Tulane, is also on the program; he’ll be speaking in a panel on “Anarchism as a Practical Philosophy,” Friday, 13 November 2026, 9:00-10:30 a.m. (Central time) in the Salon Room. Jason’s fellow panelists are Jesse Spafford, Jessica Flanigan, and Billy Christmas.

author: Valerie Anne
title: You Oughta Know That Alanis Morissette Is Pansexual
content:
feature image photo by Credit: NBC / Contributor via Getty Images

It’s official: 90s icon and present-day superstar Alanis Morissette is pansexual. The singer was a guest on the Handsome podcast, which is co-hosted by queer comedians Tig Notaro, Fortune Feimster, and Mae Martin, and they were talking about Alanis’s penchant for a post-breakup rage anthem. Fortune Feimster jokingly asked her, “Did it make you want to be a lesbian at any point?” to which Alanis replied, “I’m pansexual, so yeah.”

The energy in the room was perfect. At first, everyone thought it was a joke (or perhaps that she was being…ironic), but when they clarified that Alanis was serious, they all joked that she should have led with that. You walk into a queer podcast with the queer announcement!!

Granted, this is not the first time Alanis has said she isn’t straight. She has been talking about exploring her sexuality and being attracted to women as far back as 2008, and it was apparently at least partly her idea for her character to kiss Sarah Jessica Parker’s Carrie during her Sex and the City guest spot. It’s just the first time she’s used a specific label out loud.

I considered riddling this intro with Alanis-related puns (like the joke my friend made: she’s got one pan in her pocket…) but I’ll save you the cringe. I’ll just say this news has made me even more head over feet for her.

God is a woman, and she’s also pansexual.

You Live, You Learn (About More Gay News)

Cara Delevingne sent Reneé Rapp for a loop during a prank call in an Elle interview.

Speaking of Cara Delevingne, she also was at the red carpet premiere of Club Kid talking about the movie and also the “blue tsunami” in the midterm elections.

Beanie Feldstein and her wife welcomed a baby girl into their family (Beanie already made the “beanie baby” joke so I will refrain).

Amber Glenn took the lead in her Dancing with the Stars number on Disney night, dressed in shiny white pants, flexing her impressive-as-hell back muscles, and doing the quickstep to A Star is Born from Hercules.

Queer Swedish pop star Tove Styrke returns to music after having a baby with her partner Sanna Sikborn Erixon.

Cynthia Nixon was asked who her favorite lesbian is and she said Sappho (and also gave almost-definitely-bisexual Eleanor Roosevelt a shout-out).

The wait is almost over: Netflix’s The Body drops on Wednesday, November 11.

Queer Canadian icon Jann Arden is among the recognizable names on the guest star list for Jared Keeso’s upcoming comedy I Kill the Bear, alongside other queer-adjacent faves like Melanie Scrofano, Michelle Mylett, and Tricia Helfer.

ICYMI, WNBA players Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers have actually been broken up for quite a while, but don’t worry, they’re still friends.

author: Victoria Valenzuela
title: Incarcerated Los Angeles Youth Fought for the Right to Hug Their Parents — and Won
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Mercedes Maradiaga sat across from her 19-year-old son in the Los Padrinos Juvenile Hall in Los Angeles in complete devastation. Her son had at that point been incarcerated at the prison for two years and she had visited him every weekend. But that day in September 2024 was especially hard because it was their first visit since he had been beaten by officers earlier that week in a space in the jail where there were no cameras. The guards had jumped on and kicked him, and he needed surgery for a torn ACL. All she wanted was to give him a hug and reassure him that she was there. However, because of the no-contact visit policies at Los Padrinos, she was unable to give him that comfort.


Even during birthdays and holidays, they weren’t allowed to embrace. The boy endured the jail’s horrible living conditions — including rat infestations and flooded toilets — but couldn’t hug his mom for a moment of escape.


“I couldn’t even let him know I’m here just with the little hug,” Maradiaga said. “It would have meant everything to him. It was sad, and I did that for four years.”


Los Padrinos had

reopened a year earlier

 in 2023, after being shut down in 2019 due to conditions that violated the Board of State and Community Corrections (BSCC) standards, including abuses by staff. Six officers were criminally charged with

assault and child abuse

 for using pepper spray on several teenage girls. Reports

also cited a decreasing youth population

 as a factor for closure, yet staff

claimed to feel “outnumbered.”

 When Los Padrinos closed, youth were shuffled to another facility called Central Juvenile Hall — and then in 2023, that facility was closed down due to similar issues. Los Padrinos reopened, and just months later, the abuses restarted. In 2025,

30 officers were criminally charged

 by the California Attorney General with child endangerment and abuse, conspiracy, and battery for encouraging “gladiator fights” that pit youth against each other.


Olivia Shields, a justice transformation policy coordinator at Urban Peace Institute, described the constant closing and reopening of BSCC facilities as a “cycle of noncompliance.” Shields said the Los Angeles County Probation Department has ultimately failed with these maneuvers to address the core issue: unmet youth needs — which won’t be addressed through incarceration but through coordinated care in the form of individualized, robust support systems and resources.


“Rather than decarcerate these populations of young people and find community-based alternatives or step-downs for as many of them as possible, they basically shift the youth around from facility to facility to avoid noncompliance,” Shields said.


Long before the closing of Los Padrinos in 2019, the facility had a bad reputation among Angelenos. Maradiaga recalled hearing disturbing stories about the facility in the ’80s when she was a kid.


“I think it needs to be shut down,” Maradiaga said. “I think that there needs to be a better way for the youth. I don’t think locking them away from their family is the answer.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


Barred From Basic Human Contact


When Ilana Parach, executive director and co-founder of

Hoops 4 Justice

, went inside Los Padrinos with a basketball and mentorship program, she quickly learned about what youth were facing inside. She felt it was important to give them a platform to express their needs directly, so she pivoted to working with them on legislation.


“They made a list of specific programs they wanted — resources for their families, reentry support,” Parach said. “At the bottom of that list, they wrote, ‘We want to hug our moms.’”


Incarcerated youth directly told her that one parent who hugged her son during a visit on his birthday then had her visit terminated and future visits suspended for two weeks. She said another youth was incarcerated for three years and had no choice but to watch his mother cry during the visits because she couldn’t hug him.


Contact visitation policies vary across California and are often left at the discretion of correctional officers. Parach said youth and staff both told her that Los Padrinos stopped allowing contact visits after the pandemic. Parach said that during meetings of the board of supervisors, she heard officers citing staffing shortages …

title: In the Crosshairs of the Far-Right Advance : An Update on Anti-Fascists and Anarchists in Greece
content:
Anarchist graffiti from Athens, Greece (2026)


The anarchist movement in Greece faces a new wave of repression. Urged on by the US and its obsession with combatting “far-left extremism,” the Greek state has targeted anti-authoritarians with new legal charges and attacked demonstrations, while fascists carry out street attacks and plot their return to the halls of power. Amidst a landscape of ongoing austerity, terrorism designations, lethal prisons, and ferocious wildfires, anarchists nonetheless continue to forge a combative culture of revolutionary solidarity.


In this article, we present an interview with an anarchist comrade in Athens assessing the current situation among anarchists and anti-fascists in Greece, along with analysis of the US’s role in advancing state repression and fantasies of Western supremacy.


The US and Greece: A Right-Wing Alliance to Defend “The West”


Earlier this month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a speech at the Pnyx in Athens. With the historic Acropolis and the Parthenon—that ancient symbol of Western democracy, constructed with slave labor—in the background, he delivered a warning message to Greece’s political and business elite.


“The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline,” Rubio cautioned. “We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.” Lamenting how “nationalism became a dirty word,” he called for renewed militarism, praised Christian faith and martyrdom, and announced a new counterterrorism information-sharing program between the two countries. His statements were calculated to reinforce the colonial legacy of Western dominance over the rest of the world, while urging the worst of Greek society to imitate America’s current political trajectory.


US Secretary of State Marco Rubio constructs an elaborate photo op for his defense of nationalism, militarism, and “the West” (October 7, 2026).


The speech came in the wake of a conference Rubio convened in July that aimed to coordinate intensified repression against “far-left extremism.” The following month, the US government imposed a “global terrorist” designation on the Italy-based

Autistici/Inventati (A/I) tech collective

, which operated the free publishing platform NoBlogs.org.


Greece’s right-wing politicians and business leaders benefiting from the country’s endless austerity measures are heeding Rubio’s call to preserve the hubris of the so-called West. Meanwhile, governments are collaborating to escalate repression against any truly revolutionary movements that challenge the world’s current status quo.


Greece’s strategic importance to Western powers is rooted in its symbolic status as the birthplace of “Western Civilization,” as well as its strategic location in the world today. The country offers the US access to four military sites, including a dedicated Navy base in Crete’s Souda Bay. Those with a longer memory have not forgotten how the US supplied napalm to Greece’s fascist forces, who worked with the Nazis during World War II and later with the British and US in a Cold War anti-communist alliance. Fascists dropped American napalm on Greek partisan resistance fighters during the civil war from 1946 to 1949, scorching bodies and charring forests, leaving the countryside scarred to this day.


More recently, the Greek people were pummeled by the 2008 global economic crisis, brought on in part by Wall Street firms such as Goldman Sachs that raked in immense profits while destabilizing the world’s economy and immiserating millions. The US then contributed to the austerity measures imposed on Greece in 2010 by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), leading to years of ferocious resistance to neoliberal capitalism and government complicity.


Today, Greece’s current New Democracy regime upholds

the legacy of the brutal military junta

 of 1967-1974, promoting the image of Greece as a symbol European supremacy as invoked by Rubio. Despite its nationalist rhetoric, the government continues to lick the boots of the US, crushing opposition in the streets and enforcing a never-ending precarity on the majority of Greece’s increasingly exhausted and numb population.

author: Aline Melo
title: Organizações lançam carta defendendo projeto que regula mercados digitais
content:
A regulamentação dos mercados digitais no Brasil, os chamados

Marketplaces

, está em disputa. De um lado, empresas e organizações sociais lançam uma carta que defende a aprovação do Projeto de Lei 4.675/2025.

 A proposta cria regras para ampliar a transparência e fiscalizar a concorrência nesses ambientes, incluindo a atuação do Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica, o Cade, criando uma superintendência específica para avaliar os negócios digitais. A carta deve ser divulgada nos próximos dias, após uma reunião convocada pelo Governo Federal, por meio da Secretaria de Comunicação Social da Presidência (Secom), com representantes desses grupos para alinhar estratégias para a aprovação do PL 4675.


Do outro lado da disputa, o projeto tem sido alvo do lobby das Big Techs, que o associa ao aumento do controle estatal sobre a internet.

 A estratégia reproduz argumentos utilizados em outras discussões sobre regulação no Brasil, como ocorreu durante a tramitação do PL das Fake News, e chama o projeto de “PL da censura”.


A proposta teve origem no Governo Federal, a partir de trabalhos do Ministério da Fazenda e do Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade), e recebeu um substitutivo apresentado pelo deputado Aliel Machado (PV-PR) em agosto deste ano.


O argumento pela regulamentação dos mercados digitais


Na avaliação de Rafael Zanatta, diretor executivo da Data Privacy Brasil — uma das organizações envolvidas na carta em defesa do 4.675/2025 —,

a regulação pode beneficiar especialmente startups, desenvolvedores independentes, varejistas e empresas brasileiras que dependem de grandes plataformas para oferecer seus produtos e serviços.


“Esse PL está trazendo um ambiente digital mais competitivo, mais transparente, melhor para startups, melhor para desenvolvedores independentes, melhor para varejistas. E os únicos afetados aqui são empresas muito específicas”, afirma.


Um dos exemplos citados pelo diretor da Data Privacy é o controle da Apple sobre a loja de aplicativos do sistema iOS e as restrições impostas a desenvolvedores quanto aos meios de pagamento. Para Zanatta, a possibilidade de utilizar alternativas, como o Pix, e de reduzir taxas de intermediação pode ampliar a concorrência e diminuir custos para empresas e consumidores.


Zanatta critica a repercussão de que a proposta reproduziria modelos autoritários de controle estatal. “O Partido Novo fala que esse seria um projeto do governo para aumentar poderes, instituir censura e controle na vida do cidadão. Esse projeto não tem nada a ver com moderação de conteúdo, não tem nada a ver com controlar a vida das pessoas. Estão falando que o PL é inspirado nas ‘ditaduras’ da China e Cuba”, afirma.


Na realidade, a proposta brasileira tem como referência experiências regulatórias adotadas em democracias europeias, especialmente o Digital Markets Act (DMA), legislação da União Europeia em vigor desde 2023. A norma estabelece obrigações para grandes plataformas digitais classificadas como controladoras de acesso (gatekeepers), com o objetivo de tornar os mercados digitais mais competitivos e impedir práticas comerciais consideradas desleais. Entre as regras estão a proibição de favorecer serviços próprios em detrimento de concorrentes e a possibilidade de desenvolvedores utilizarem sistemas de pagamento alternativos nas lojas de aplicativos.


O projeto brasileiro também prevê instrumentos de atuação preventiva do Cade sobre grandes grupos econômicos, com obrigações específicas voltadas à proteção da concorrência. Embora existam diferenças entre os dois modelos, ambos tratam da regulação econômica de mercados digitais e da limitação do poder de grandes plataformas, não do controle sobre conteúdos ou opiniões publicados por usuários.


“O PL 4675 protege o Pix, protege infraestruturas públicas digitais e protege que empresas brasileiras possam surgir e crescer sem serem limadas desse processo, ou mesmo compradas”, acrescenta.


Segundo Zanatta, o projeto também daria ao Cade instrumentos para impedir ou reverter operações de fusão e aquisição que possam prejudicar a concorrência, inclusive quando grandes grupos econômicos tentarem comprar empresas brasileiras emergentes. Ele cita como exemplos hipotéticos uma eventual aquisição do Jusbrasil pelo Google ou da Magazine Luiza pela Amazon.


Além da Data Privacy Brasil, participaram da articulação da carta organizações como Artigo 19, Ctrl+Z e Instituto Brasileiro de Defesa do Consumidor (Idec), e …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Milton Tolomeo en huelga de hambre: exigen al SPF que cumpla lo ordenado por el Poder Judicial
content:
Desde la Coordinadora contra la Represión Policial e Institucional (CORREPI) y la Gremial de Abogados y Abogadas denuncian el grave empeoramiento de las condiciones de detención de los presos políticos y el incumplimiento del Servicio Penitenciario Federal y su superior, el Ministerio de Seguridad Nacional, de lo ordenado por el Tribunal Oral Federal nº 6.


Milton Tolomeo


Compartimos el comunicado:


Informe sobre la situación de Milton Tolomeo, preso político en huelga de hambre: EXIGIMOS AL SPF QUE CUMPLA LO ORDENADO POR EL TRIBUNAL ORAL FEDERAL


El 8 de noviembre, Milton Iván Tolomeo, preso político por haberse manifestado contra la infame reforma laboral el 11 de febrero de 2026, inició una huelga de hambre en su actual lugar de alojamiento, el nuevo Complejo Penitenciario VIII de Marcos Paz.


Milton, igual que Eneas Gallo, permanece detenido, con prisión preventiva, desde el 14 de febrero pasado. Se lo acusa por los delitos de resistencia a la autoridad, intimidación pública y tenencia de material incendiario. Los primeros dos delitos son parte del “combo” habitual aplicado a manifestantes, y el tercero surge de una irregular identificación efectuada por las fuerzas de seguridad a partir del ciberpatrullaje y tecnología de reconocimiento antropométrico altamente cuestionable.


No conforme con eso, el fiscal de instrucción, el inefable Stornelli, agregó la agravante genérica de “acto terrorista” al propiciar la aplicación -por primera vez a nivel nacional desde su sanción en 2011 y ampliado en 2024- del art. 41 quinquies, que duplica el mínimo y máximo de la pena en expectativa, con lo que ambos enfrentan hoy una sanción penal de hasta 30 años de prisión.


Esa agravante ya había sido descartada por el juez instructor inicial de la justicia de Ciudad y la Cámara de Apelaciones, pese a lo cual fue incorporada al requerimiento de elevación a juicio. Cabe agregar que esa agravante, conforme la letra del mismo artículo, no es de aplicación cuando el hecho ocurre en el marco de la defensa de derechos humanos o constitucionales, como, en el caso, los derechos laborales.


Después de un largo mes recluido en el SIGPPLAR (Sistema Integral de Gestión para Personas Privadas de la Libertad de Alto Riesgo), verdadero Guantánamo “a la Bullrich” creado en 2024, que significó la privación de todo contacto personal o telefónico con familiares y hasta sus defensores, con 20 horas de aislamiento y sólo 4 al día de “recreo” para acceder al patio, a los sanitarios y a los sectores para preparar alimentos, logramos que Milton fuera trasladado a pabellón común en el CPF II de Marcos Paz, donde pudo retomar el derecho a las visitas familiares y de organismos de DDHH, la comunicación telefónica y el acceso a alimentación adecuada provista por sus allegados, elementos de higiene personal y limpieza.


Pero el 11 de octubre pasado, de manera totalmente discrecional, el Servicio Penitenciario Federal decidió su traslado al nuevo complejo federal, inaugurado a las apuradas para descomprimir la superpoblación de la cárcel de Devoto en vísperas de la anunciada visita del papa León XIV a ese penal, donde hoy apenas 70 internos quedan alojados.


El traslado, entre gallos y medianoche, se produjo dejando atrás la totalidad de sus pertenencias (ropa, calzado, libros, elementos de cocina, de higiene y limpieza, radio, etc.). En el nuevo lugar de alojamiento hay elementales carencias básicas de infraestructura y servicios. No hay libre acceso al agua potable, a los depósitos de mercadería de sus familiares las instalaciones sanitarias no están terminadas y se limitaron los días y horarios de visitas.


Desde su defensa denunciamos el grave empeoramiento de las condiciones de detención al Tribunal Oral Federal nº 6, que de inmediato envió varios oficios al servicio penitenciario exigiendo resolver esa situación y requiriendo informes, y los propios internos interpusieron un recurso de Habeas Corpus correctivo que tramita ante el Juzgado federal nº 1 de Morón.


Ante la falta de respuesta del SPF, el 8 de noviembre Milton decidió iniciar una huelga de hambre, negándose a ingerir alimento alguno.


Informado de la situación, en el día de ayer el Tribunal Oral Federal inmediatamente requirió al servicio penitenciario que las autoridades del CPF VIII efectúen los controles médicos correspondientes cada 24 horas, remitiendo informes periódicos; insistió en el cumplimiento de lo ordenado en lo ordenado por el Tribunal con fechas 13 y 15/10/2026 y …

author: Administrador
title: UNA DISCULPA
content:
A los colectivos de familias y familiares buscadoras de la Glorieta de las y los Desaparecidos.

Una disculpa. O muchas, de modo que alcancen a todas y cada una de las familias buscadoras que se congregan en la Glorieta de las y los Desaparecidos.

Nosotros nos sentimos agredidos y lastimados. Respondimos, a través mío (los compas suelen ser más duros) y ustedes se sintieron igual o más ofendidas.

En lo que se refiere a nuestras palabras, la responsabilidad es totalmente mía, capitán insurgente primero de infantería Marcos. Mis palabras fueron interpretadas como agresiones hacia ustedes. De verdad lo lamento.

De corazón les pido disculpas por haberles ofendido, lastimado y agredido. De nada sirve decir que no era la intención o poner de pretexto “el estrés” por las agresiones de los 3 niveles de gobierno. Debí ser más cuidadoso y prudente en el uso de las palabras y en el tono. Espero me sirva para aprender a dirigirme con delicadeza y cuidado a quien busca verdad y justicia.

Está claro, creemos, que hay que respetar modos, geografías y calendarios. Por nuestra parte les decimos con sinceridad que esperamos que tengan éxito en su empeño y que encuentren a todas las ausencias posibles. Y que siempre encuentren la forma de abrazar a quien busca sola, sin más apoyo que su rabia.

Porque a veces puede olvidarse que de eso se trata todo: de encontrar a quien falta.

Les reitero mis disculpas. Espero deveras que encuentren en sus corazones la bondad suficiente para aceptarlas.

Por lo demás, cada quien su modo, su calendario, su geografía… y su agenda.

Desde las montañas del Sureste Mexicano.

Capitán Insurgente Marcos. México, noviembre del 2026.

P.D.- En lo que se refiere a la iniciativa, no tenemos más contactos al exterior que el Frayba, nadie más. Sólo cuando se concreta un punto en la agenda, hacemos contacto directo con los grupos y colectivas de familias buscadoras o con familias buscadoras en particular, pero siempre avisando al Frayba, que es quien lleva el registro.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Repudio europeo al INTA por la exoneración de Virginia Aparicio: "Los hallazgos de la investigación no fueron convenientes para muchas personas y sectores"
content:
Por Natalia Concina


Violette Geissen, profesora de la Universidad de Wageningen (Países Bajos) y coordinadora general del proyecto internacional Sprint (Transición Sostenible de Protección Vegetal, por sus siglas en inglés), calificó de “injusta” la

exoneración del INTA Virginia Aparicio

, la investigadora que coordinó en Argentina el estudio sobre exposición a plaguicidas. Geissen defendió el desempeño científico de Aparicio, aseguró que cumplió rigurosamente con los protocolos establecidos por el consorcio internacional y cuestionó la decisión del organismo de apartarla. “Virginia Aparicio es una investigadora excelente”, afirmó Geissen desde Holanda, en diálogo con Tierra Viva.


“Hicimos protocolos para armonizar los métodos y que se realizaran en todos los países de la misma manera. Virginia siguió esos protocolos al pie de la letra”, sostuvo la investigadora, que también cuestionó la decisión institucional de abandonar el proyecto.


“El INTA firmó su ingreso al consorcio conociendo qué se iba a hacer y cuáles eran los objetivos. Ese contrato no lo firmó Virginia, lo firmó el responsable del organismo. Por lo tanto, no se entiende cómo luego quieren irse”, planteó.


La coordinadora de Sprint también reveló que el caso argentino no es el único que generó consecuencias para los investigadores involucrados. “Otro investigador perdió su trabajo y otras personas sufrieron hostigamiento”, contó. Y vinculó esas situaciones con los resultados de la investigación: “Es claro que los hallazgos de Sprint no fueron convenientes para muchas personas y sectores”.


El proyecto Sprint fue financiado por la Unión Europea y reunió a instituciones científicas de diez países europeos, además de Argentina. Su objetivo era desarrollar una herramienta para evaluar los riesgos de los agroquímicos a partir del análisis de residuos y mezclas de plaguicidas en el ambiente, los animales y las personas.


La Argentina fue elegida por el consorcio por su relevancia en el mercado internacional de soja. La incorporación del INTA fue aprobada en 2020 mediante la Resolución 477, firmada por la entonces presidenta del organismo, Susana Mirassou. Aparicio quedó a cargo de la coordinación local y durante 2021 se realizaron muestreos en el sudeste bonaerense a 73 voluntarios, entre productores convencionales y agroecológicos, trabajadores rurales y consumidores. También se analizaron muestras de agua, suelo y aire.


Los inconvenientes comenzaron a partir de los primeros resultados

, en junio de 2023. Aparicio había convocado a los participantes para presentarles los hallazgos, pero el INTA ordenó suspender la reunión. Seis meses después, el organismo decidió retirar a la Argentina del consorcio y abrió una investigación administrativa contra la científica. El argumento institucional fue que el proyecto involucraba investigaciones con seres humanos que excedían sus incumbencias, pese a que la participación había sido aprobada previamente.


El sumario concluyó con ocho imputaciones contra Aparicio, entre ellas presuntas irregularidades en el manejo de información confidencial, el envío de muestras al exterior y los procedimientos de evaluación.

La investigadora rechazó las acusaciones

 y sostuvo que había actuado de acuerdo con los requerimientos del proyecto. Finalmente, el 26 de octubre de 2026,

el Consejo Directivo del INTA dispuso su exoneración

, la sanción disciplinaria más grave del régimen de empleo público.


Para Geissen,

los resultados científicos de S

print

 permiten dimensionar la importancia del trabajo realizado y las preguntas que todavía deben responderse. “Es el primer estudio mundial que demostró que existen múltiples plaguicidas en todas las matrices y que se acumulan en las casas”, señaló. La investigadora explicó que uno de los aportes centrales fue estudiar la exposición combinada a distintas sustancias, en lugar de analizar cada producto por separado.


“Lo que hemos visto es que la inhalación puede causar más residuos de plaguicidas que lo que se ingiere”, afirmó. También sostuvo que las personas están expuestas a mezclas de sustancias por distintas vías y que en los hogares pueden encontrarse hasta 120 combinaciones diferentes de plaguicidas.


La coordinadora mencionó, además, los experimentos realizados en modelos animales con concentraciones que habían sido consideradas seguras para los seres humanos. Según relató, en las pruebas con ratas preñadas se observaron casos de leucemia entre las crías.

author: Rizomatica
title: Sobre la propuesta de modificación al artículo 13 de la ley indigena 19.253
content:
La propuesta de modificación al artículo 13 de la ley 19.253 impulsada en el gobierno anterior a través de la denominada Comisión para la Paz y Entendimiento, fue una iniciativa transversal de la clase Política que incluyó a personeros de todo el espectro político Chileno como propuesta para el desarrollo en materia indígena.


Está propuesta ha sido fomentada por el actual gobierno de tinte ultraderechista con la finalidad de instalarla cómo política pública para el pueblo mapuche. Prueba de ello es que hace pocos días se reunieron en Temuco diversos personeros del gobierno con la finalidad de promover una consulta para dar implementación a esta medida.


El artículo 13 de la ley 19.253 es la normativa que regula y contiene restricciones respecto del dominio y uso de los terrenos indígenas. Este artículo contiene una protección exigida por el interés nacional del cual son sujetos los terrenos indígenas que impide que estos sean sometidos a enajenaciones, embargos, gravámenes, ni ser adquiridas por prescripción, salvo entre comunidades o personas de una misma etnia.


En términos generales, hasta ahora, el artículo 13 ha sido una salvaguarda para el dominio de la tierra indígena en manos de los pueblos originarios, por cuánto la ley en este aspecto tiene un carácter imperativo y obligatorio de protección.


No obstante aquello, esto no ha significado una protección completa ya que a través de diversos artilugios legales se han registrado casos en que a pesar de sus diversas prohibiciones, si se ha logrado enajenar (

vender

) terrenos indígenas a personas no mapuche. Esto ha sido en virtud de vacíos contenidos en la normativa que dejan espacios a artilugios legales que diversos abogados han utilizado para realizar esas ventas en vulneración al espíritu de la ley.


Un caso emblemático a este respecto fue el mediático caso de la venta realizada por la viuda chilena de un mapuche después de su muerte en la comuna de Pucón al ex subsecretario Ubilla durante el gobierno del expresidente Piñera.


Está venta de un terreno indígena a un chileno dejó de manifiesto lo frágil de la ley respecto de la real protección a los terrenos indígenas cuando hay intereses económicos importantes de por medio. Esta venta se pudo realizar en el contexto de lo que en derecho civil se conoce como liquidación de una sociedad conyugal y adjudicación por disolución de esta.


Volviendo a la propuesta de modificación al artículo 13, lo que preocupa es el aparente sentido inocuo de dicha medida, ya que directamente no habla de

enajenación

 o

venta

 de un terreno indígena a una persona o entidad no mapuche, sino que el énfasis ha sido puesto en la posibilidad de

arrendamiento

 de un terreno indígena a personas

no indígenas

 o

personas


jurídicas

 de diversa índole.


Está situación es más compleja de lo que parece a simple vista porque abre una posibilidad de vulneraciones difíciles de prever a futuro.


Lo que señala la propuesta de modificación es que los terrenos indígenas podrán ser arrendados a cualquier persona no indígena o persona jurídica por un plazo de hasta 10 años y 25 años con consulta al órgano técnico encargado en materia indígena que es la Conadi.


El argumento para esto, es que en las condiciones actuales de restricción que contiene la propiedad indígena ha sido muy difícil incorporar estos terrenos a los beneficios que contempla la ley y a diversas medidas administrativas de los órganos y servicios del Estado en materia de fomento productivo, acceso a vivienda, acceso a crédito, transferencia tecnológica y oportunidades de desarrollo en general. En la visión de los promotores de esta iniciativa se sostiene que esto ha sido el principal elemento de tope que han tenido los mapuche para hacer productivas sus tierras e incorporarlas eficientemente al circuito productivo de la economía local y regional.


Para ello se propone bajar el nivel de restricciones que contiene la ley en materia de protección y permitir arriendos en condiciones de mercado actuales y competitivos.


Esto en teoría significaría regular de forma más eficiente situaciones de arriendo irregular que hoy pudiesen existir y por otra parte mejorar los promedios de los valores de los precios de arriendo para el arrendador y conceder garantías tanto de tiempo como de condiciones jurídicas que permitan al arrendatario realizar una labor productiva con seguridad en un tiempo acorde a dicha inversión, pudiendo ser por un lapso de hasta 25 años.

author: La Zarzamora
title: Lanzamiento de Black Onions, un listado de sitios web anarquistas y antiautoritarios con extensión .onion
content:
Publicado originalmente en Montréal Contre-information

Nos complace anunciar el lanzamiento de Black Onions, una nueva iniciativa que tiene como objetivo ofrecer una lista estable y actualizada periódicamente de sitios anarquistas y antiautoritarios con extensión .onion. Los sitios .onion son sitios web accesibles a través del navegador Tor mediante direcciones que terminan en «.onion».

En los últimos meses, algunos gobiernos han atacado las infraestructuras de comunicación de nuestros movimientos con renovado vigor; buena prueba de ello son la conferencia internacional sobre el «terrorismo de extrema izquierda» celebrada en Estados Unidos en julio, así como la inclusión del proveedor de servicios de alojamiento militante italiano Autistici/Inventati en una lista de sanciones relacionadas con el terrorismo a finales de agosto.

Para bien o para mal, la comunicación pública de nuestros movimientos tiene lugar en gran medida en Internet, lo que la hace vulnerable a los mecanismos tecnológicos de censura. A diferencia de los sitios web convencionales, los sitios .onion son menos vulnerables a la censura, ya que no utilizan nombres de dominio y permiten ocultar la ubicación del servidor, del mismo modo que el navegador Tor oculta tu propia ubicación al visitar el sitio. Consideramos que los sitios .onion son nuestra mejor baza para seguir comunicándonos en línea dentro del movimiento anarquista, especialmente si los intentos de censura se intensifican en el futuro.

El problema recurrente de los sitios .onion es que sus direcciones, compuestas por 56 caracteres aleatorios, son imposibles de memorizar. Black Onions tiene como objetivo resolver este problema. Te recomendamos guardar en los marcadores del navegador Tor, o en un archivo en tu ordenador, las direcciones .onion que utilizas habitualmente; pero si necesitas una dirección que aún no has guardado, ¡encuéntrala en Black Onions!

Accede a Black Onions a través de cualquiera de las siguientes direcciones:

– blackonions.gd – blackonions.li – blackonions.st – (próximamente, una dirección .onion)

Para establecer una base de confianza en esta nueva iniciativa, los siguientes proyectos anarquistas han avalado nuestra propuesta mediante declaraciones firmadas con PGP: Act For Freedom Now!, un proyecto de contrainformación activo desde 2008 , y el No Trace Project, un proyecto contra la represión activo desde 2021.

¡Utiliza sitios .onion! ¡Resiste a la censura!

author: anred
title: Condenan al policía que gaseó a una nena de 10 años: es la primera condena por la represión a las protestas en el gobierno de Milei
content:
El policía federal Cristian Miguel Rivaldi fue condenado a un año y tres meses de prisión en suspenso por haber rociado con gas pimienta a Fabrizia Pegoraro, de 10 años, y a su madre durante una movilización en defensa de las jubilaciones frente al Congreso, el 11 de septiembre de 2024. El juez federal Daniel Rafecas lo encontró responsable de los delitos de incumplimiento de los deberes de funcionario público y lesiones leves, y dispuso además su inhabilitación especial por dos años y seis meses. Es la primera condena contra un integrante de las fuerzas de seguridad por su accionar en las protestas frente al Congreso durante el gobierno de Javier Milei.

El fallo llega después de más de dos años de una causa atravesada por la defensa oficial del accionar policial y versiones del gobierno nacional que intentaron atribuir el ataque a una manifestante. Sin embargo, los registros audiovisuales, los testimonios y la documentación médica permitieron reconstruir lo ocurrido: Fabrizia y su madre estaban sentadas en el suelo, sin agredir ni ofrecer resistencia, cuando el efectivo les disparó gas irritante a corta distancia. La niña debió ser atendida en el Hospital Oftalmológico Santa Lucía, donde le diagnosticaron conjuntivitis química. Por ANRed.


El policía federal

Cristian Miguel Rivaldi fue condenado a un año y tres meses de prisión en suspenso por haber gaseado a Fabrizia Pegoraro, una niña de 10 años, y a su madre durante una movilización en defensa de las jubilaciones frente al Congreso, el 11 de septiembre de 2024

. El juez federal

Daniel Rafecas

 lo encontró responsable de los delitos de incumplimiento de los deberes de funcionario público y lesiones leves. Además, dispuso su inhabilitación especial por dos años y seis meses. Se trata de

la primera condena contra un integrante de las fuerzas de seguridad por su accionar en las protestas frente al Congreso durante el gobierno de Javier Milei

.


El ataque ocurrió durante la jornada de movilización contra el

veto presidencial a la Ley de Movilidad Jubilatoria

. Fabrizia y su madre,

Carla Mariana Pegoraro

, estaban sentadas sobre la avenida Rivadavia, en las inmediaciones del Congreso, cuando los efectivos avanzaron para despejar la calle. Rivaldi, que integraba la División Operaciones Urbanas de Contención de Actividades (DOUCAD) de la Policía Federal, utilizó el aerosol disuasivo que tenía asignado y roció a ambas en el rostro. Las dos debieron recibir asistencia y la niña fue atendida posteriormente en el Hospital Oftalmológico Santa Lucía, donde le diagnosticaron conjuntivitis química.


La condena se produjo después de un juicio correccional que comenzó y terminó este miércoles 11 de noviembre. La acusación estuvo a cargo del fiscal federal

Eduardo Taiano

 y del abogado

Gregorio Dalbón

, representante de la niña y su madre. Durante la investigación

fueron fundamentales los registros audiovisuales, que permitieron identificar al efectivo y reconstruir la secuencia

.

La documentación médica también acreditó las lesiones sufridas por Fabrizia

. En su dictamen para llevar al policía a juicio, Taiano sostuvo que había actuado «de forma desmedida e injustificada, y a una corta distancia», y que ambas víctimas estaban «sentadas en la vía pública sin agredir a la autoridad ni ofrecer resistencia alguna».


El caso tuvo además un recorrido atravesado por el

intento del gobierno nacional de desligar a las fuerzas de seguridad de lo ocurrido

. Tras la difusión de las imágenes,

la entonces ministra de Seguridad, Patricia Bullrich, cuestionó a la madre por haber llevado a su hija a una manifestación

. Desde el Gobierno también

se sostuvo que el gas habría sido arrojado por una mujer que participaba de la protesta y vestía de naranja

. Esa versión fue desmentida por verificaciones periodísticas de AFP, que analizaron registros audiovisuales y material de periodistas presentes en el lugar y concluyeron que el gas que afectó a la niña había sido arrojado por un policía. Dos años después, la sentencia judicial confirmó la responsabilidad de Rivaldi.

Durante la instrucción, el efectivo negó haber visto a la niña y sostuvo que, de haber advertido su presencia, la habría apartado para evitar que resultara herida. También intentó justificar su accionar en el cumplimiento de las órdenes recibidas durante el operativo …

content:
