Iniciada esta semana em Antália, na Turquia, a 31ª Conferência das Partes da Convenção das Nações Unidas sobre as Mudanças Climáticas (COP31) não está gerando o mesmo burburinho que sua versão anterior, realizada em Belém. No ano passado, ativistas do mundo todo viajaram ao Pará. A

COP30

, a primeira a ser realizada na Amazônia, teve um simbolismo enorme, com intensa mobilização popular. Ainda que as esperanças por soluções ousadas contra o aquecimento global não tenham se concretizado naquele momento, vemos agora que as negociações ocorridas no Brasil abriram alguns caminhos promissores.


O marco alcançado em Belém foi evidenciar o buraco nas negociações sobre o uso de combustíveis fósseis. Parece uma loucura que os países se recusem até agora a falar em um mundo sem petróleo e carvão, considerando que esse objetivo levou à criação da Convenção Quadro das Nações Unidas para as Mudanças Climáticas (UNFCCC) na Cúpula da Terra, a Rio 92.


Em grande medida, a proposta de pôr fim aos combustíveis sujos só se tornou possível  através da pressão da sociedade civil, que teve presença histórica na COP de Belém. A mobilização conseguiu empurrar a pauta um pouco além da exasperante inércia do atual arranjo multilateral.


Além disso, a aceleração do processo global de aquecimento, levando ao registro do ano mais quente da História em 2024 contribui para criar um senso de urgência. Da maneira como as coisas caminham, com o Super El Niño atingindo o auge nestes últimos meses, 2026 deve ser o novo ano mais quente de todos os tempos. 


Também faz pouco que

soubemos que, pela primeira vez

, o limite de 1,5 °C da temperatura média global, estabelecido como um teto de segurança, será ultrapassado. Ainda não sabemos por quanto tempo ficaremos acima deste limite, mas já temos indícios de que desastres climáticos de grande magnitude seguirão ocorrendo.


Por isso, a COP31 deve ser importante para confirmar o compromisso dos países em achar um caminho de transição a um mundo com menos emissões de carbono. O problema, como sempre, é se essa busca vai ocorrer em tempo hábil e com que recursos financeiros.


Representantes de povos indígenas durante a Cúpula de Líderes sobre Florestas da COP31, no Centro de Exposições de Antália, na Turquia


O mapa do caminho


Em Antália, o tema sobre o fim da era dos combustíveis fósseis continua sobre a mesa, embalado pela iniciativa do Brasil de apresentar o chamado mapa do caminho. Foi uma iniciativa voluntária da presidência da COP30 para não deixar a discussão sobre como banir os combustíveis fósseis minguar. Uma menção explícita sobre este objetivo ficou de fora do texto acordado em Belém, mas o governo brasileiro se uniu a outros governos para apresentar uma proposta sobre como os países podem fazer uma transição para uma economia mais limpa.


Apresentado poucos dias antes da COP31, o mapa do caminho sugere que todos os países  façam nos próximos anos grandes avaliações sobre a complexidade de mudar a demanda de energia, o suprimento de energia e a economia.

 A partir destes diagnósticos, cada nação deve, até 2030, incluir metas para extinguir o uso de combustíveis fósseis em seus planos nacionais de redução de emissões. A iniciativa brasileira foi bem recebida pela sociedade civil organizada. O

Observatório do Clima elogiou a liderança brasileira

 e mencionou que ela deve servir de guia para ações daqui para frente para os países membros da Convenção do Clima.


Livrar o mundo da dependência de petróleo e do carvão não é realmente trivial. Não há economia nas quais a gasolina e o diesel não estejam presentes. Térmicas a carvão ainda geram eletricidade nas nações mais populosas, China, Índia e Estados Unidos. O Brasil, com suas vantagens comparativas – sol, vento e potencial hidrelétrico – pode clamar certa liderança, ainda que na prática esteja investindo no aumento da produção de petróleo. Não creio que haverá pressão popular que poderá reverter a exploração de petróleo na Foz do Rio Amazona, o que mostra a contradição em curso das políticas energéticas de Lula.


As análises mais recentes do perfil de emissões do Brasil, lançadas esta semana

pelo Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões e Remoções de Gases de Efeito Estufa (Seeg),

 mostram que o Brasil não está cumprindo inteiramente a meta …

title: YRK: Iranian attacks caused extensive damage in Merîwan
content:
The East Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) released a statement announcing the aftermath of Iranian attacks on several villages in the Merîwan (Marivan) region. According to the YRK Command, troops of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards targeted the villages of Qamîşele, Henarşêxan and Gagal with drones and heavy weapons on Wednesday.


According to the statement, the attacks caused extensive damage to numerous residential buildings, as well as gardens, vineyards and agricultural land belonging to the villagers. The YRK forces suffered no casualties in the attacks, the statement added.

author: groundxero
title: The Enemy at Home
content:
The belief that Democrats will dismantle a system designed to serve the rapacious greed of the war machine and the ruling billionaire class is a mirage.


 


CHRIS HEDGES


Nov 12


 


Power does not rest in the Congress. It does not rest in the courts. It does not even rest in the imperial presidency. It rests in the hands of Wall Street financiers, Silicon Valley, private equity firms, the fossil fuel industry, the predatory health care and pharmaceutical giants, agribusinesses and, most of all, the war industry.


 


No mainstream politician, including Bernie Sanders, dares utter a word against our entrenched militarism. If you do, you end up like Ralph Nader, who was turned into a pariah by a compliant media and our corporate-indentured political parties. Nader spoke the truth. He paid for his honesty.


 


We are about to witness the

largest increase

 in war spending in American history with a proposed $1.5 trillion budget. The average taxpayer already shells out over $4,000 a

year


to the war industry as consumer and environmental agencies are

dismantled

, health care and education are defunded and programs such as

Medicaid


and

food stamps

 (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) are slashed.


 


The new Pentagon budget will

hand

 $58.5 billion to artificial intelligence and military command-and-control centers and see the effective

merging

 of the United States and Israeli military industrial complexes. Seventy-four percent of the increase in the proposed $1.5 trillion budget

will go to

 private contractors,

including

 those who are building massive data centers on military bases.


 


None of this is good for us or good for the planet. The Pentagon, powered by the fossil fuel industry, is the world’s

largest institutional polluter

, emitting an estimated

66 million metric tons


of carbon dioxide in 2024.


 


Americans, meanwhile, struggle with rising prices — nearly 30 percent of people go

into debt

 to buy groceries. An estimated 114,174. Americans

die

 each year due to lack of health insurance or inadequate health care while a single-payer universal health care system could cover every American, save more than 100,000 lives a year, and reduce annual health expenditures by $1.04 trillion, or nearly 20 percent. Twenty-five percent of Americans are

functionally unemployed

. The minimum wage remains frozen, despite Democratic Party promises to raise it, at $ 7.25 an hour.


 


The elites use war not only for personal enrichment, but to stifle class conflict.


 


War, as W.E.B. Du Bois said, diverts the poor from their real interests. It funnels national frustrations into the “heroic” battle against a common enemy. The nationalist cant, with its endemic racism, seduces those who are alienated or on the margins of society into feeling they suddenly belong. It entices them to sacrifice themselves for a “noble” cause. They becime the architects of their own enslavement. They march like sheep into war’s purgatory.


 


By the time they wake up, it is too late. They are cast aside, as so many of our

veterans

 have painfully discovered, like human refuse.


 


But as a tactic to consolidate power and enrich the billionaire class, it is unbeatable.


 


Wars will only be curtailed, if not halted, when we nationalize the weapons industry and dramatically reduce the military budget. Until then, nothing, absolutely nothing, will change.


 


Indeed, things will only get worse.


 


No one in Congress — or any other branch of government — will do this for us.


 


The masters of war sitting in the boardrooms of Boeing, General Dynamics or Northrop Grumman are not praying for peace in the Middle East or coexistence with China and Russia. The generals — who build their careers by orchestrating wars and post military careers enriching themselves working for defense contractors — are not seeking a cessation of global conflicts. They are seeking hundreds of billions in taxpayer dollars and government debt to fuel the self-defeating cycle of endless war.


 


The corporate vultures — especially the war makers — are, as I write, descending on Congress. They are meeting with Democratic Party leaders and holding out promises of millions in cash. They will corrupt, neutralize and compromise most. They will destroy the careers of the very few who refuse to do their bidding.


 


They hold the real power. They have no intention of surrendering it.

author: John David Parol
title: 1,000 puno sa Marikina puputulin para sa ₱8.5-B ADB bridge project
content:
Sa kahabaan ng St. Mary Avenue sa Provident Village, nakabalot sa mga puno ng Narra at Balete ang mga telang may panawagang: “Save me! Say no to tree-cutting!”

Para sa mga residente ng subdivision na sinalanta ng pinakamatinding baha sa kasagsagan ng Bagyong Ondoy at Ulysses, ang natural canopy at ugat ng mga punong ito ang huling buhay na panangga laban sa pag-apaw ng Marikina River.

Subalit sa ilalim ng Metro Manila Bridges Project (MMBP) ng Department of Public Works and Highways, puputulin ang mahigit 500 puno sa lugar upang itayo ang tulay na magbubuhos ng mga sasakyan mula Marcos Highway diretso sa loob ng kanilang komunidad.

Sa isang pamayanang dati nang nalubog sa pagbaha, pinangangambahan ng mga residente ang epekto sa kanilang kaligtasan ng naturang tulay na bahagi ng ₱8.5-bilyong proyektong pinondohan ng pautang mula sa Asian Development Bank (ADB).

Nangunguna sa barikada at pagtutol ang koalisyong Marikina Kontra Agos (MKA) sa ilalim ng panawagang “Save the Trees, Stop the Bridge!”

Unang lumabas sa Provident Village ang kanilang panawagan nang maimbitahan silang magsalita sa “PA-X-PLAIN: A Forum on Pax Silica” sa inisiyatiba ng Silangan Against Pax Silica noong, Oktubre 17 upang mas magpalalim sa malawak na ugnayan at banta ng Pax Silica at Luzon Economic Corridor sa lupa, kalikasan, kabuhayan, at pambansang soberanya.

Para kay Carlo Maningat ng MKA, ito ang kauna-unahang pagkakataon na nagbahagi ang grupo sa labas ng sariling subdivision upang ilantad ang banta ng proyekto.

​”Mawawala ang canopy cover sa tinatayang 17 ektarang lupain kung puputulin ang mahigit 1,000 puno sa Marikina na magpapalala sa init sa lungsod at bulnerabilidad natin sa baha.”

Ilan sa mga ito ay daan-taon na ang tanda (century-old) at itinuturing nang national heritage na hindi na makaliligtas sa earth-balling, dahilan upang igiit ng grupo ang interbensyon ng National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) upang protektahan ang mga ito laban sa pagputol.

Bukod sa mga puno, higit 70 kabahayan sa Marikina ang nakatakdang ma-demolish.

​Sa Provident Village, inireklamo ng mga apektadong residente ang isyu ng illegal taking at kabayaran: tanging ang mismong parte lamang ng ari-arian na gigibain ang babayaran ng gobyerno, habang iiwanang nakatiwangwang at hindi na mapakikinabangan ang natitirang bahagi ng kanilang tahanan.

​Kinuwestiyon din sa presentasyon ang ligalidad ng pagpapatupad ng pampublikong proyekto sa pribadong lupain nang walang kaukulang deed of donation, certificate of acceptance, o resolusyon mula sa konseho ng lungsod na nagpapatibay sa donasyon ng lupa ng Provident sa Marikina LGU, batay na rin sa legal precedent ng Korte Suprema sa kasong Quezon City Government vs. Rainier L. Madrid.

Hindi lamang isa, kundi tatlong tulay ang plano ng DPWH at ADB.

​Ang Bridge 1, na nagkakahalaga ng humigit-kumulang ₱1.69 bilyon, ang pinaka-kontrobersyal dahil direktang magbubuhos ito ng trapiko mula SM Marikina sa Marcos Highway papasok sa St. Mary Avenue.

​Kasunod nito ang Bridge 2, na mag-uugnay sa Homeowners Drive at A. Bonifacio Avenue. Tumatagos ang linyang ito sa mga barangay ng Calumpang, Tañong, at Jesus dela Peña.

​Sa hilaga naman, itatayo ang Bridge 3 na tatawid mula Kalayaan at Kabayani Street sa Nangka (Balubad) patungong Matandang Balara at Capitol Hills sa Quezon City.

Ayon sa breakdown ng MKA, aabot sa eksaktong 1,069 puno ang nakalinyang putulin sa pitong barangay: 514 sa Bridge 1; 232 sa Bridge 2; at 350 sa Bridge 3.

​Ang kontrata para sa civil works ng mga naturang tawiran ay naigawad sa mga kumpanyang mula sa Tsina, kabilang ang Hunan Road and Bridge Construction Group Co., Ltd.

Batay sa datos ng pagpopondo para sa Metro Manila Bridges Project, umaabot sa kabuuang ₱12.028 bilyon ang inilaang pondo para sa proyekto. ​Sa nasabing halaga, ₱8.5 bilyon ang magmumula sa pautang ng ADB, habang ₱3.52 bilyon naman ang magiging counterpart fund ng gobyerno ng Pilipinas. Nasa ₱3.36 bilyon pa lang ang kabuuang pondong nailabas para sa mga taong 2025 at 2026 upang pondohan ang implementasyon ng proyekto.

​Nagsimula ang mobilization at pre-construction activities noong 2024, habang nakatakdang tapusin ang konstruksyon ng Bridge 1 at Bridge 2 sa Setyembre 2027. Target namang makumpleto ang kabuuang proyekto, kabilang ang Bridge 3, pagsapit ng 2028 bago sumapit ang loan closing date.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Unnamed Military Exercises Aim to Intimidate Taiwan Ahead of Elections, While Avoiding International Outcry
content:
ACCORDING TO TAIWANESE Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo, China is currently engaged in area access denial drills around Taiwan.

Such drills involve more than 100 naval and coast guard ships operating in waters around Taiwan. These exercises include the deployment of the Liaoning, China’s first aircraft carrier, and its carrier group.

Last week, on November 3rd, images of Chinese naval vessels deployed around Taiwan were released by National Security Council head Joseph Wu. Wu also drew attention to a large number of air sorties that had taken place on November 3rd, with 49 sorties of Chinese aircraft that entered Taiwan’s Air Defense Identification Zone and crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait.

Previously, news reports had indicated that China may have been practicing for a potential blockade of Taiwan in late October and early November, through exercises that coordinated between its eastern, northern, and southern theater commands. According to national security officials, these drills were larger than previously named large-scale drills by China, such as the 2025 Justice Mission.

Indeed, it is notable that China has not formally announced any military drills to date. China normally conducts at least two named large-scale military exercises per year, in the spring and the fall. This has not occurred this year yet, though it might be expected that China would conduct a large-scale set of exercises before the end of the year.

It is possible that China is stepping up military activity as a show of force before the Taiwanese local elections set to take place later this month. Indeed, probably as a means of intimidating Taiwan and flexing muscles, one has in short order seen Pakistan briefly revoke permissions for Taiwanese airlines to fly over its airspace, Papua New Guinea order the closure of Taiwan’s representative office, and reports that Lithuania requested that Taiwan change the name of its representative office in what would have been read as a form of diplomatic downgrading.

Likewise, domestically in Taiwan, one has seen incidents of transnational repression. These include political commentator Akio Yaita being attacked at the venue of a talk, a comedian who mocked Chinese president Xi Jinping in his stand-up routine having feces and paint thrown at the venue where he was performing, and a plot to ram the same comedian with a vehicle and hospitalize him.

China may be stepping up efforts to intimidate Taiwan then–including familiar military threats. But not formally announcing a new set of military exercises may be a means of avoiding strong reactions to Chinese military exercises that might backfire for the CCP, in which members of the public rally behind the DPP and Lai administration rather than being cowed into voting for the KMT.

Either way, Chinese naval movements go to show that Chinese threats against Taiwan have not ceased, shortly before elections. Furthermore, that there is little attention from the world in a time of significant military exercises should be concerning, in that the sources of information about military activity remain confined to state actors, and China is able to prevent any outcry about its military activity if it does formally announce military exercises.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Witness tries to disprove Sara’s Gencorp stake
content:
Criminal charges may be awaiting Gencorp Industries Inc. counsel Atty. Suzette Balucanag-Punay as she insisted that Sara Zimmerman Duterte Carpio does not own a single share of stock in the company but admitted that Sara received P2,142,369.14  as “return of capital” from the company from 2022 to 2025, broken down as follows: P337,500 in 2022; P555,750 in 2023; P612,419.14 in 2024, and; P636,700 in 2025. Under the law, Sara cannot engage in business or earn additional compensation from the government while occupying the vice presidency.


Twisting herself in knots, Punay said the payments were for the return of capital to Sara, who invested in one company which failed to secure a Jollibee franchise. Her investment later jumped to Gencorp, whose owner is closely linked with the Dutertes. Punay claimed that through all those years, Sara was not a stockholder, officer or director of Gencorp, a company controlled by a businessman who was named by detained ex-president Rodrigo Duterte as his envoy to China to attract investments.


Punay’s statement contradicts Sara’s admission in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) that she was a stockholder and director of the company. She executed her SALNs under oath. Yet, Punay insisted that Sara’s name did not appear in the company’s General Information Sheets (GIS) from 2022 to 2025. She also said Gencorp did not declare dividends during the same period, raising another question why Gencorp paid Sara P2.1-million during the same period for “return of capital.” However, Sara’s SALNs showed her annual “return of capital” might even be higher than the dividends for Gencorp stockholders who belong to one Chinese-Filipino family. The ties that bind them and Sara are worth investigating.


Punay’s pained defense of Sara as not being a beneficial owner of the company will not stand on the basis of her SALN disclosure. Her absence during stockholders’ meetings, board meetings, management or decision-making is of no consequence to the impeachment trial. Her unilateral declaration that she was a Gencorp stockholder in her SALN “doesn’t make her one?” Or is this the same as saying standing in a garage doesn’t make a woman a car?


Kapunan asked why Punay did not bring Duterte’s declaration of GenCorp ownership in her SALNs to the company’s attention. She said it was not her duty to examine other people’s SALNs and adjust GenCorp’s corporate records based on their declarations. “I believe that my function as counsel of GenCorp, Your Honor, does not involve looking at other people’s SALNs and adjusting our records just because somebody declared that he is a stockholder of our corporation,” she said. Kapunan then asked why Sara had declared herself a GenCorp stockholder if she had no shares in the company. Again, Punay said she is not Sara’s keeper.


From 2022 to 2025, Punay disclosed, Gencorp did not declare dividends but gladly paid huge amounts to Sara. Moreover, Sara did not participate in the management of the corporation, she added, which is irrelevant to the issue of her failure to divest herself of any business interest when she became vice president in 2022. Supposed to be an eagle-eyed counsel, Punay could not say with certainty how a corporation with a paid-up capital of only P1.25-million managed to wangle five Jollibee franchises since each franchise is estimated to cost a minimum of P35-million. She claimed she could not find any record of Sara’s investments in Gencorp. The impeachment court might as well summon such records to check on the veracity of her assertion. GenCorp operates five Jollibee branches in Davao City: Bolton, Matina Crossing, G-Mall, Times Square, and Abreeza.


Asked if Duterte had shareholdings or other interests in previous Jollibee franchisees or in the specific branches, Punay answered “no.” She wasn’t aware that another Jollibee branch in Quezon City was also operated by Gencorp. Prosecution counsel Lorna Kapunan pounced on Duterte’s investment, noting that Sara’s president’s original capital contribution to Davao Bounty was only P46,875 but Gencorp.’s return on her “loose investment” ran into millions in just four years. An evaluation of the original Gencorp records might reveal the falsity of Punay’s claims or challenge the reliability of the defense’s argument that the investment was above board and did not violate the constitutional ban on vice presidents engaging in business while in office.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Groups defy gov’t plea to postpone mass actions
content:
Progressive groups led by Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) protest outside the House of Representatives while lawmakers’ briefing on Pax Silica is ongoing on Wednesday, November 11. (Charles Edmon Perez/Pinoy Weekly)

Where is the respect for farmers and Aytas who will be evicted from their communities because of Pax Silica?

This is the response of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) in Malacañang’s recent public statement to “show courtesy” as the Philippines hosts the 49th ASEAN Summit from November 15 to 18.

“We will hold protests before, during, and after the ASEAN Summit and Trump’s visit,” the group said in a statement. US President Donald Trump is expected to arrive in the Philippines next week.

In a press briefing on November 10, Malacañang’s Press Officer Claire Castro appealed to the protesters not to schedule rallies during the arrival of the international delegations and “show the genuine hospitality and good character of the Filipino people.”

“Respect for visitors? How about respect for vendors and urban poor displaced by ‘clearing operations’? Where is the respect for farmers and Aytas who will be evicted from their communities because of Pax Silica?” Bayan asked.

Bayan, together with multi-sectoral groups, launched the 12 days of protest which kicked off on November 4. The group stressed that the Philippine government should not welcome “war criminals and foreign plunderers” like Trump at the expense of the Filipino people’s welfare and their right to protest.

The Philippine National Police increased the number of personnel to more than 23,000, coming from the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO), Armed Forces of the Philippines, Bureau of Fire Protection, and other concerned agencies.

Human rights group Karapatan described the ASEAN preparations as “over-the-top” and are reminiscent of the huge police deployment during the State of the Nation Address (SONA) last July.

“And we all know how that played out. Fifty-one protesters were arrested even before the protest program began, with many of those arrested taken merely because they wore black,” said Cristina Palabay, secretary-general of Karapatan. “This is our country, and we have every right to protest, especially when the policies and actions of these very visitors threaten our people’s rights and interests. US President Donald Trump is not merely a guest whose presence demands deference. The US is actively intervening in our country’s affairs, advancing its economic and military interests at the expense of Filipino sovereignty and people’s rights.”

The United States leads the Pax Silica Initiative, which plans to establish a 4,000-acre industrial hub within the Philippines’ Luzon Economic Corridor. Described as the first “AI-native industrial acceleration hub,” the proposed site is being positioned as an economic security zone intended to strengthen shared supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, electronics, and other goods.

Read: ‘Pax Silica’ initiative seen as war production, environment destruction

Progressive groups also assailed the worsening economic situation amid grand preparations for the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Independent think tank group IBON Foundation said that the current low wages failed to keep up with the country’s inflation — climbing up to 7.8 percent in October from 7.2 percent in September. The group stressed that rising prices of these commodities, along with rice, are affecting poor and low income families.

The unemployment in the country also increased by almost 909,000, according to the data of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), though the IBON Foundation argued that the number could be higher.

The number of unemployed Filipinos has raised the Philippine unemployment rate to 5.4 percent, making it the highest among its Southeast Asian neighbors based on the latest data in Indonesia (4.8%), Malaysia (2.9%), Vietnam (2.2%), Singapore (2%), and Thailand (0.9%).

The Philippines is also performing the poorest in terms of economic performance, compared to its counterparts in Southeast Asia. It has among the lowest GDP growth in the region at 2.1 percent compared to Brunei (0.02%), Thailand (1.9%), Malaysia (5.3%), Singapore (5.4%), Indonesia (5.5%) and Vietnam (10%).

“The government’s business-as-usual approach is worsening joblessness, eroding incomes and making the cost of living soar for millions of Filipinos,” said IBON Foundation, warning the administration of Ferdinand Marcos Jr …

author: rti_admin
title: A Ballot and the Barricade
content:
Quite often, as I stand at the edge of Jantar Mantar and watch a police officer tighten the barricades across the road, I see space. It surprises me, for, like democracy or citizenship or the human right to protest, space is not supposed to be seen. It is not that standing in New Delhi, this capital of monumental avenues, government buildings and carefully cultivated national spectacles, has given me some special ability to see what I had not been able to see before. It is just that, when the police begin deciding where people can stand, how far they can walk and how long they can remain together, space suddenly acquires a very visible grammar. Everything competes with it for visibility: placards, police uniforms, detention vans, commuters searching for an alternative route, journalists trying to document an unfolding confrontation and, of course, the institutions that seem much easier to approach in a textbook than on the street. Light, which can illuminate a public institution, cannot necessarily illuminate the distance between that institution and the people who wish to question it. On 10 October 2026, as protesters gathered in Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the disputed Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, this distance acquired a material form. Barricades obstructed routes, police detained protesters, and restrictions on transport and mobile internet affected the city’s circulation. The Election Commission maintained that electoral revision was intended to improve the accuracy of voter lists; critics questioned its implementation and warned of possible disenfranchisement. The disagreement was therefore not simply about a list of names. It concerned the conditions under which people could make claims about their own political existence-and whether the institutions responsible for administering citizenship could be held publicly accountable for the ways in which they did so.

This disorientation is followed by anger and confusion, of the body as much as the mind, which coagulate into a mixture of disbelief and reluctant familiarity. We have become accustomed to seeing democracy represented through the visual grammar of elections: the inked finger, the queue outside a polling booth, the electronic voting machine, the triumphant party headquarters. The ballot is photographed; the voter is counted; the result is announced. But what happens when citizens attempt to question the procedures through which the electorate itself is constituted? Who gets to count the people who count? The question sounds like a riddle, but its consequences are administrative, material and profoundly political. When a revision of electoral rolls is contested, the dispute concerns not only the accuracy of a database but also the relationship between documentary legibility and the right to participate. A person may exist socially, work, pay rent, raise children and belong to a neighbourhood, yet still find that their political existence depends upon whether their name appears in the appropriate column. James C. Scott’s Seeing Like a State (1998) helps explain how governments make complex populations administratively legible through standardised records, categories and measurements. Such legibility is indispensable to many public functions, including the maintenance of electoral rolls. But a list is never the population itself; it is a representation of the population, constructed through rules that can be examined, challenged and corrected. The democratic question is not whether electoral lists should be accurate. Of course they should. It is whether the procedures used to make them accurate are themselves sufficiently transparent, accessible and accountable to those whose political standing depends on them.

How is one to draw space in place of the barricade? Henri Lefebvre’s The Production of Space (1974) offers a useful starting point, because it refuses to treat space as an innocent container into which social life simply pours. Space is produced through power, labour, planning and everyday practice. A road is not merely a road: it is a worker’s route to a shift, a vendor’s access to customers, a commuter’s connection between home and employment, and, under particular circumstances, a place where citizens assemble to make a claim upon the state. The barricade brings these otherwise overlapping uses into conflict. It announces that the road is public, but that its publicness can …

author: Jasmine Duff
title: Bosses are pushing for a hard-right government in Victoria
content:
Australia’s business elite and right-wing press are gunning to end Victorian Labor’s twelve-year reign and install a Liberal government. They’re pushing for harsh cuts to services for working-class people. Victoria’s Chamber of Commerce published a 

wish-list

 for the election, demanding exemptions from the payroll tax, reversing Victoria’s state debt, and drawing in data centre investment. The Murdoch and Channel 9 media conglomerates have helped the Liberals make crime and debt central election issues.

They’re pushing at an open door because both major parties are helping the bosses to generate a harsher right-wing political climate. Under Ben Carroll’s leadership, Victorian Labor has attempted to appease business. In his four months as premier, Carroll has launched a Royal Commission into the CFMEU, increased police funding, tightened bail laws, and cut services for kids with disabilities. Both Carroll and his predecessor Jacinta Allan attempted to suppress the wages of teachers during their recent enterprise agreement campaign.

But for Australia’s business elite, this isn’t enough. They want a change of government. And if the polls are to be believed, they’re going to get one. 

Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson has, for now, stabilised her party after years of embarrassing internal strife. Her campaign relies on heavy fear-mongering about youth crime and presenting Victoria as drowning in debt. Wilson is often described in the press as a moderate Liberal because she appears less socially reactionary. She matched Labor’s pledge to make abortions free, neutralising Labor’s attempt to make it an election issue. 

But Wilson is a blue-blood, ruling-class figure. She was raised in the Liberal Party and was backed by the hard-right Institute of Public Affairs (IPA) while head of the Young Liberals. Before being elected to the blue-ribbon seat of Kew, she served as executive director of policy at the Business Council of Australia. Her husband works for the IPA, and hard-right Liberal powerbroker James Paterson is a close collaborator and godfather to her children. In power, she’ll serve the interests of big business.

The Liberals have pledged to return Victoria’s budget to surplus by 2032. They also plan to lift the threshold for the land tax and payroll tax and cut the metropolitan payroll tax rate. These are all measures which would hand money to businesses and large landowners. They’ve also pledged to hire 3,000 new police officers. 

To pay off the debt while taking these measures would require drastic cuts elsewhere. While the Liberals have mostly avoided outlining where they would make cuts, they’ve already pledged to increase the workloads of civil servants through a hiring freeze covering thousands of positions. It’s likely they will propose further cuts that will affect social services and undermine working-class living standards. 

Alongside cuts, the Liberals want to create a more authoritarian political climate. Wilson has pledged to ban the slogan “globalise the intifada” and introduce move-on powers to crack down on protests. She will scrap the Victorian Treaty process. And she plans to introduce legislation that expands the list of offences for which children will be subjected to adult courts and adult sentencing.

It’s not just the Liberals. One Nation is also doing a service to the bosses by shifting the debate even further to the right. Despite the media’s portrayal of the party as “populist” disruptors, they’re on board with the agenda of reshaping Victoria in the interests of business. 

The bosses have faced little resistance so far in making their concerns central to the terrain of the election. This only serves to entrench a feeling of resignation about the impending right-wing wave. But if significant forces were prepared to launch a fightback, they could likely get a hearing. Only a small minority agree with the Liberals’ plan to scrap Treaty, but there have so far been no rallies to defend it. Progressive NGOs have not led marches against racism or to defend migrants. Nor have unions organised mass meetings or strikes to resist the bosses’ offensive. Instead, when Victorian teachers fought to improve their pay and working conditions, their union’s leadership encouraged them to back down and accept crumbs. 

The institutional weakness of the left and the decline of union militancy put the bosses and their backers in a powerful position. They’ve set the tone for this election, and the …

author: Cas Smith
title: Doctor says Israeli cluster bombs, with Australian tungsten, are targetting Palestinian children
content:
Dr Farah Abdul Aziz, Perth-based general and breast surgeon, volunteered twice in Gaza, including a harrowing period of service in the enclave’s “red zone” from December 2024 to January 2025.

Aziz told Green Left that working in the north of Gaza was “just awful”.

“There were just continuous attacks across the zone from sundown to sunrise, and even during the day. Medical staff could not go out of the hospital at all, because we could easily get bombed at any time.”

Aziz, a member of Palestinian Australian New Zealand Medical Association (PANZMA), was largely tasked with treating head, abdominal and chest injuries.

“The patients I received were the ones who had just survived the blasts that we were hearing all night. It was usually multiple shrapnel injuries, but they were still alive. Then, during the day, it would be single-shot bullet injuries.

“Because I’m not a neurosurgeon, I didn’t treat children who had received a single shot to the head, but I still saw them when my colleagues received them.

“Some had received a single shot to the abdomen or chest; these are little children, you can imagine snipers sniping them from two, three hundred meters away.”

The October protest against the Land Forces weapons expo in Perth condemned Australian governments for embracing the weapons industry and their involvement in supply chains connected to Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

But information about the specific weapons used, and Australian companies’ involvement their manufacture, is scarce.

Aziz said that because there is a significant proportion of children in Gaza, they made up 87% of her patients.

One particularly horrifying aspect was trying to treat children who had been targeted by cluster bombs as tiny, cube-shaped tungsten shrapnel was spread throughout their bodies.

“It’s well documented that these cluster bombs come from quadcopters, which are basically big drones that follow people around in Gaza,” Aziz said.

“This little kind of bomb cluster will actually open up and fire hundreds of little cubes. They’re about two millimetres small and they’re made from tungsten. Because of this they are very dense, but also high-velocity, because they’re so tiny.”

The latter factor meant that the shrapnel penetrated multiple organs and was extremely difficult to get rid of.

“I had one patient, who I remember really well, because the cubes just went every single angle of his bowel,” Aziz said. “Every single time, I would run the bowel from top to bottom to look for things that I had missed and I would find another hole and another hole.

“I had never experienced anything like that; usually, you have a bullet wound with an entry wound and an exit wound. Instead, this shrapnel would move in multiple tangents around the body. So, it’s obviously produced to cause maximum injury.”

Aziz said the tungsten making up this shrapnel was sourced from far north Queensland, and specifically the Mount Carbine Tungsten Mine. Activists say the wolfram ore concentrate from the mine is sent to US tungsten fabricator Elmet Technologies, where it is turned into warhead parts, tank parts and tiny tungsten cubes.

Speaking of the resilience of Palestinian people, Aziz noted that the majority of patients would carry information that enabled them to support doctors treating their illnesses, including cancer.

Many people had sought out Aziz’s expertise as a breast cancer surgeon. “They would come to me with a piece of paper with their history — their ultrasound, their mammogram, their biopsies — and they would show me their CT scan and their mammogram on their phone.

“Kudos to the local doctors as well; whenever they report a patient’s scan, they will get the family in to take a video of them scrolling down their scans, because they know that the patient has to move around from one place to another, seeking medical help.

“In spite of what’s going on, the [Palestinian patients] have a really good understanding of what they need to do. If they have a medical condition, they will go from one hospital to another, seeking help.”

Palestinian Australian New Zealand Medical Association

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: The “two souls” of the Spanish general strike
content:
A 24-hour general strike is set to take place across the Spanish state on 11 November, sparked by recent struggles over housing. In the lead-up to the general strike, 

Red Flag

’s 

Jordan Humphreys

 spoke to Germán 

P. Montañés

, a member of the revolutionary organisation Anticapitalistas, about the unfolding situation.

Red Flag

:

 Rising rents and house prices are affecting people across the globe. Why has it become such a flashpoint in the Spanish state in particular? What is the housing situation like there?

Germán

 

P. Montañés:

 Housing in the Spanish state has been a structural problem for a long time. One of the most visible impacts of the 2008 financial crisis was a wave of mortgage evictions. Today, mortgage-related evictions are less common, but renting has become much more widespread.

Even so, renting remains less common in Spain than in cities like Berlin or New York, where tenant voting blocs have played a major political role. In Spain, home ownership is the norm even among much of the working class. This stems from a strategy popularised during the dictatorship—echoing Margaret Thatcher’s later policies in the UK—summarised by a government minister’s famous quote: “I want a country of homeowners, not proletarians”. This high level of home ownership has somewhat cushioned the crisis; without it, the social situation likely would have collapsed much sooner.

Still, the crisis remains severe for two main groups: young people, who are locked out of home ownership and forced to pay exorbitant rents; and low-income workers and migrants, who face the worst housing instability.

The modern housing movement began around 2008 with anti-eviction campaigns such as the Plataforma de Afectados por la Hipoteca (PAH). Later, tenants’ unions emerged from these struggles—founded in 2017 in hubs like Madrid and Barcelona, and expanding across the Spanish state over the past few years.

A major tipping point occurred in late September, when police evicted 87-year-old María del Carmen (Maricarmen) Abascal from her home in Madrid. She had lived there for nearly 50 years under a rent-controlled agreement, but after an investment fund bought the building, her rent drastically increased. On the fourth attempt, police successfully removed her. This high-profile eviction sparked widespread outrage across the country. In response to the growing public backlash, the prime minister brought the general elections forward to 29 November.

RF

: 

Could you give us a better idea about the tenants’ unions—what kind of organisations are they, and what relationship do they have with the revolutionary left?

GPM:

 The emergence of tenant unions reflects the limits of the previous housing movement, which focused almost exclusively on stopping evictions. The problem with focusing on evictions is that the movement arrives far too late: by the time a family is facing removal, the police are already at the door.

The founding principle of the tenants’ unions was to adapt the most effective elements of trade unions to housing—arriving early to conflicts and organising people sooner. Rather than a diffuse social movement, housing activism needed a formal union. Members pay a monthly contribution, providing a financial base that allows staff to work full time and maintains an ongoing presence.

They also drew heavily on US labour tactics, focusing on entire buildings or properties owned by the same investment fund or landlord family to intervene long before eviction day.

They’ve been very successful recently in Madrid. Around September, they had about 2,000 to 3,000 members, and over the last two months of conflict, that number doubled to roughly 6,000. To clarify: these are financial members, not dedicated militants—there are perhaps 100 to 150 core militants—but the growth is significant.

The mainstream political left has no militant presence inside these spaces and does not control them; it tries to exert influence from the outside through government institutions and political pressure.

The revolutionary left isn’t broadly present either, though our organisation is the only one with a real foothold inside the unions. Our influence extends beyond raw numbers: we’ve maintained a dialogue with the union leadership for ten years. While the leaders come from autonomist or anarchist traditions, key militants in leadership positions allow us to maintain a solid presence. Our goal is to build a revolutionary current inside the …

author: Jerome Small
title: Carroll’s royal commission: an attack on effective unionism in Victoria
content:
The Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria was announced by Victoria’s Labor Premier Ben Carroll in August: his first act as the incoming premier. 

Carroll’s announcement was a response to a years-long media campaign against the CFMEU, the main construction union. It was also part of a wholesale lurch to the right by an already neoliberal Labor government. And it is a blatant attack on any idea that unions should act to raise wages. 

If proof is needed, just look at the first day of the current bloc of hearings. I attended the first day of the commission back in September and sat through the proceedings yesterday via livestream.  

Literally the main point of yesterday’s hearing was how terrible it was that the CFMEU stopped a major construction job—the Gap Road level crossing removal in Sunbury—for a day and a half in June 2022, and that this resulted in traffic controllers winning an increase in wages from the award rate (at that time $26 per hour) to around $49 per hour. 

The horror. This equates to a full-time wage of $1,862 per week, slightly above Australia’s average full-time wage of $1,835 in 2022. It’s an OK wage, though no king’s ransom. With allowances, shift and casual loading, and the plentiful overtime that construction sites run on, this can add up to a decent wage if you’re prepared to work long hours.

To listen to Chris Young, the counsel assisting the royal commission, a union winning this sort of wage for a blue-collar worker through industrial action in 2026 is a threat to all that is right in the world. So much so that two weeks of the royal commission’s rather expensive time is being devoted to investigating how this could possibly have come about, with the express intention of ensuring it never happens again. 

Young spent yesterday sifting through the circumstances leading up to this supposed affront to decency. The CFMEU had a lot going in its favour. 

Railway crossing removals happen on a tight timetable, planned up to a year in advance. The two companies doing the work—John Holland and CPB—wanted to deliver the job on time in order to secure further work. The labour market was tight in Victoria. The CFMEU had already been successful in securing enterprise agreements with most of the big companies doing this sort of work in Victoria. From the evidence led by counsel assisting, it sounds like the CFMEU judged the moment perfectly—just like any union which is serious about taking action to raise wages should, and historically has. 

Both the CFMEU and the Australian Workers’ Union (AWU) cover workers working on civil construction projects like level crossing removals, and since 2014 the CFMEU has been trying to expand its coverage at the expense of the AWU. The Victorian Labor government at that time was uninterested in helping the AWU maintain coverage over these jobs—like Gap Road—and over traffic control work in particular. 

This was a positive for the workers at Gap Road, and more broadly. The royal commission was told that Zoom Recruitment, one of the AWU-aligned labour hire companies providing traffic control at Gap Road, was operating on a long-expired enterprise agreement that paid only the legal minimum specified in the construction award. 

This is utterly consistent with the business model of the AWU for the past century or more in construction, which is to undercut the wages and condition of the CFMEU and its predecessor unions. And to their credit, for most of that time, the CFMEU and their predecessors generally ignored the AWU’s claims to coverage on “civil” infrastructure work (roads, rail, bridges and tunnels).

The commission heard yesterday that the Labor government’s largely hands-off attitude to this demarcation dispute in 2022, which effectively favoured the CFMEU over the AWU, may have been because of factional alignments within the ruling Labor Party. This is hardly a crime, or even a novel tactic in Australian union politics.  

The AWU has used exactly the same approach, of translating political clout in the Labor Party into industrial coverage (and vice-versa), for its entire existence. The conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Union (SDA) follows the same path. The only difference is that the AWU and the SDA have an appalling record of lifting wages—in fact the SDA did the opposite, helping employers undercut legal minimums, until a path-breaking legal case in the Fair Work …

title: Solidarity shown to climate action group Rising Tide
content:
Many community-based groups are showing their support for climate action group Rising Tide, which is battling NSW Labor, Newcastle City Council and NSW Police to organise a peaceful protest on Newcastle Harbour, the world’s biggest coal port, on November 14.

You can register for the Paddle for the Planet here, and sign the petition to reverse Newcastle Council's ban on Rising Tide events here.

Below are some of the solidarity statements.

Sydney Students for Climate stands with Rising Tide against the outrageous decision by the City of Newcastle to permanently ban climate protests from council-owned land.

The undemocratic attack on protest rights was passed by the mayor’s deciding vote, after a 6–6 split at the November 10 council meeting. The motion could effectively ban all protests on Newcastle council land.

It was supported by NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns, who wrote a letter endorsing the motion.

Minns has consistently tried to shut down peaceful protests for climate, Palestine and other issues.

We also note that NSW Police are taking Rising Tide to the Supreme Court to try and shut down the November 14 paddle out for the planet.

With the climate hurtling towards disaster and NSW Labor continuing to approve new coal and gas projects, we will fight these anti-protest restrictions and continue demanding action for a safe climate.

SSFC will be at the Paddle for the Planet this Saturday, and the People’s Blockade of the World’s Largest Coal Port in February, and we encourage all to join us.

Socialist Alliance stands with Rising Tide and all groups protesting against the expansion of coal and gas, and for funding a just transition for fossil fuel workers in Muloobinba/Newcastle.

The City of Newcastle’s decision on November 10 to ban Rising Tide, and other groups, from protesting on “community-owned land” is draconian and dangerous.

The motion — adopted by a the independent Mayor’s casting vote — represents yet another attack on citizen’s democratic right to protest in NSW. Three Labor councillors did not support the Mayoral minute, only given half an hour before the meeting, but one did.

While the motion singled out Rising Tide, it said “affiliate groups” were also banned from protesting on council land. When pressed, Mayor Gavin Morris confirmed he also wanted to stop protests that support Palestine.

NSW Labor Premier Chris Minns’ record on trying to stop peaceful protests — on Palestine and for a safe climate — shows just how dangerous he is.

For three years Minns has tried to stop citizens from protesting the genocide in Gaza. He has been spectacularly unsuccessful because he has been challenged, and the courts, including the Supreme Court, have ruled against his efforts to stop people from mobilising together to express their view — the Sydney Harbour Bridge march for humanity being the most prominent example.

Minns is a big fan of coal, and he is now trying to introduce a new law to circumvent a High Court decision stating that NSW planning must take all emissions into account.

Minns has wanted to stop Rising Tide’s peaceful protests for a safe climate at the Newcastle Harbour. For several years he has been pushed back.

Newcastle City Council’s decision to prevent Rising Tide from using foreshore land now and into the future will not deter climate activists.

The NSW Police has lodged an objection in the Supreme Court to also disallow the Rising Tide protest on November 14.

But climate activists will continue to protest NSW Labor’s addiction to fossil fuels, which includes expanding coal mines in the Hunter Valley in a climate crisis.

As COP31 begins in Turkey, Rising Tide is seeking to draw attention to Australia’s complicity in fueling dangerous climate change. Minns is also complicit.

Socialist Alliance has long supported Rising Tide and will be joining the family-friendly flotilla protest at the world’s largest coal port on November 14 at 10am.

author: Odessa Bishop-McMurray
title: “If they won’t give us a future, we will build one right here” - why the French revolt should inspire high-schoolers everywhere
content:
As one of the organisers of the upcoming nationwide 

Students Say No to Hanson

 demonstration on 12 November, I’ve had to endure a lot of inanity from the media and the right. Amongst snide remarks about the stages of brain development and warnings of the mortal dangers of missing two periods of class, one accusation keeps coming up: that we’re plotting to bring “French-style riots” to Australian cities. 

Right-wing journalists seized on an Instagram post we made on 11 October, conveying the inspiration we draw from French student protesters fighting government austerity and the far right. 

Cue an avalanche of hysterical headlines and news segments: The Murdoch-owned Adelaide 

Advertiser

 warned readers to brace for “walkouts ‘inspired’ by violent French protests”. Pauline Hanson went on Brisbane’s 4BC Radio to rip into us:

“...They are saying they are inspired by what’s going on in France. What? The 

looting

? The 

burning

? The 

destruction

? They’re 

inspired

 by that?”

Well, we’re not sorry for being inspired by French students. Everyone who wants to see a better world should identify with their struggle. 

Young people everywhere are facing a dire future, and revolt is rightly spreading. It’s clear even to some in the establishment that what’s happening in France is part of a global wave of protest with deep roots. As former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown wrote this week in 

The Guardian

: “A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken—and they know it.”

Both far-right governments and “sensible centrists” are taking us on the same trajectory: more racism, more militarism, and more austerity. 

When states aren’t attempting to re-introduce conscription, as in Germany, they’re funnelling billions into the military-industrial complex while schools crumble. In France, students endure classrooms infested with cockroaches, mould and overcrowding, sometimes numbering 35 students to a class. 

We’ll likely never be able to afford secure housing or sufficient healthcare. We’ve watched politicians choose fossil fuel companies over the habitability of our planet. For many of us, the establishment’s unanimous endorsement of Israel’s genocide in Gaza was the final nail in the coffin.

It’s obvious that the journalists’ and politicians’ pearl-clutching about a few broken Parisian shop windows is a means of avoiding discussion of these issues. And their condemnation of violence rings hollow when they decline to comment on the vastly greater violence that the system inflicts on people daily. 

There’s the violence that is inherent in running such an unequal society. French youth linger without a future in the slums while the richest 500 families own nearly half the country. Schools and hospitals in France are crumbling, but the latest budget announcement includes 54 billion euros in further cuts to public spending. The police systematically brutalise Black and Arab working-class migrants. The high-profile killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, which sparked a nationwide revolt in 2023, is part of a long history of racialised policing. 

When these injustices generate resistance, there’s one public service the government can guarantee: the bludgeoning of protestors, tear gas, and potentially lethal stun grenades; exploding a student’s hand, breaking another’s jaw and leaving two 16-year-olds blinded for life. 

This is an inherent admission that the ruling class has no genuine plan to improve society. They just want resignation from ordinary people, and when that fails, tear gas is their backup plan.

But French students have shown that resignation gets us nowhere; Our power comes from the streets, and that’s a lesson the ruling class desperately does not want students to learn.

Already, France has shown small glimpses of how these movements can win real gains. While still hoping to crush the movement, the government has already been forced to make concessions. They’ve announced plans to cap class sizes, hire more teachers, and create more university places. This is a tiny fraction of what the movement is demanding, but it proves a timeless truth: a month of rebellion can win more change than decades of asking nicely.

A grassroots student movement in Serbia just ended the 14-year rule of the repressive Vučić regime. In Brazil, thousands of students flocked to the streets to successfully halt the advance of far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

It seems like …

author: Sagar Sanyal
title: Emergency and autocracy in Modi’s India
content:
The far-right government in India led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been increasingly repressive and anti-democratic over recent months. Commentators are asking if the country is in the grip of an ‘

undeclared Emergency

’, a reference to the 1975-77 period of ‘Emergency rule’ by then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in which activists and trade unionists were simply rounded up and jailed. 

The current repression is a response to the student and youth protests that erupted in the capital, New Delhi, in late July. They were sparked by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), a satirical movement that began on social media a couple of months earlier. The scale and intensity of the protests surprised the regime, as did the mocking anti-Modi tenor of popular chants. While the protest demand was for the resignation of the education minister over exam leaks, the protesters were motivated by visceral opposition to Modi, who has ruled since 2014. The police lashed out using the sort of 

force

 that they typically use in repressed regions like Kashmir. Police fired pellet guns, used nail-studded batons and sexually assaulted women protesters. 

Despite the repression, tens of thousands mobilised daily for five days—high school and university students, middle-class and working-class youth. Not only in Delhi, but in dozens of cities around the country. Alongside clips of police brutality circulating on social media, there are clips of youth chasing police off the streets with their sheer numbers and bravado. There are clips of cheeky middle-class youth approaching police who are away from the heat of the action to ask mocking questions like “Dear Mr. Officer, are you planning to tear gas protesters today?” The government is tracking down incriminating and embarrassing recordings of those events and asking social media platforms to 

remove them

.

Public opinion has turned strongly against Modi’s repression. Among the Hindi-speaking, middle-class, upper-caste Hindus who have been the most secure vote base of the BJP, parents now saw their own children being beaten—just for demanding a fair opportunity in college exams! Ultimately, the administration conceded the protest demand to sack the education minister, a humiliating 

defeat

 for Modi. It gave the lie to the “unstoppable strongman” image of him so carefully crafted by pro-Modi big media. 

Less than three months after the July protests, a new protest movement gripped the nation. It demands the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner of India, Gyanesh Kumar, who has been highly partisan to Modi and his 

Hindu nationalist

 Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and, according to some parties, rigged state elections in Bihar (May 2025) and West Bengal (April 2026). In West Bengal, the BJP won for the first time due in part to the chief election commissioner disqualifying millions of names from the eligible voters list. Deletions disproportionately targeted Muslims, who are an ideological enemy of Hindu nationalists, and who were also an important vote base of the party the BJP displaced—the Trinamool Congress (TMC). 

Following a late September 

expose,

 which revealed that the chief election commissioner had overruled the protestations of even his fellow election commissioners, the CJP and left student groups took up vote-rigging as a national campaign to channel the energy from the July student movement. Demands for the chief election commissioner to resign have been taken up by all opponents of the BJP. 

When a large protest was called for 

10 October

, the state responded by locking down New Delhi. Around 40,000 paramilitary and police laid siege to a sizeable area around the “designated protest site” of Jantar Mantar in the centre of the city. They blocked roads and shut down local internet mobile services (India is 

among the worst

 states for this). They closed over 40 metro train stations in Delhi and stopped over 200 inter-city trains from reaching Delhi. They threatened activists in their homes on the night before the march, this coming on top of regular arbitrary detention of prominent leaders of the protest movement (from the CJP and the left parties). 

Undeterred

, protestors appeared in their tens of thousands and were again met with batons and tear gas, and thousands were detained.

Sizeable protests have continued sporadically since 10 October, some called by the CJP or student organizations of the left, 

others

title: Bodrum Emek ve Demokrasi Güçleri: HABAŞ’ta yaşanan kaza değil iş cinayeti
content:
Antalya – İzmir Aliağa HABAŞ Demir Çelik Fabrikası’nda meydana gelen patlamada 19 işçinin hayatını kaybetmesi ve en az 15 işçinin yaralanması sonrası Bodrum Emek ve Demokrasi Güçleri, basın açıklaması ve eylem yaptı. Açıklamada, “Üretim zorlaması, taşeronlaştırma ve denetimsizlik nedeniyle yaşanan bu facia bir kaza değil, göz gör e göre gelen bir iş cinayetidir” diyerek yaşanan işçi ölümlerine tepki gösterildi.

Bodrum Emek ve Demokrasi Güçleri adına Belediye meydanında açıklamayı yapan Hakkı İlbeyi, aynı fabrikada son 10 yılda en az 7 işçinin daha hayatını kaybetmiş olmasının, ihmallerin sistematik hale geldiğini göstergesi olduğunu belirterek, “üretimin büyük ölçüde taşeron firmalar üzerinden yürütülmesi, bakım çalışmaları sırasında dahi üretimin durdurulmaması ve makine ile ekipmanların denetlenmemesi işçilerin yaşam hakkını hiçe saymaktır” dedi.

HABAŞ’taki güvencesiz ve denetimsiz çalışma düzeninin, başta Bodrum olmak üzere tüm Muğla genelinde de hüküm sürdüğünü belirten İlbeyi, “Bodrum’daki şantiyelerde, otellerde ve turizm işletmelerinde; Muğla genelindeki Yeniköy, Kemerköy ve Yatağan termik santralleri ile maden ve mermer ocaklarında işçiler kadrolu, taşeron ve yüklenici ayrımıyla ağır koşullarda çalıştırılmaktadır. İş güvenliği önlemlerinin maliyet unsuru olarak görüldüğü bu düzen devam ettiği sürece, bölgemizde de benzer faciaların yaşanması kaçınılmazdır” diye konuştu.

Emek Partisi Bodrum ilçe örgütü de eylem sonrası dağıttığı bildiride yaşanan işçi ölümleri, işçi cinayetlerine değinerek “Bodrum’daki inşaat ve turizm alanları başta olmak üzere Muğla’daki tüm termik santrallerde, maden ve mermer ocaklarında derhal gerçek bir denetimin yapılması ve denetim sonuçlarının şeffaf biçimde kamuoyuyla paylaşılması” çağrısı yaptı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Freedom Editor
title: A day of general strike in Spain
content:
A chronicle of pre-dawn picket lines, massive demonstrations, persistent rain, and sharply differing figures on participation

The strike began before dawn. By midnight, the first picket lines were already being organized. In Valencia, the CGT union had called for pickets at the Mercavalència wholesale market starting at 2:00 a.m., and at the EMT (municipal transport) depots in San Isidro from 5:00 a.m. Subsequently, access routes into the city—including the V-21 highway and the Ronda Nord—were blocked. The coverage in Valencia tracked the movement from the wholesale markets to the municipal transport network.

In Catalonia, actions were concentrated from the early hours at the Mercabarna wholesale market, various workplaces, and along roadways. According to updates published throughout the morning, more than thirty locations across the road network were affected by blockades. In Madrid, “informational” picket lines gathered at the EMT transport depots in Fuencarral and Carabanchel; the CCOO and UGT unions reported police charges and the use of pepper spray against participants.

At the Mercamadrid wholesale market, unions also reported police intervention. Reports concerning the Madrid transport depots include statements from the organisations involved. Tension spread to Málaga, where reports emerged of police charges near the EMT (municipal transport company) depots, and to Zamora, where early reports indicated two arrests and four people requiring emergency medical attention following an incident involving a transport picket line. In the Basque Country, the Ertzaintza (Basque police) reported thirteen arrests as of mid-morning, eight of which took place in Portugalete. These were preliminary tallies from different regions and points in time.

Initial reports from labour unions indicated high participation in certain industrial sectors. CCOO and UGT estimated that 90% of workers in the automotive and port sectors, and 85% in the meat-processing industry, participated during the early shifts. The CGT also reported high levels of work stoppages and picket activity. These estimates come from the organisations themselves, refer to specific sectors and shifts, and do not, on their own, confirm the overall percentage of workers on strike. The initial industrial report provides further detail on its source.

In the Valencian Community, the figures varied significantly. UGT-PV reported over 70% participation in industrial firms with union representation, while the employers’ association, CEV, estimated a 2.57% participation rate across the region’s entire economic sector during the early hours. Later, CCOO and UGT reported an average participation rate of 60% in the region. These figures are not directly comparable, as they differ in scope, the population observed, and the timeframes considered. Examining both sets of figures helps to explain these discrepancies.

The strike also affected public media. Canal Sur Televisión interrupted its regular programming around 8:20 a.m. while the show Despierta Andalucía was airing. In Valencia, nearly fifty students staged a sit-in at the Faculty of Geography and History at the University of Valencia in support of the strike. Picket groups focused on commercial areas moved through the streets and neighbourhoods of various cities. In the Vila de Gràcia neighbourhood, the mobilisation coincided with the postponement of an eviction.

The struggle for housing did not emerge as an issue separate from working conditions. Tenants’ unions, labour unions, and neighbourhood assemblies brought demands against high rents to the picket lines, alongside the defence of wages, public services, and labour rights. In Bilbao, groups converged in front of the Arriaga Theatre before heading toward the Basque Government headquarters. In Pamplona (Iruñea), a protest in front of CaixaBank ended with one arrest, according to reports on the day’s events. In Barcelona, ​​a main picket line moved through the commercial district; in Madrid, there were blockades on the Gran Vía and the Carrera de San Jerónimo.

By the afternoon, the strike had reached the major avenues.

Barcelona saw one of the largest marches. Groups arriving from various neighborhoods converged at the Jardinets and the Passeig de Gràcia. The Tenants’ Union (Sindicat de Llogateres) estimated the turnout at 400,000 people, while the local police (Guardia Urbana) provided an estimate of 55,000. These figures come from different sources, with no …

title: Huelga de hambre en Marcos Paz: “no se pueden avalar estas condiciones por una visita papal”
content:
Milton Tolomeo, preso hace nueve meses por protestar contra la Reforma Laboral, inició el domingo un ayuno indefinido. Desde la cárcel, explica que los 1.500 internos del Complejo 8 atraviesan una situación “tortuosa” tras el traslado forzoso del 12 de octubre.

Por Elisa Corzo, para Canal Abierto.


Este miércoles 11, último día del Papa León XIV en Argentina y el mismo día que visitó el penal de Devoto,

Milton Tolomeo –preso hace nueve meses por protestar contra la Reforma Laboral-

 inició su cuarto día de huelga de hambre en reclamo por las condiciones de detención

. Denuncia que, justamente tras

el traslado forzoso desde el penal porteño

, en condiciones deplorables, del 12 de octubre, la situación de los 1500 presos del nuevo complejo VIII de Marcos Paz se volvió “tortuosa”.


En diálogo con

Canal Abierto

, luego de que se restablecieran las líneas telefónicas que habían sido interrumpidas, señala que lo que piden, de mínima, es que se restablezcan las condiciones que tenían en el complejo en el que estaban antes, que era de máxima seguridad.


“Nosotros salimos de máxima seguridad y en este que es un modelo de media tenemos muchas peores condiciones. Perdimos el acceso a la educación, el acceso al trabajo, el acceso a la proveeduría donde compramos la mercadería que no puede ingresar de afuera como huevos, harina y condimentos. Perdimos lo que es recreación, la posibilidad de tener celdas abiertas, que ahora están cerradas todo el tiempo. Seguimos reclamando por agua potable. O sea, las condiciones se agravaron mucho”, sostiene.


Milton que estuvo un mes en el pabellón para presos de alto perfil -para terroristas- de Ezeiza, señala que el 8 no es muy diferente. “Esto es un modelo perfil más modernizado, con población y con teléfono”, grafica. “Desde la estructura de las mesas, el tema de las puertas, el patio, es lo mismo. Nosotros no tenemos vista a la naturaleza, el patio y el pabellón es un tercio de lo que teníamos allá (en el 2). Son cajas de zapatos, es todo muy tortuoso mentalmente”.


El joven sobre quien pesa una acusación terrorismo por participar en la protesta del 11 de febrero contra la Reforma Laboral cuenta que la huelga no inició por la visita del Papa pero sí tiene la esperanza de que se pueda visibilizar lo que pasa en Marcos Paz.


“Es una cuestión humana. O sea,

cualquier persona que sea católica, que crea en esta religión, no puede avalar estas condiciones por una visita papal

. Las condiciones de los 1500 detenidos no pueden venir de la mano una visita del Papa… esta tortura. Calculo que la visita del Papa no es para torturarnos a nosotros los 1500. Esto tiene que ver con el funcionamiento de todo el sistema de penitenciario, que bastante mal uso y mal manejo tiene”.


“Pero bueno, entiendo que esto viene de la mano de estas políticas de mano dura, como dicen ellos, del que “las hace, las paga”. Pero acá hay muchos detenidos que no tienen nada que ver. Algunos que son laburantes y están detenidos por causas totalmente ilógicas. Y tenemos una Justicia que lo que hace es culpar a los que menos tienen, a los que más desfavorecidos están, mientras protege a personajes internacionales que se dan a la fuga, a funcionarios del Gobierno que tienen millones que no pueden declarar, a gente que tiene vínculos con el narcotráfico. Y ellos están libres en su casa mientras nosotros somos los que estamos acá padeciendo esta tortura del nuevo régimen penitenciario”.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Canal Abierto (@canalabierto)


“No entiendo la acusación de terrorismo”


En comunicación con este medio también se refirió a la causa penal por la que está preso, al igual que Eneas Gallo, y por la que ambos podrían enfrentar penas gravísimas de entre 10 y 30 años, tras el pedido de que se les aplique la figura de Terrorismo, a pedido del fiscal Carlos Stornelli y por aceptación del juez Ariel Lijo

.


En ese marco, su familia, organismos de Derechos Humanos y la Coordinadora por la Libertad de lxs Presxs Políticos repudia que se mantenga la prisión preventiva. Y también reclaman que se restablezcan las visitas de los organismos de Derechos Humanos.


“Me genera mucha angustia –afirma Milton- porque no entiendo del porqué de esa acusación de terrorismo. Yo soy una persona que trabajaba cuatro horas de lunes a viernes como ayudante encargado de edificio. Después tenía mi profesión de masajista, la cual estaba tratando de desempeñarme y que crezca para …

author: CNT Bilbao
title: La clase trabajadora para en el 11N: huelga, calle y organización
content:
Bilbao y Euskal Herria han vivido hoy una jornada de huelga general con las ciudades paradas y manifestaciones masivas. El bloque propio de CNT en la manifestación ha contado con una gran participación. Han sido horas de movilización en las que también hemos tenido que denunciar las actuaciones de la Ertzaintza contra huelguistas y manifestantes.


Según la información de nuestras secciones sindicales, el seguimiento en la CAPV ha sido desigual según los sectores. En la enseñanza, los centros han funcionado con servicios mínimos y el seguimiento ha sido muy alto, casi absoluto. En la industria, los centros han superado el 50 % de seguimiento de forma generalizada, con alguna excepción de poco seguimiento en centros pequeños, de menos de 50 personas trabajadoras. En el transporte público han pesado los servicios mínimos. En la sanidad el seguimiento ha sido irregular, aunque muy notable en el ámbito administrativo, y conviene recordar que el sector mantiene sus propias huelgas. En el comercio, donde ha habido manifestaciones el cierre ha sido absoluto y en muchos barrios las persianas han estado bajadas por la mañana. En la hostelería, algunos bares se habían comprometido a cerrar y otros no.


Esa irregularidad no es casual. Hoy hemos hecho huelga y hemos salido a la calle porque los derechos no se piden: se conquistan y se defienden. La jornada de ocho horas, las vacaciones pagadas o la protección frente al despido no fueron regalos, sino fruto de huelgas, cajas de resistencia y décadas de organización colectiva. La huelga es mucho más que una movilización: es la protesta que interrumpe la producción, la que duele a la patronal cuando se refleja en sus cuentas, la que sale de las grandes manifestaciones y entra en los centros de trabajo. Demuestra que somos quienes hacemos funcionar la economía y que tenemos la capacidad de pararla.


Sabemos también que no todo el mundo puede hacer huelga. Las mujeres migrantes sin papeles, atrapadas por la Ley de Extranjería, se juegan mucho más que el salario de un día. Lo mismo ocurre con quienes tienen contratos tan precarios que ejercer su derecho puede costarles el empleo, con los falsos autónomos sin protección, con las trabajadoras de los cuidados y del hogar, sin convenio ni interlocutor, con quienes quedan atrapadas en cadenas de contratas y subcontratas, o con quienes temen las represalias de empresas que han hecho de la amenaza una forma de gestionar las relaciones laborales. Que no puedan hacer huelga demuestra que la precariedad está diseñada para que defender los derechos salga caro. Quienes hoy hemos podido parar hacemos nuestra también su lucha, porque el apoyo mutuo es la base de nuestro sindicalismo.


Desde CNT exigimos lo que en justicia nos corresponde: salarios y pensiones dignos, reducción de jornada sin bajar el sueldo, y trabajo y vivienda para todas las personas. Entendemos además que el Estado no es una institución neutral, y no aceptamos que la patronal y el Estado hagan con nuestros derechos lo que quieran, devolviéndonos nuestras demandas recortadas y irreconocibles. Tampoco aceptamos que se nos divida dejando a las trabajadoras migrantes sin derechos. Queremos todo para todas, y solo lo conseguiremos juntas, mediante la acción directa y en organizaciones propias de clase, independientes de gobiernos, instituciones y partidos.


Para CNT, la huelga de hoy es un punto de partida. Veinticuatro horas de paro no bastan, pero son un comienzo. Mañana tenemos que seguir juntas, quienes hemos podido parar y quienes no, reforzando la organización en nuestros centros de trabajo a través de las secciones sindicales y las asambleas, y en barrios y pueblos a través de redes de solidaridad vecinal. Que esta huelga se haya organizado de abajo arriba demuestra que la horizontalidad, las asambleas y el apoyo mutuo son la clave. La huelga es nuestra herramienta, la solidaridad nuestra fuerza y la organización nuestro camino. ¡Fuerza, compañeras!


La entrada

La clase trabajadora para en el 11N: huelga, calle y organización

 se publicó primero en

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.
