title: Συγκέντρωση ενάντια στο κλείσιμο του προγράμματος στέγασης «HELIOS JUNIOR», Πέμπτη 12/11, στις 18.00, στην πλατεία Βικτωρίας
content:
Κάλεσμα/Αφίσα από

Solidarity with Migrants:


Συγκέντρωση 12/11, 18:00, Πλατεία Βικτωρίας:


Ενάντια στο κλείσιμο του προγράμματος στέγασης «HELIOS JUNIOR»


Στις 9 Νοεμβρίου, το πρόγραμμα «HELIOS JUNIOR» τερματίστηκε επίσημα. Οι ένοικοι (περίπου 200 πρόσφυγες, ηλικίας 18-21 ετών) ενημερώθηκαν μόλις 5 ημέρες νωρίτερα ότι πρέπει να εγκαταλείψουν τα σπίτια τους, χωρίς να προβλέπεται κάποιο άλλο πρόγραμμα στέγασης. Επιπλέον, το Υπουργείο Μετανάστευσης δήλωσε ότι το κλείσιμο των δομών στέγασης αποτελεί πολιτική απόφαση, παρά το γεγονός ότι υπάρχουν διαθέσιμα κονδύλια από την ΕΕ. Μέχρι στιγμής, κανείς δεν έχει αποχωρήσει από το σπίτι του, ενώ οι άνθρωποι αυτοί αναζητούν εναλλακτικές λύσεις.


Την περασμένη εβδομάδα συναντηθήκαμε με αρκετούς από τους ενοίκους και αποφασίσαμε να καλέσουμε σε συγκέντρωση την Πέμπτη, στις 18:00, στην Πλατεία Βικτωρίας, για να αντιταχθούμε στο κλείσιμο του προγράμματος και να διεκδικήσουμε τη συνέχιση της παροχής στέγης για τους ασυνόδευτους νεαρούς πρόσφυγες στην Ελλάδα.


Η εκκένωση των κατοικιών με τόσο σύντομη προειδοποίηση είναι απαράδεκτη. Είναι ανεπίτρεπτο η κυβέρνηση να πετάει ανθρώπους στον δρόμο, χωρίς να προσφέρει καμία εναλλακτική λύση. Οι γειτονιές μας γίνονται όλο και περισσότερο στόχος θεσμικού ρατσισμού, ”εξευγενισμού” (gentrification) και της κρατικής βούλησης να αποκλειστούν οι μετανάστες από το κέντρο των πόλεών μας. Το κλείσιμο του HELIOS JUNIOR αποτελεί πολιτική επιλογή και απαιτεί συλλογική απάντηση.


Γι’ αυτό καλούμε σε συγκέντρωση την Πέμπτη, στις 18:00, στην Πλατεία Βικτωρίας, ως μια πρώτη δημόσια δράση.


Ενάντια στο κλείσιμο του προγράμματος στέγασης «HELIOS JUNIOR»


Στέγη για όλους – ντόπιους και μετανάστες μαζί.


Solidarity with Migrants


Gathering 12.11, 18:00 Plateia Victoria:


Against the closing of the HELIOS JUNIOR HOUSING Program


On November the 9th the HELIOS JUNIOR PROGRAMM officially closed. The residents (around 200 refugees in the age 18-21) were informed 5 days before, that they need to leave their houses and no further housing program is planned. Furthermore, the ministry of migration stated that it is a political decision that the housing structures are closing and that the money would be available from the EU. So far no one left their house and the people are trying to find other solutions


In the last week we met with several residents and decided to call together for a gathering on Thursday at 18:00 in Plateia Victoria against the closing of the program and to demand a continuation of a housing program for unaccompanied young refugees in Greece. The closure of the houses with such a short notice is not acceptable. It is not acceptable that the government throws people on the streets, without providing any alternative.


Our Neighborhoods are further and further targeted by institutionalized racism, Gentrification and the will of the state to exclude migrants from the center of our cities. The closing of HELIOS JUNIOR is a political choice and needs a collective answer.


Therefore we are calling for a gathering, Thursday 18:00 in Plateia Victoria as a first public action.


Against the closing of the Helios Junior Housing Program!


Housing for everyone, locals and migrants together.


Solidarity with Migrants

title: Incekara: Determination of young people proves that resistance is possible
content:
Protests launched by high school students in Paris against poor educational conditions have had a domino effect, spreading across France and to other countries. What began as a protest over education has developed into broader opposition to the system, encompassing the rising cost of living, declining wages and the housing crisis. These developments have also drawn attention to Turkey, where exploitation and inequality are even more deeply entrenched. University students took to the streets in Istanbul on the anniversary of the establishment of the Council of Higher Education (YÖK), an institution created in the aftermath of the fascist military coup of September 12, 1980. Students protested against the government's increasingly repressive measures. Demonstrations in Beyazıt Square and Beşiktaş were particularly marked by anger over a directive issued by the Ministry of Interior concerning universities in September. Istanbul University student Yasin Incekara spoke to ANF and said, "The determination shown by young people during the March 19 protests demonstrated that it is possible to resist the repressive regime being established in Turkey and showed how these blockades can be broken."


'Young people face similar forms of repression worldwide'


Yasin Incekara, a second-year sociology student at Istanbul University, said that young people taking to the streets across Europe and other parts of the world reflected the problems they share. Incekara emphasized that although Europe is often portrayed as a prosperous society, young people there also struggle with poverty and the problems created by the capitalist system. He said, "Over the past few months, we have seen young people taking to the streets against poverty, the lack of a future and repressive policies, not only in the Middle East but also in Europe, which is presented as prosperous. The youth uprising that has emerged particularly in France shows that young people face similar forms of repression not only in Turkey but in many parts of the world."


'March 19 showed young people's determination to seek freedom'


Incekara said that although resistance in Turkey has been weaker than in other countries, the March 19 protests demonstrated how young people could break through the restrictions being imposed on them. He described the March 19 protests and subsequent developments as evidence of young people's determination to pursue freedom in the face of oppression. Incekara said, "Through their determination to demand freedom against oppression, young people demonstrated during the March 19 protests that it is possible to resist the repressive regime being established in Turkey and showed how these blockades can be broken."


'Repressive directives seek to label revolutionary students as terrorists'


Incekara said that the authorities had intensified repression through various mechanisms in response to the determination shown by young people in their struggle. He pointed to the 17-article directive sent to universities by the Ministry of Interior in September, which he described as fascist, as the latest example. He argued that the directive sought to label students involved in progressive and revolutionary activities at universities as "terrorists." Incekara said: "The directive explicitly refers to providing private security personnel at universities with training similar to that given to police officers, as well as intensifying efforts to recruit informants and pressure students into becoming collaborators. It also opens the way for officers from the Anti-Terrorism Branch to set up information stands at universities under the pretext of awareness-raising and preventive activities, allowing them to conduct intelligence operations. Through these stands, the police aim to criminalize students involved in political struggle in the eyes of newly enrolled students, portraying them as marginal groups associated with terrorism and manipulating newcomers with warnings to 'stay away from them.' Of course, this does not reflect reality. If there is any group seeking to spread terror today, it is the capitalist state and the police themselves."


'Families are also pressured to inform on their children'

title: MED TUHAD-FED: Son iki yılda 15 hasta mahpus yaşamını yitirdi
content:
MED Tutuklu ve Hükümlü Aileleri ile Hukuki ve Dayanışma Dernekleri Federasyonu (MED TUHAD-FED), son iki yılda cezaevlerinde 15 hasta mahpusun yaşamını yitirdiğini açıkladı. Federasyon, ağır hasta mahpusların sağlık durumlarına rağmen tahliye edilmediğini belirterek Adalet Bakanlığına çağrıda bulundu.


Hasta mahpus Tuncer Sağlam toprağa verildi


8 Kasım 2026


Mezopotamya Ajansının haberine göre, cezaevinde bulunduğu sırada ağır sağlık sorunları yaşayan ve tedavi gördüğü hastanede hayatını kaybeden Tuncer Sağlam'ın ardından federasyon temsilcileri cezaevlerindeki hak ihlallerini değerlendirdi.


MED TUHAD-FED Eşbaşkanı Kerem Canpolat ile yönetim kurulu üyeleri Mahsum Oruç ve Şafi Hayme, Barış ve Demokratik Toplum Süreci kapsamında cezaevlerindeki koşulların iyileştirilmesi ve hasta tutukluların tahliyesi için somut adımlar atılmasını istedi.


“Cezaevlerinde yüzlerce hasta mahpus var”


Federasyon Eşbaşkanı Kerem Canpolat, devam eden siyasi sürecin toplumda umut yarattığını ancak cezaevlerindeki koşullara olumlu bir etkisinin olmadığını söyledi.


Cezaevlerinde sağlık sorunları nedeniyle günlük ihtiyaçlarını tek başına karşılayamayan yüzlerce mahpus bulunduğunu belirten Canpolat, kanser ve kronik hastalıkları olan kişilerin uygun tedavi koşullarına erişemediğini ifade etti.


Canpolat, bazı mahpusların cezaevinde kalamayacaklarına ilişkin sağlık raporlarına rağmen tahliye edilmediklerini söyledi.


Cezaevlerinde hem adli hem de siyasi mahpusların hak ihlallerine maruz kaldığını söyleyen Canpolat, devletin tutukluların yaşamını ve sağlığını koruma yükümlülüğünü hatırlattı.


73 yaşındaki hasta tutuklu Abdullah Tırpan yaşamını yitirdi


26 Ekim 2026


“Her ölüm toplumdaki güveni zedeliyor”


Barış ve Demokratik Toplum Süreci'nin başlamasından bu yana cezaevlerinde 15 hasta mahpusun yaşamını yitirdiğini belirten Canpolat, sağlık hakkına erişim ve tahliye uygulamalarının yeniden düzenlenmesi gerektiğini söyledi.


Canpolat, cezaevlerindeki ölümlerin toplumsal güveni de olumsuz etkilediğini belirterek sürecin ilerleyebilmesi için devletin somut adımlar atması gerektiğini ifade etti.


Avrupa İnsan Hakları Mahkemesi (AİHM) kararlarının uygulanmamasını da eleştiren Canpolat, hasta tutukluların tedavilerinin cezaevi dışında, ailelerinin yanında sürdürülmesini talep etti.


İzmir Barosu, hasta mahpus Yıldırım'ı ziyaret etti: "Zamana yayılmış idam cezası"


27 Ağustos 2026


“400 ila 500 ağır hasta mahpus bulunuyor”


MED TUHAD-FED Yönetim Kurulu Üyesi Mahsum Oruç, cezaevlerinde 400 ila 500 arasında ağır hasta tutuklu bulunduğunu belirtti.


Oruç, sağlık sorunları nedeniyle cezaevinde kalamayacak durumda olan kişilerin tahliyesinin çeşitli idari ve hukuki uygulamalarla engellendiğini söyledi.


Yaklaşık dört ay önce TBMM'de kabul edilen yasal düzenlemeye işaret eden Oruç, düzenlemenin uygulanmasının çeşitli kurulların değerlendirmelerine bağlı tutulduğunu ve bu nedenle tahliyelerin gerçekleşmediğini söyledi.


Oruç, söz konusu düzenlemenin etkili biçimde uygulanması halinde Tuncer Sağlam'ın yaşamını yitirmemiş olabileceğini ifade etti.


Tuncer Sağlam'ın ölümü


Federasyon temsilcileri, Tuncer Sağlam'ın sağlık durumunun ağır olmasına rağmen tahliye edilmediğini belirtti.


Sağlam'ın avukatı tarafından 23 Eylül'de yapılan tahliye başvurusunda, vücudunda 10 santimetrelik kitle bulunduğu, damar invazyonu ve olası metastaz bulgularının tespit edildiği aktarıldı. Sağlam, 7 Kasım'da tedavi gördüğü hastanede yaşamını yitirdi.


Mahsum Oruç, Sağlam'ın yaklaşık iki yıldır cezaevinde bulunduğunu ve sağlık durumunun yetkililer tarafından bilindiğini belirterek gerekli tedavinin sağlanmadığını savundu.


TAHLİYESİ ÜÇÜNCÜ KEZ ERTELENDİ


Hasta mahpus Mehmet Sait Yıldırım kalp krizi geçirdi


25 Ağustos 2026


“Tahliyeler için mekanizmalar oluşturulmalı”


MED TUHAD-FED Yönetim Kurulu Üyesi Şafi Hayme de hasta mahpusların tahliyesi için gerekli mekanizmaların kısa sürede oluşturulabileceğini söyledi.

author: anred
title: ¿Qué pasó en Guernica?, el gobierno de Alberto y la represión a la última ola de tomas de tierras
content:
Sergio Berni, entonces ministro de Seguridad bonaerense, se jactaba de desalojar cinco tomas de tierra por semana. Era plena pandemia, cientos de miles de familias que no podían pagar alquileres o vivían hacinadas buscaron una salida en la ocupación de terrenos. Ocurría la última gran ola de “tomas de tierras” durante el gobierno de Alberto Fernández que terminó marcada por la represión, las promesas incumplidas y el abandono. Guernica se convirtió en el caso visible y emblemático de aquella crisis: la organización de más de 2 mil familias en tierras “compradas” en dictadura destinadas a un country, la resistencia al desalojo y la exposición mediática obligaron al gobierno provincial a abrir una negociación que estuvo atravesada por titubeos, dilaciones y propuestas que no resolvían el problema habitacional. Por ANRed | Imagen: German Romeo Pena


Primero es necesario contar que la “ocupación de tierras “ tras la dictadura fue una modalidad habitual de las clases trabajadoras más empobrecidas para adquirir sus viviendas ante la sucesiva falta de respuesta habitacional que dieron las democracias posteriores, es decir ni el Estado y menos el mercado resolvieron la crisis habitacional. Para aquel entonces los últimos datos eran delCenso Nacional de 2010, el déficit habitacional alcanzaba 3,5 millones de vivienda entre ellas 1,3 millones de viviendas faltantes y 2,2 millones de viviendas que no proveían  las condiciones mínimas para mantener un nivel de vida digno. 9 millones de personas que eran inquilinos, cifras que actualmente se han agravado en el último censo del 2022.


Luego el desenlace del conflicto en Guernica, disputa que estuvo atravesado por la crisis política y económica que sacudía al gobierno de Alberto Fernández. En septiembre de 2020, la disparada de los dólares paralelos, la presión empresaria y la preocupación oficial por la inestabilidad económica habilitaron una ofensiva política contra las tomas de tierras. Sergio Massa, junto con la intendenta de Presidente Perón, Blanca Cantero, impulsaron una posición de endurecimiento frente a las ocupaciones. Cantero convocó a intendentes del conurbano que reclamaban una respuesta judicial y policial, mientras se consolidaba un bloque político que exigía terminar con la toma y enviar una señal contra nuevas recuperaciones. Guernica comenzaba a ser presentada como un antecedente peligroso que debía clausurarse para evitar que se multiplicara.


14 intendentes piden desalojar tomas de tierras y Berni se publicita defendiendo la «propiedad privada»


La tensión se agravó en octubre con la ocupación de la estancia Casa Nueva, perteneciente a la familia Etchevehere, en Entre Ríos. La iniciativa fue impulsada por Dolores Etchevehere junto al Proyecto Artigas, con el acompañamiento de Juan Grabois y militantes vinculados del Movimiento de Trabajadores Excluidos (MTE), que proponía desarrollar un proyecto agroecológico en esas tierras. La reacción de empresarios y la derecha política que venía presionando por desalojar Guernica reaccionó de inmediato: el conflicto se convirtió en una bandera contra las recuperaciones de tierras y en una supuesta amenaza generalizada a la propiedad privada. La disputa con los Etchevehere intensificó la presión política y mediática sobre el gobierno nacional. Dentro del Frente de Todos también se profundizaron las diferencias: mientras un sector intentaba sostener la negociación y encontrar una salida habitacional, Massa, Berni y los intendentes reclamaban hacer cumplir la orden judicial. Las negociaciones impulsadas inicialmente desde Nación, con participación de funcionarios vinculados al Movimiento Evita, contemplaron una posible relocalización colectiva, pero naufragaron en medio de las disputas internas entre el Movimiento Evita y La Cámpora. Desde septiembre, Andrés Larroque quedó al frente de las conversaciones provinciales, cada vez más condicionadas por la presión judicial y política.


Finalmente, el 28 de octubre, cuando todavía se discutía una última prórroga y existían conversaciones para evitar una intervención violenta, la Justicia rechazó el pedido de postergación y la gobernación cancelo las negociaciones inventando justificaciones. En la madrugada del 29, unos 4.000 efectivos de la Policía Bonaerense.. La decisión terminó imponiendo la línea de Berni y de los intendentes: el desalojo como respuesta disciplinadora frente a las recuperaciones de tierras, antes que una solución de fondo a la emergencia habitacional. title: „So kann man nicht mehr leben“: Auch in Portugal wird gegen steigende Lebenshaltungskosten und Wohnungsnot protestiert
content:
Dossier


„

Seit Jahren werden wir durch steigende Immobilienpreise und Lebenshaltungskosten ausgebeutet. Wir arbeiten uns zu Tode und rackern uns ab, um mit unserem Gehalt bis zum Monatsende durchzukommen, die steigenden Kraftstoffpreise und die Grundausgaben zu bewältigen und unsere Wohnung nicht zu verlieren. Uns bleiben nur Schulden und Sorgen, während die Aussicht auf eine bessere Zukunft schwindet.

Coimbra bleibt nicht außen vor! Wir rufen alle dazu auf, sich am kommenden *Mittwoch (14.) ab 17:30 Uhr auf der Praça da República* zu einer Malaktion sowie zum Anbringen eines Transparents und anderer Materialien zu versammeln

.“ portug.

Aufruf zur Demo am 10. Oktober


 der Instagram-Plattform „Não dá mais para viver assim“ („So kann man nicht mehr leben“) und mehr dazu:


In Portugal schließen sich die Kämpfe gegen Lebenshaltungskosten und für öffentliche Infrastuktur zusammen – ein Generalstreik spätestens am 24. November nicht ausgeschlossen 


Portugal: Nach der gewaltsamen Räumung kämpfen neue Protestlager gegen Wohnungsnot und Mietengesetz in Lissabon und Porto auch fürs Demonstrationsrecht


Wohnungskrise in Portugal: Protestcamp oder Weihnachtsmarkt?


„

In Portugal hat die Aktivistin Renata Cambra vor Gericht einen symbolischen Sieg errungen: Ihr Zelt auf einem zentralen Platz in Lissabon darf aufgebaut bleiben. Aber genau dort soll bald der Weihnachtsmarkt stehen. Sie ist zur Symbolfigur der Proteste gegen die Wohnungskrise in Portugal geworden. Die Aktivistin Renata Cambra verbucht einen juristischen Erfolg, denn ihr Zelt auf der Praça do Rossio in Lissabon darf aufgebaut bleiben. Genug Solidarität für ein neues Protestlager gab es zunächst aber nicht. Das Gericht entschied, ihr Zelt sei keine illegale Besetzung des öffentlichen Raums, sondern ein symbolisches Element des Protests. Die Entscheidung beschränkte die Erlaubnis jedoch auf die Demonstrantin, die den Antrag gestellt hat. author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Indigenous youth, Elders join national protests against Bill C-39 at Prime Minister’s Office
content:
Indigenous youth, Elders, environmental organizations and labour leaders rallied outside the Prime Minister’s Office Thursday as part of a national day of action against Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act.


Opponents say the legislation would override Treaty rights, weaken environmental laws and expand Cabinet power to fast-track major projects.


Hand-drummers from the Ottawa River Singers opened the demonstration. 


Speakers warned the omnibus bill would give the government broad new authority to designate “regions of national interest,” suspend or amend key environmental protections, and override the inherent, Treaty and constitutionally protected rights of First Nations.


Dara Wawatie-Chabot, an Indigenous youth speaker, told the crowd the legislation threatens protections across the board.


Dara Wawatie-Chabot at a rally outside the Prime Minister’s Office on a day of action against Bill C-39 on Nov. 12, 2026. Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.


“Bill C-39 would go right through any type of protections, whether it is environmental protections, labour protections or Indigenous rights,” she said. “They are just going to be completely bypassing all of that in order to get access to resources that are going to just make things worse for everybody on this planet.”


Introduced in September, Bill C-39 expands powers created under last year’s Building Canada Act. It would allow Cabinet to designate “regions of national interest” where certain projects — including pipelines, energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks and industrial developments — could be pre-approved or accelerated under a one-year decision timeline.


It’s really not shocking,” she said. “What Mark Carney represents is this legacy of Canadian settler violence and resource extraction, to be honest.”


Prime Mark Carney in effigy huggling a gas container at a rally held outside the Prime Minister’s Office on a national day of action against Bill C-39. Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.


Approximately 100 protesters attended the protest carry signs that read “seniors for climate action now” and “open up your hearts and listen to the people.” Eventually, a teenager came out imitating Prime Minister Mark Carney. The character had many different props that he pulled out from a box titled “Liberal Priorities.” 


The Carney character eventually pulled out and hugged a red gas container while simultaneously stomping on a stuffed fox and orca. 

The Carney character, who used a paper mache mask, was “dragged over to the Senate” to continue the demonstration. 


Elder Naanii Rose Lockyer delivered a direct message to the government.


“Stop the destruction. We’re at a point in time where if we keep on going in the direction we’re going, we can’t turn back,” she said. “They cannot predict what’s coming. And their fear-based response is to amp up surveillance and control of the masses. They’re pushing people over the edge. You have to look at the poverty crisis, the hunger crisis that all people are facing now. It’s not just First Peoples that are being offered up. The poor are on the chopping block as well. We have how many homeless people? It’s crazy.”


“They’ve tried assimilation, that didn’t work. They’ve tried colonization that was moderately successful. He [Carney] basically declared war on all of us, not first peoples but all people. This Mother Earth supports us all, and that’s what people are trying to protect today.”


Naanii Rose Lockyer outside the Prime Minister’s Office on a day of action against Bill C-39 on (Nov. 12, 2026). Photo: Mark Blackburn/APTN.


Her message to the Carney government on Bill C-39 was concise: “Hear the people. Lead with your heart, not your wallet.”


What the bill would do


Critics say C-39 would enable ministers to set aside or amend conditions under the Species at Risk Act, the Fisheries Act and other environmental laws if they are judged too financially or practically challenging. It also strengthens the federal government’s ability to end legal strikes.


The Assembly of First Nations, the Chiefs of Ontario, the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations, the Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador and Nishnawbe Aski Nation have all rejected the bill, arguing it subordinates the honour of the Crown and free, prior and informed consent to commercial timelines.

title: Protests in several cities: Guarantee the right to life of ill prisoners
content:
Human rights organizations and political initiatives have protested in several cities across Turkey and Northern Kurdistan against ongoing human rights violations in Turkish prisons. The demonstrations highlighted demands for medical care for prisoners with health conditions, the release of seriously ill inmates and an investigation into the death of Tuncer Sağlam, who died at Sincan Prison in Ankara on November 7. Protests demanding the release of ill prisoners had already taken place in several cities the previous day.


The organizations also called for an end to the obstruction of medical treatment and the implementation of legal measures adopted as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.


Izmir: Criticism of delayed releases


Outside the courthouse in the Bayraklı district of Izmir, Ayfer Yıldırım, Co-Chair of EGE TUHAYDER (Association for Solidarity and Cooperation with Families of Prisoners and Convicts in the Aegean Region), stated that Tuncer Sağlam had not received adequate medical treatment despite suspected pancreatic cancer. Because no definitive diagnosis was established, he was not released, Yıldırım said and called for an investigation into the responsibility of the prison administration, judicial authorities and healthcare institutions involved.


She also drew attention to the situation of other ill prisoners: Pınar Tikin, who has an arachnoid cyst in her brain and saw her release postponed for the second time, and Evin Zapsu, who had to undergo a biopsy due to suspected cancer. Yıldırım called for the release of both women and criticized the continued imprisonment of seriously ill people as incompatible with the objectives of the peace process.


DEM Party MP Ibrahim Akın criticized the fact that the framework law, adopted nearly four months ago, had still not been implemented. He called for the legal provisions to be applied and court rulings to be enforced.


Call for an investigation into the death of Tuncer Sağlam


The death of Tuncer Sağlam was also the focus of a public statement in Muş. Barış Kılıç, Co-Spokesperson of TUHAY-DER, called for an investigation into possible failures that may have led to Sağlam’s death. He also demanded that Evin Zapsu be provided with adequate medical treatment and released, along with other seriously ill prisoners.


In Adıyaman, members of the Democratic Institutions Platform gathered outside the prison. They called for the removal of legal and administrative obstacles preventing the release of seriously ill prisoners. DEM Party MP Ali Bozan made serious allegations against those responsible. He stated that Sağlam’s death was not merely the result of negligence but should be regarded as a killing. Bozan called on the government to release seriously ill prisoners immediately.


Further protests in Urfa and Iğdır


In Urfa, TUHAY-DER organized another protest. In Iğdır, the DEM Party and the Free Women’s Movement (TJA) took to the streets together. The participants demanded effective guarantees for ill prisoners’ right to life and access to medical care. They also called for a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding Tuncer Sağlam’s death and the removal of legal and administrative obstacles to the release of seriously ill prisoners.,

author: Andrea DiP
title: Protestos de jovens pelo mundo demonstram que ainda se pode sonhar com o futuro
content:
Uma onda de protestos liderados pela Geração Z está se levantando pelo mundo, trazendo uma lufada de ar fresco e remodelando cenários políticos. 


Nós vimos isso

no Brasil com os atos encabeçados por movimentos estudantis que puxaram milhares de pessoas para as ruas e atuaram fortemente nas redes pela democracia e pela reeleição de Lula.


Na Itália, as jornadas estudantis pedem mais verbas para a educação pública

, melhorias em infraestrutura escolar e medidas contra o altíssimo custo de aluguéis e moradias estudantis.

Na França, protestos que começaram em setembro também por demandas de melhor educação, melhor infraestrutura nas escolas e mais investimento, têm se intensificado e tomado as ruas de todo o país

 –  só no último dia 05, reuniram cerca de 600 mil pessoas, segundo números oficiais.

Na Alemanha, o movimento Gen Z Regelt (Algo como “A Geração Z Resolve”) realizou atos em 34 cidades para protestar contra o serviço militar obrigatório e exigir mais investimentos em educação

, e no dia 31 de outubro botou nas ruas cerca de 120 mil pessoas.


Na Índia, o movimento Partido do Povo Barata (CJP, na sigla em inglês para


Cockroach Janta Party

) também tem levado milhares de jovens às ruas de Mumbai e Nova Deli para denunciar irregularidades na educação

, pedir a saída do ministro da Educação, Dharmendra Pradhan, e uma reforma no sistema de exames. O CJP é um movimento político liderado pela Geração Z indiana que surgiu a partir de declarações feitas em maio pelo presidente do Supremo Tribunal da Índia, que usou o termo “barata” para descrever jovens desempregados que se dedicam ao ativismo.


Os protestos movidos pelos GenZ – nascidos entre 1997 e 2012 – geralmente levantam pautas relacionadas à educação, mas também pedem a cabeça de líderes autoritários, atenção à emergência climática, às desigualdades sociais e abordam conflitos como o Genocídio em Gaza. São campanhas horizontais, sem um líder específico, e que usam as redes sociais para se organizar.


A repressão também tem sido violenta. Não é possível dizer o número certo de prisões porque os atos seguem acontecendo, mas estima-se que mais de 6 mil pessoas foram presas somente na França, sendo 87% delas menores de idade.


Em uma

análise recente, a Civicus,

 organização sem fins lucrativos que monitora as liberdades civis globais, afirmou:

“Como questionam a distribuição do poder econômico e político, os protestos liderados pela geração Z invariavelmente são recebidos com violência estatal”.

 O relatório relaciona a violência infligida aos jovens manifestantes com seu foco em sistemas e instituições que há muito tempo estavam simplesmente sendo aceitos.


Protestos liderados por movimentos estudantis não são novidade, claro. Mas o que torna essa nova onda interessante é o momento em que ela se levanta. 


Em um mundo que tem sido assolado por governos autoritários e populistas que fazem conchavos com Big Techs para intermediar todas as relações humanas e interferir na soberania de países, que incentivam o ódio, a misoginia, criam e alimentam um ambiente tóxico e violento para mulheres e LGBTQIA+, em um momento de múltiplas instabilidades, guerras e crises – climáticas, econômicas, institucionais, crises que desafiam o que entendemos por democracia e como víamos a política institucional e crises que atingem em cheio o modelo capitalista neoliberal que nos engole com seu ultra individualismo –

os jovens vêm cobrar o que nunca lhes foi prometido. Eles vêm dizer que querem eles mesmos criar futuro. 


Pode parecer óbvio, mas não é.


Porque a essa geração foi oferecido pouco espaço para utopia, pouca imaginação de futuro, pouco encantamento.

 Para usar o termo que Paolo Demuru cunha em seu livro “Políticas do Encanto”: pouca perspectiva. Afinal, vivemos muitos pontos de não retorno. 


Ao mesmo tempo, o futuro baseado em um passado fantasioso prometido pela extrema direita, em que a emergência climática é mentira, que diz que é só expulsar imigrante que o emprego vem e a economia melhora, ou, na sua versão tecno-solucionista, que a IA resolveria todos os males do planeta, simplesmente não está acontecendo.


É nesse vácuo que

a Geração Z ocupa as ruas, recusa tanto o passado inventado da extrema direita quanto o futuro tecno-solucionista das Big Techs, e reivindica o direito de imaginar. 


Bonito ver esses jovens devolverem à política algo que parecia perdido: a ideia de que o futuro ainda está em disputa e que dá para construí-lo …

author: Assembly in memory of Kyriakos Xymitiris and in solidarity with the persecuted of the Ambelokipi case
title: To the second anniversary of the death of our comrade Kyriakos Xymitiris
content:
[german below]
On 31 October 2024, two years ago, the anarchist Kyriakos Xymitiris lost his life. We want to keep remembering him and therefore publicly commemorated this anniversary together in front of NY/ Bethanien, here in Berlin, where he was active for many years.


Kyriakos died as an armed guerrilla fighter. During his years in Germany from 2015 to 2021 he was first and foremost a sociable and politically active Berliner. Soon after his arrival, he became part of the anarchist movement and initially contributed to grassroots struggles against the state and capital. Before long, he became fully involved in the local militant movement and was a familiar face at events, demonstrations and struggles on the streets.


In 2021, he returned to Athens, where he was born and raised. There, he continued what he had begun in Berlin, following his imaginative and cheerful path towards a struggle in which personal risk becomes secondary to the importance of the goal. In this context, it is understandable that his political analysis, the many street battles and the violent repression eventually led him to the decision to take up arms and familiarise himself with explosives. Looking at the history of the movement, particularly the more recent Greek movement, this decision was by no means purely individual, as many people before him had already chosen armed struggle, and many after him will do so as well.


On 31 October 2024, tragedy struck. An explosive charge that Kyriakos was handling detonated in his hands and killed him.


“Kyriakos Xymitiris, one of us!” is a slogan that has been shouted in many places around the world since that day. Today, Kyriakos‘ name stands for the continuity of struggles for freedom, even in places conceived as the peaceful hinterland of white imperialism. Kyriakos fell on the margins of Europe during a period of upheaval, in which war and genocide are openly and controversially discussed here. His decision not only to participate in the discourse but instead to sharpen the sword is remarkable. But it is also challenging. Challenging for those in power, who constantly declare resistance dead. But also, and much more importantly, challenging for the oppressed, who find themselves stumbling in the dark along the endless paths of their search for solidarity.


As the assembly in memory of Kyriakos Xymitiris, which organised the gathering on October 31, we find ourselves, two years after the difficult loss of a valued comrade for many of us, facing the question of how we want to remember Kyriakos in the future. What significance do his decisions and his death hold for the movement here in Berlin?


These are questions that must be answered by that part of society which wants to overthrow the system and build a free and solidaristic life in its place. We were not many here in the commemoration, but the protests and riots, conscientious objection to military service, strikes and sabotage spreading across the world show that the struggle continues. In the demonstrations which took place alongside our gathering, the flame of action and the warmth of solidarity, for which Kyriakos fought for many years here in Berlin, continue to live on. In every emerging revolt, in everyday acts of resistance and in every uprising that will hopefully soon take place in Berlin again, Kyriakos himself lives on.


Perhaps the memory of Kyriakos will help the new movement prepare itself for the system’s counterattacks. Perhaps his example will contribute to arming both thoughts and actions in such a way that temporary uprisings become a permanent condition, in which the armed force of the state is pushed back further and further, and the warmongers and exploiters can no longer live without fear.


On this second anniversary, we contributed to preserving Kyriakos‘ memory by gathering in a place that holds significance for grassroots struggles in Berlin. Kyriakos himself attended many meetings at NewYorck, and this place was also a regular starting point for him to head out into the streets of Kreuzberg.


Also, NewYorck is connected to our comrade Nicole, who lived and was active there until her death in 2023, as well as to our comrade Devran, who lived and was active on Adalbertstraße until her death in 2025. Both were militant figures whose stories intersected with Kyriakos’s for several years.

title: Two political prisoners released after decades of imprisonment
content:
Political prisoners Aydın Kudat and Zübeyir Idem have been released from Turkish prisons after serving 34 and 30 years, respectively. In both cases, the responsible Administrative and Observation Boards had repeatedly blocked their release despite the completion of their regular prison terms.


Aydın Kudat released after 34 years


Aydın Kudat was released from the T-type prison in Karabük on Wednesday and was welcomed by his family outside the facility. He was arrested in 1992 in the Bismil district of Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) and subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment by the then State Security Court (DGM).


His release was originally scheduled for September 6, 2022. However, the responsible prison board denied his release a total of six times. The stated reason was Kudat’s refusal to sign the so-called declaration of remorse demanded by the prison administration.


The long-term prisoner was finally able to leave prison following a new decision by the board. He was scheduled to return to Amed on Wednesday evening on a flight via Istanbul.


Zübeyir Idem released after two postponements


Zübeyir Idem has also regained his freedom after 30 years in prison. He was released from the prison in Espiye, Giresun province, after the responsible Administrative and Observation Board approved his release.


Idem had already completed his 30-year prison term on June 2, 2026. Nevertheless, two separate decisions by the board postponed his release by three months each.


Following his release, Idem was welcomed by family members. He then traveled to Adana to visit the graves of his mother and father, both of whom had died during his decades of imprisonment.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Newest report from correctional investigator says 10 year review of prison life shows little has changed
content:
The newest report from Canada’s federal prison watchdog says that despite 49 recommendations over 10 years, there has been “an absence of progress” in reducing the over-incarceration of Indigenous Peoples.


Valerie Phillips, who was the interim head of the

Office of the Correctional Investigator (OCI)

, wrote that findings indicated Correctional Services Canada (CSC) “remains predominantly risk-averse, security-driven, and institution-centred, with Indigenous-specific initiatives operating at the margins rather than as core system functions.”


“The central finding of this report is clear and consistent. A persistent gap remains between policy commitments and what is experienced on the ground,” she wrote. “This gap is the defining challenge of federal corrections.”


The OCI acts as a watchdog for the federal corrections system, taking complaints from prisoners and prison workers and visiting prisons to assess living conditions and trends, such as the over-incarceration of Indigenous Peoples.


Every year, the office releases an annual report which summarizes findings from the last year, paired with recommendations for Corrections Service Canada (CSC) to help address issues or gaps.


Phillips released the 2025-2026 annual report on Oct. 26, the first since former correctional investigator Ivan Zinger took his retirement in February.


This time, she wrote her report based on findings from the last decade.


In the

206-page document,

 she concluded that there is no behind-bars support that can replace community-based alternatives.


Indigenous Peoples remain over-represented throughout the entire legal system because of a lack of community-based supports, as well as risk assessment tools which advocates believe are rooted in outdated, colonial practices.


Sen. Kim Pate said she found the report “disheartening.”


“The situation keeps getting worse because we need the courage and the conviction to actually recognize that what has happened for decades has been not only ineffective, it’s been damaging and has made people who already have significant past trauma and histories of abuse in situations of more risk of not having their needs met,” she told APTN News.


“And until we do that and until we address those in the community and provide support to folks to have those, have their needs met, we will continue to see more of the same.”


Nicole Kief, the executive director of

Prisoners’ Legal Services (PLS)

, had a similar reaction and said the report didn’t “surprise her at all.”


PLS is a clinic operated by the Vancouver-based West Coast Justice Society, which offers prison-related legal aid to Indigenous and non-Indigenous clients.


“As I’m reading through these reports, I just find myself nodding and nodding and nodding and nodding, because this is all consistent with what we see in our own work,” Kief said.


From the perspective of an advocate who sees the barriers faced by people in incarceration on the day-to-day, she said what is often the biggest challenge is the “gap between policy and practice.


“That’s what stands out to me,” she said.


Sen. Kim Pate reads a letter from an incarcerated person in her Ottawa office in 2023. She said the 2025-2026 annual report from the OCI was “disheartening.” Photo: APTN File.


In the report’s section on Indigenous corrections, Phillips wrote that there have been gains when it comes to corrections officers being more culturally informed with the help of increased training introduced as recently as the fall of 2025.


For example, a higher number of Indigenous Peoples in incarceration had access to cultural resources because corrections officers were better equipped to recognize and place people in programs at an earlier stage than before.


For example, that year, 37 per cent of high-risk Indigenous offenders participated in the

Pathways initiative

, an Elder-driven cultural healing program for those preparing to transfer to a lower security facility.


In the 2022-2023 fiscal year, fewer than 10 per cent of Indigenous offenders accessed the program, which means there was almost a 30 per cent jump in two years.


However, the progress is undermined by risk assessment tools and written legislation that isn’t being changed, she continued.


In 2025-2026, the Pathways program only increased capacity from 350 to 366 people at one time, nationally, and 76 people “remained waitlisted despite operating at approximately 86 per cent capacity,” Phillips wrote.


The …

title: ICE’s Own Investigations Reveal Deaths in Custody Caused by Medical Neglect
content:
Internal ICE investigations have found that 23 individuals died in 2025 after a lack of proper medical care.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The San Francisco Chronicle has obtained internal ICE investigations into the deaths of dozens of people in its custody during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term, finding that 23 of the 29 individuals died after a lack of proper medical care.

Guards, medical providers, and staff at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities failed to provide emergency care, failed to send individuals to the emergency room, or ignored other critical warning signs, the report indicates. According to ICE’s own investigations, deficient medical care directly contributed to 20 of 23 of the deaths. The six other individuals who died in 2025 had received care within sufficient limits, the agency claims.

The Chronicle acquired the reports through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request. The findings contradict the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)’s claim that its immigration jails provide “timely and appropriate medical care” and that “the medical care in ICE detention is the best care” that many immigrants “have received in their entire lives.”

The Chronicle previously reported on 48 deaths in ICE custody since Trump’s second term began, finding that delayed medical care and failure to provide critical care contributed to 17 of these deaths and that there was not enough information on at least 15 cases. This report, from April, came before the outlet obtained ICE’s own investigations into the 2025 deaths, which reported an even larger number directly caused by medical neglect.

At least 62 people have died in ICE custody since the start of Trump’s second term, more than double the amount of deaths from the first Trump administration and the highest rate in over a decade.

ICE has not investigated all of the deaths caused by the agency and its immigration jails. For example, Prisciliano Trejo Ricano died shortly after ICE released him from custody while he was in a coma; his name has not been counted among those who died in custody after the agency changed its policy in June to no longer report and investigate deaths of individuals who died within 30 days of release. Similarly, at least two disabled people died in 2026 shortly after ICE released them into freezing weather, and were not counted among ICE’s official death count.

In the second half of October alone, three people died in ICE detention: Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old permanent resident from Mexico who died on October 17 at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas, whose family reported that he was denied medication and care; Luis Sandoval, a 48-year-old Salvadoran who died on October 23 in ICE detention in Georgia and, according to DHS, died by suicide; and Roberto Jimenez Gutierrez, a 43-year-old Guatemalan who was found unresponsive on October 24.

In some cases, prison staff mocked individuals who called for help and who later died after their neglect. In others — like the deaths at Camp East Montana in Texas, which have been referred to as suicides — conditions included medical neglect, solitary confinement, and physical and sexual violence.

People imprisoned inside ICE jails have launched hunger strikes in protest of the conditions inside, including medical neglect and unlawful, prolonged detention. In May, over 300 detained people launched a hunger and labor strike at New Jersey’s Delaney Hall, which lasted approximately a month and brought national attention to conditions in immigration jails. In September, immigrants being detained at the El Valle Detention Facility in Texas launched a hunger strike; and in October, at least 73 people launched a hunger strike at a processing center in Georgia. Other hunger strikes have been reported in immigration jails in Pennsylvania, Michigan, California, and Washington — with one immigration jail in Tacoma, Washington, witnessing at least 20 hunger strikes in 2026.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share …

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: a10 – Solidarity is how we win  – Slingshot talks with a Stop Cop City RICO 61 defendant on resisting political repression
content:
In December 2025, the racketeering charges brought against 61 people indicted as co-conspirators in the Stop Cop City movement were dismissed as procedurally invalid. This marked a major victory for the movement and the co-defendants’ collective defense strategy. It might go without saying, but I’ll say it anyway: we do not always lose these big repression cases, and it is important that we emphasize the wins just as loudly as we decry justice denied. Moreover, talking openly about people’s experiences with criminalization and working together to craft collective strategies rooted in solidarity can help us feel less afraid in the face of legal repression. Backing down is not an option, so how do we contend with the terrain we must navigate to keep fighting?

With this in mind, two members of Slingshot Collective (Sirkka and Antonio) talked with Hannah Kass: a former defendant in several prosecutions of Stop Cop City activists on RICO and arson charges.

Note: this interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Slingshot: To get us started, could you give us some background on the Stop Cop City RICO case and its outcomes?

Hannah: Yeah for sure. Over the course of the struggle to stop Cop City there were a number of arrests on different charges, starting from babypants criminal trespassing charges but then escalating to a point where people started getting felony domestic terrorism charges just from being at protests in proximity to property destruction; just for being in the forest and being part of this forest occupation, allegedly. There were other arrests that weren’t domestic terrorism charges though too. They raided the bail fund – the Atlanta Solidarity Fund – and charged them with baseless financial crimes like charity fraud and money laundering. Then, you know, they picked up people who were doing basic first amendment activities like passing out flyers naming the officers who murdered Tortuguita, and charging them with felony intimidation.

After all these separate arrests, all of us were then rounded up in this giant RICO (Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations) case of 61 people, basically alleging that this movement to stop Cop City and defend the Welaunee Forest, if you’re a part of it, then you’re part of a terrorist criminal organization and conspiracy. It basically uses the fundamental tenets of how social movements work, you know: resource mobilization, social coordination, relationships, etc., against us. And using conspiracy law, specifically RICO, to criminalize being part of a protest or a social movement had such a devastating effect on the movement.

Slingshot: Could you say more on that, why do you think the RICO case had the effect it did?

Hannah: Sure. Of course, there were actions that happened after the RICO indictment. Some effective ones too: in November 2023 like 12 Ernst concrete trucks got burned and they dropped their contract right away, and they were pouring concrete for Cop City. So it definitely wasn’t a sudden like “oh man, we’re RICO’d, game over” but the RICO case sucked energy out of the movement, and it also produced fear and trauma in people. I mean, I’m still dealing with that trauma to this day, and I know a lot of other people are. And not just the emotional trauma but the way that it impacts your life to be labeled a domestic terrorist or to be in a RICO case, you know that’s basically being labeled as a terrorist organization, it’s really hard to get a job, and get housing. It’s hard to participate in society, this kind of repression is designed to produce social death for anyone who resists the expansion of a police state, essentially. Or whatever other monstrosity they’re trying to push through.

Slingshot: How do we push back against this? We would love to hear your reflections on the state of political repression in the U.S. right now more broadly, and what this means for continued resistance and movement strategy. What do we need to be thinking about as we face the escalation of domestic “lawfare” against political movements?

Hannah: Yeah, I think lawfare is a great way of putting it. I’ve been thinking a lot about lawfare with regard to these prosecutions, and also how we’ve beaten them back. So first with the question of where the case is today and where we’re going: The RICO case was dragged out for two years but it was ultimately dismissed on a technicality. Now it is on appeal, but chances are good that the appeal will also be dismissed because …

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Peasant organizer persists despite surveillance
content:
Jesus Monasterial. (Photo from Photo from Tanggol Magsasaka-TK)

Repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety.

When he was a university student, he questioned the purpose of agricultural education. Now he is organizing landless farmers and fisherfolk.

Jesus Monasterial has spent more than two years working with rural communities in Southern Tagalog. However, his work resulted in repeated surveillance by state forces, peasant groups said.

On October 31, Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan reported that a police intelligence operative identified as “Bruno” had been asking about Monasterial’s whereabouts in Lian, Batangas. The operative was reportedly previously assigned in Nasugbu.

At the time, Monasterial was assisting a protest camp in Barangay San Diego, where farmers, fisherfolk, and residents opposed the possible demolition of several houses.

“I was on my way back to the people’s protest camp in San Diego when news reached us that someone had been asking about my personal information,” he said.

The camp was established by Samahang Mangangawil 1979 and the San Diego Homeowners’ Association, with support from the Katipunan ng mga Samahang Magbubukid sa Timog Katagalugan (KASAMA-TK) and Pambansang Lakas ng Kilusang Mamamalakaya ng Pilipinas–Timog Katagalugan (PAMALAKAYA-TK).

The incident prompted fellow organizers to discuss security measures. They also plan to file a complaint before the Commission on Human Rights (CHR).

Monasterial’s involvement in peasant organizing began at the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) where he was enrolled in BS Agricultural Biotechnology.

Coming from a family of farmers in Bicol, where his grandparents worked as agricultural tenants, he became increasingly critical of an agricultural education system that he said served the interests of transnational corporations rather than addressing farmers’ lack of land and government support.

Through the League of Filipino Students–UPLB, he became involved in social issues action and joined community immersions with farmers in Tartaria, Silang, Cavite, as well as Mangyan communities in Mindoro and Dumagat communities in Rizal.

These experiences led him to leave his studies and become a full-time organizer. He now serves as deputy secretary-general of KASAMA-TK.

His work involves staying in communities, conducting consultations and political education, and helping establish local farmers and fisherfolk associations.

“Being a full-time organizer means devoting my entire time to the communities and being far from my loved ones,” he said, adding that he had to set aside his plan to finish college.

The October 31 incident was not the first reported surveillance involving Monasterial.

On July 19, 2026, soldiers from the 16th Infantry Battalion of the Philippine Army reportedly sought to identify the organizers of KASAMA-TK’s Regional Peasant Consultation in Barangay Malinis, Lemery, Batangas.

On September 21, a man introducing himself as “Del” Dela Cruz reportedly approached a member of Sugarfolks’ Unity for Genuine Agricultural Reform (SUGAR-Batangas), attempting to persuade the member to leave the organization and provide information about its activities.

According to Tanggol Magsasaka–Timog Katagalugan, the man showed footage of a protest outside the Department of Agriculture regional office led by the Alyansa ng Magsasaka para sa Kumpensasyon (AMK), SUGAR-Batangas, KAISAHAN, and KASAMA-TK. He allegedly warned the member against working with Monasterial, claiming that the organizer was “already drawing attention.”

The protest resulted in a dialogue with government representatives to demand agricultural inputs and implements for farmers and farmworkers affected by successive calamities.

The groups also cited previous incidents in Barangay Casile, Laguna; Lupang Ramos and Tartaria, Cavite; and Coron, Palawan.

Monasterial said that the repeated surveillance restricted his movements and caused anxiety over his family’s safety. “Repeated surveillance limits my movements as an organizer and makes me fear returning home to my family because they might also be targeted by the state due to my advocacy.”

Despite the threats, Monasterial said that his work remains rooted in the struggles of farmers and farmworkers.

In Batangas, he witnessed sugarcane cutters and loaders receiving only P350 to P400 for every ton of cane harvested and loaded onto trucks. Their wages are paid at the …

George Sand

Pour savoir précisément où nous en sommes, mais aussi faire face à ce qui nous arrive, alors que l'intelligence artificielle étend son emprise sur le monde et les vies, nous avons besoin d'un sémaphore.

On dit que l'expression « intelligence artificielle » a été lancée par John McCarthy, en 1956, lors de la conférence de Dartmouth, coup d'envoi du programme de recherche consacré à la reproduction algorithmique de la pensée humaine. Nous dirons donc, quant à nous, que l'histoire de l'I-A commence à la fin du xixe siècle, lorsqu'un philosophe visionnaire, cheminant à flanc de montagne, a compris qu'on pouvait arracher au cri de l'âne sa puissance d'exclamation intempestive – et qu'il y avait là, pour nous, un grand danger

There is no alternative

Il arrive aussi, on le sait, que l'âne se cabre. L'I-A approbatif que dénoncent les philosophes est la forme mutilée de ce « hi-han ! » qui est à la fois refus catégorique et cri pour l'autonomie et la liberté. author: EDRi
title: Data retention is mass surveillance of people’s phone and internet activity
content:
In 2014, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) declared mass retention of internet traffic and location data as contrary to the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Any proposal for a new EU instrument harmonising data retention must respect the boundaries of CJEU jurisprudence and uphold the rights to privacy, data protection and freedom of expression. Read more in EDRi’s new publication.

It is the legal requirement for internet service providers to retain metadata about their users beyond what is necessary for the provision of the service (e.g. billing or network optimisation and security purposes) and to keep it solely so that it can later be accessed by law enforcement bodies and intelligence services.

Metadata is data generated for the purpose of transmitting content in electronic communications services and networks. This includes mobile numbers of the sender and recipient, the time and duration of a call or an internet session, websites accessed, and the location of mobile devices. On a technical level, metadata is no longer needed once the transmission ends.

Metadata is very revealing about people’s private lives.

Systematic recording of location data will reveal a person’s permanent and temporary places of residence, political and religious preferences (e.g. participation in public demonstrations and religious ceremonies), health status (e.g. visit to a specialised clinic), sexual orientation (e.g. LGBT+ venues), or other sensitive aspects (e.g. visit to a lawyer’s office).

Metadata contains information about social or professional relations with other people (“social graph”).

Usage patterns for website visits and other internet services reveal an enormous amount of information about a person’s interest and state of mind.

Metadata is more revealing than the content of communications, especially because metadata is highly structured, which makes it easy to analyse. Governments can easily profile and categorise entire populations solely based on metadata.

The Court of Justice of the EU rightly described metadata retention as creating a feeling of being under constant surveillance. This has a chilling effect on participation in public life, as individuals restrict their own civil liberties to avoid surveillance.

While data access requests may be specific and targeted, general and indiscriminate data retention treats everyone as a potential suspect. Surveillance without suspicion violates the presumption of innocence, which is an essential right in democratic societies.

Retention of vast amounts of personal data inevitably creates huge vulnerabilities to cyberattacks. Malicious actors can gain access to massive amounts of data and abuse it for identity theft or blackmail.

Data retention severely undermines the possibility of online anonymity. Anonymity is a question of safety for many, even a matter of life or death: investigative journalists, whistleblowers, crime survivors, political opponents, refugees, victims of transnational repression, artists, human rights defenders, and more. It supports the exercise of key fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and the freedom to receive and impart information.

US telecom company AT&T was hacked by an attacker who stole the logs of calls and texts to more than 100 million customers over a six-month period in 2022.

In 2024 the Garda Síochána Ombudsman Commission (Ireland’s police watchdog) accessed journalists’ phone records to identify their sources as part of its own investigation into the Irish police, even though the journalists were not accused of any criminal offence.

In 2013, the Polish Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) obtained access to billing data of a journalist who had reported on irregularities in the intelligence services. The CBA’s aim was to uncover their source’s identity. The journalist won the case in court, and the CBA published an official apology.

The Berlin Data Protection Authority reported that most cell tower dumps (law enforcement requesting information on all the devices that connected to a particular cell site during a specific time period) by German authorities between 2009 and 2011, when data retention was in place in the country, were unlawful. The German police used this surveillance technique as an everyday investigative tool despite its very intrusive nature, and systematically failed to meet several legal requirements. Data retention enabled this abuse.

author: Unknown
title: Lilia Folt - On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness
content:
Author

: Lilia Folt

Title

: On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness

Date

: September 27

th

, 2026

Notes

: Originally published in

Dissonant Times

, a grassroots journalism and counter-info project from the Willamette Valley of Oregon.

Source

: Dissonant Times, Retrieved on 11/5/2026 from https://dissonanttimes.org/anarchic-reflections-on-anti-surveillance-mindfulness/


 Surveillance has become a ubiquitous feature of everyday life in America. Cameras watch us from businesses and homes, from bus stops, from cars, from traffic lights. Bluetooth trackers ping our smartphones as we pass by, mapping our movements. The phones themselves illuminate our paths through society by continuously pinging cell towers, providing our cell providers our location data, information that is only a subpoena away, if that. In countless ways, we’ve been made to both passively accept and actively participate in our own surveillance. This vast complex of surveillance doesn’t just gather information about us, it also shapes our behaviors, temperaments, and ways of moving through the world. Surveillance molds us down to the level of subjective, sensory, embodied experience. At that same level we can begin to shake off its hold on us and reclaim ourselves. For that, I am offering a practice I’m calling “anti-surveillance mindfulness,” a form of walking meditation that builds mindful awareness of surveillance cameras. This practice, if taken up consistently, opens onto a broader project of transforming our relationship to the places we live in, a project that itself naturally blossoms into materially transforming public space, as self expands to world in the moment-by-moment practice of mindfulness.


Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness


 Readers may or may not be familiar with the Panopticon. Designed by 18

th

 century English liberal Jeremy Bentham, the Panopticon was a model for an institutional building designed so that a single prison guard can watch all the inmates from a central watch tower. The inmates, meanwhile, cannot tell whether or not they are being watched, and therefore could be watched at any moment. To quote Bentham:


 The more constantly the persons to be inspected are under the eyes of the persons who should inspect them, the more perfectly will the purpose of the establishment have been attained. (...) This being impossible, the next thing to be wished for is, that, at every instant, seeing reason to believe as much, and not being able to satisfy himself to the contrary, he should

conceive

 himself to be so.


 A lot has changed since the 1700’s, but the disciplinary paradigm of surveillance has remained the same. If anything, it has expanded beyond specific institutions to encompass much of society.


 There are cameras everywhere, and we are being watched, and while we are aware of this, we tend to see it as normal and unremarkable, an inevitability we must resign ourselves to. Consciousness of being surveilled fades into the background, becoming a constant assumption of being watched that we internalize. This surveillance consciousness is running us all the more effectively because it is not distinct, because it is

un

conscious. That is why the first step in anti-surveillance mindfulness is becoming conscious of surveillance.


 Mindfulness is at the same time a means and an end, the seed and the fruit. When we practice mindfulness in order to build up concentration, mindfulness is a seed. But mindfulness itself is the life of awareness: the presence of mindfulness means the presence of life, and therefore mindfulness is also the fruit. — Thích Nhất Hạnh,

The Miracle of Mindfulness


 “Mindfulness” is a practice originating in various sects of Buddhism. The mindfulness practices and concepts I’m familiar with have largely been within the school of Zen Buddhism

[1]

.


 The classic mindfulness practice is watching the breath, and that is a great starting point. Take a breath in, the air entering through your nose, your stomach and chest softly expanding as you inhale. Then exhale through the mouth, the stomach and chest settling back down, gently exhaling for a little longer than your inhale. Repeat this several times, deepening your breaths slightly. From there, start to check in with your body. Notice how it feels to be sitting down, or to be standing if you are standing; notice how it feels to be holding this piece of paper, holding your phone, or looking at your computer, however it is that you are reading …

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Air Creebec hit by administrative data breach affecting employees and passengers
content:
Air Creebec, a regional Quebec airline owned by the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee, reported a data breach Wednesday affecting both customers and staff.

In a press release, the company announced “an unauthorized intrusion targeting some of its administrative systems.”

The release stresses that the breach did not compromise any systems associated with aircraft, flight operations or flight safety, noting the company’s administrative systems were not connected with aircraft and flight systems, which it said operate independently.

“Initial findings indicate that administrative files were exfiltrated,” states the release. “These files may contain personal information relating mainly to current and former employees, as well as passengers. Others may also contain operational, administrative or financial information related to customers and partners. The review is ongoing.”

Based in the airport of Val d’Or in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region of western Quebec, roughly 520 kilometres northwest of Ottawa, Air Creebec offers flights to 16 destinations in Quebec and Ontario. The company’s fleet consists of 21 Dash-8 turboprop regional airliners, along with one ATR 72 turboprop air-freighter for cargo, and carries 200,000 passengers per year.

Cybersecurity experts assessing damage

Air Creebec director for Marketing and Business Development Edward Trahan said the breach was identified in October after which company officials immediately brought in cybersecurity experts to analyze the situation.

“They’re currently evaluating what’s going on and what the breach actually contained,” Trahant told APTN News. “The experts are still conducting their review, so there’s no numbers [of victims] at this time that we can give.”

He added that for security reasons, he was not presently willing to name the cybersecurity team currently helping with post-breach recovery.

He said because the attack was designed to go undetected it was hard to determine the date upon which it began, and for how long attackers were able to access Air Creebec’s systems prior to being discovered.

“What I can assure you of is that as soon as [we were] made aware of [it], we acted immediately and did not wait.”

At the moment, Trahant said the attack appeared to have stolen information “related to our employees, past employees too, and maybe even our passengers.”

“But it’s hard to confirm at the moment.”

Company will contact affected parties

He added that a priority for Air Creebec is contacting every one of their staff or customers whose information has been compromised, which cybersecurity experts would undertake to carry out as soon as possible.

“A part of what the cybersecurity experts are doing for us is gathering information to [determine] what kind of protection packages we can provide to people that had their information involved,” said Trahan.

“Those people will be directly contacted in probably the next few days — [but] probably more like [the next] day — about what package they will receive, what protection they’re going to have and how long it’s going to last.”

Trahan said the cybersecurity team was currently in the process of securing all possible intrusion points, but he said the nature of cybersecurity is that 100 per cent protection is impossible.

“It’s just the way of the world,” he said, “but they are closing every possible way to get in and they are getting to the very end of that. As for how they got in initially, we don’t know yet and I don’t want to speculate while the review is still underway.”

Trahan said he and Air Creebec are taking the situation very seriously and are committed to supporting all those affected, and the company said it would be in touch with affected people to offer “appropriate protective measures,” including the possibility of credit-monitoring and identity-protection services.

“Those services will be based on the nature of the information exposed and the risks that were identified,” he said. “So individuals that are eligible to receive this protection will be informed directly and will be given a list of steps to follow in the very near future.”

Jesse joined APTN as a producer after 16 years as a print and web journalist. During seven of those years, he covered the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee for community newsmagazine The Nation. Jesse’s writing on Indigenous issues has also appeared in Canadian Geographic, the Toronto Star, the Rover, The Eastern Door, Metro, and the Huffington Post.

author: Scott Timcke
title: The Stories Shaping Africa’s AI Future
content:
In the boardrooms of Addis Ababa and the tech hubs of Nairobi, a new worldmaking project is underway. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the central arenas where African states negotiate their position in an unequal global order. To speak of “AI in Africa” is not simply to describe the arrival of a technology, but to encounter a set of competing discursive frames through which political desires, developmental ambitions, ethical claims, and governance priorities are translated into technical agendas. As national strategies and regional protocols are rolled out, what comes into view is a struggle over how Africa is imagined within this machine age, and what kinds of futures that imagination makes thinkable.


These frames are not simply different ways of describing a new technology. They are competing scripts for what Africa is, what AI is for, and who ought to shape its future. Some cast the continent as a site of leapfrogging and renewal; others as a zone of exposure, extraction, sovereignty, moral repair, or improvised adaptation. Each brings some actors and possibilities into focus while pushing others to the margins. That is why the issue is not only what AI means for Africa, but what pictures of Africa are being called into view through AI discourse.


The first terrain is shaped by promise and protection. One of the most pervasive registers is promissory. In the African renaissance 2.0 frame, visible in the

AU Continental AI Strategy

, AI appears as a

leapfrogging

 device through which Africa can bypass the chokepoint of traditional industrialization and enter prosperity through technical modernization. Here, the ethical subject is the developmental state or planner charged with delivering growth, inclusion, and renewal. What comes into view is capacity, competitiveness, and beneficial transformation. What recedes from view are the historical and political-economic conditions that make acceleration so attractive in the first place: debt, infrastructural dependence, uneven ownership, and the possibility that AI may deepen rather than overcome inherited asymmetries.


Running alongside this is a protective register. In this vulnerability frame, Africa is not late but exposed to surveillance, bias, exclusion, and systems introduced into settings where safeguards are weak and redress is limited. As the

CIVICUS report on AI surveillance in Africa

 suggests, the issue is not only future risk but already existing forms of technologically mediated harm. The ethical subject here is the harm-bearing population—the data subject, precarious worker, surveilled citizen, and linguistically marginal user most likely to absorb the costs of badly governed AI. This frame is ethically indispensable because it foregrounds rights, harm, and institutional fragility, including the uneven but growing architecture of data protection on the continent. Its limit, however, is that it can cast Africa chiefly as a site to be protected rather than one from which technological futures are actively contested and shaped.


A second terrain is shaped by structure and sovereignty. Alongside these promissory and protective registers sits a more structural critique. In the

anti-colonial frame

, AI appears as a socio-technical order built through unequal material relations: not only data extraction, but also mineral supply chains, outsourced labor, environmental degradation, foreign-owned infrastructures, and asymmetrical control over the institutions that govern digital life. From this perspective, Africa is not outside the AI order looking in; it is already deeply inserted into it, though often on subordinated terms. The ethical subject is the dispossessed worker, community, or polity whose labor, resources, and data are drawn into AI systems while ownership and value are captured elsewhere. What becomes visible is the political economy of AI—an approach that makes it harder to sustain the comforting idea that Africa’s main problem is simply one of readiness or delayed entry. But the frame has limits. In foregrounding dispossession, it can flatten internal differentiation, externalize agency too completely, and become so totalizing that the uneven realities of negotiation and strategic inhabitation recede from view.


The sovereignty frame shifts the question from extraction to control: AI is cast as a problem of authority over infrastructure, procurement, standards, and rulemaking, a concern visible in South Africa’s

National …

author: Dinah Gardner
title: The Other China We Need to Talk About
content:
WHAT IF I told you that there was a chance—not a very high chance, but a real chance nonetheless—that if you visited the People’s Republic of China today you might be kidnapped, blindfolded, driven to a specialized facility and subjected to six months of psychological torture. All on the orders of the state.

It sounds unbelievable, doesn’t it?

But this is what happened to at least several dozen foreign citizens in recent years. It is what happened to American scholar Min Zin this past June, when he landed in Yunnan province on the invitation of a Chinese academic institution to attend a conference. And it is also what happened to half a dozen people who appear in the latest edition of the book The People’s Republic of the Disappeared, which we just published on 28 October.

This important book is a collection of mostly first-person stories that expose the psychological horrors of being held in the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) feared secret detention system called Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL). The system permits police to hold an individual in complete isolation, no contact with family or lawyers, to be interrogated for hours at will.

The individual is under 24-hour guard: this includes being watched all day every day, all night every night, whether you are asleep, sitting quietly in your cell or even on the toilet. The CCP intentionally uses RSDL to strip away every last shred of human dignity. RSDL is designed to break a person’s will to extract a confession for crimes imagined by the state

For more than a decade, the CCP has used RSDL against its own people, in particular human rights defenders. It is now increasingly using it against foreign citizens to exert its will across borders and as a kind of hostage diplomacy. Michael Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who wrote the foreword to this edition, is one of its most well-known examples.

In editing the stories for this book, I was struck again and again by how similar everyone’s experience was. This speaks to the uniformity of the RSDL system:

The removal of the temporal world. “There are no clocks in RSDL” is the title of Australian TV anchor Cheng Lei’s chapter. She would guess and count breaths to keep track of time.

The removal of the physical world. There are no windows in RSDL or they are covered in thick blackout curtains. Japanese scholar Hideji Suzuki cried when he was granted 15 minutes of sunlight, the only time in his seven months’ incarceration when he was allowed to see the sky.

The removal of yourself. Michael Kovrig noted: “There are no mirrors—not even the reassurance of seeing your own face.” Chinese activist Li Qiaochu writes how she was simply called “target”.

Filling the space left by these absences was a current of fear. Endless rules, the lack of privacy yet total isolation (guards were forbidden from talking to prisoners), reduced nutrition, sleep deprivation, lack of fresh air, and the padded suicide-proofed walls. Several of the detainees wrote while they could never see outside their RSDL facility, at nighttime they would often hear gunfire or the barking of dogs.

“In my mentally exhausted state, the sounds of gunfire would constantly startle me and even cause me to imagine that I was about to be executed,” wrote Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che.

But something else struck me as I read through their testimonies. However harrowing these stories of suffering are, they are also evidence of human resilience in the face of horror.

Cheng Lei writes about how she would escape into her mind, translating poems, reliving her former TV interviews and making up stories in her head. Similarly, Michael Kovrig meditated, sang songs to himself, and remembered past moments in his life, as if it was a recording playing in his mind.

“I learned to meditate on the movies I had watched and the poems and novels I had read,” wrote Li Qiaochu. “Those precious memories allowed me to gradually filter out the brainwashing, to preserve my vitality and to keep myself from being transformed into their machine.”

Feedback from earlier editions informed us that rights activists use the Chinese editions of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared to prepare for and strengthen their mental resolve and courage in case one day they too are taken into RSDL. Knowing that others have gone through this and come out the other side can be an immense help. It’s for this reason that the Chinese edition of this book will be …
