author: Marcelo Oliveira
title: Suposta ligação com o crime organizado pode barrar posse de 10 candidatos em 2027
content:
O Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) pode impedir que 10 candidatos eleitos nas últimas eleições e investigados por ligações com organizações criminosas, tomem posse no ano que vem. Entre eles, dois tiveram suas candidaturas impugnadas pelo Ministério Público Eleitoral (MPE) e depois deferidas pela Justiça Eleitoral de seus estados: o ex-prefeito de Embu das Artes (SP), Ney Santos (Republicanos), candidato a deputado federal, e

Márcio Canella

 (União), ex-prefeito Belford Roxo (RJ), que se candidatou a deputado estadual.


Outras seis candidaturas que conseguiram votos suficientes para se eleger, cinco no Rio de Janeiro e uma no Mato Grosso do Sul, foram impugnadas pelo MPE e indeferidas pela Justiça Eleitoral regional, porém, entraram com recurso no TSE e puderam concorrer “sub-judice”. Ou seja, disputaram as eleições sabendo que a Justiça Eleitoral poderia barrá-los a qualquer momento. Nos oito processos, o MPE sustenta no TSE que as candidaturas devem ser impugnadas definitivamente.


Os dois últimos casos em análise no TSE por supostas ligações com o crime organizado são dos deputados federais eleitos Antonio Rueda (União/RJ) e Márcio Rezende (PSD/RJ). Ambos tiveram os registros das candidaturas deferidos pelos Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais, porém eles foram questionados por terceiros no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral.


Em 2026, 42 candidatos, de 10 estados do país, foram impugnados pelo Ministério Público Eleitoral (MPE) por vínculo com organizações criminosas.

 Do total, 22 deles tiveram os registros barrados pela Justiça Eleitoral ou renunciaram.


Duas candidaturas que tiveram o indeferimento defendido pelo MPE no TSE por terem sido permitidas pela Justiça Eleitoral não conseguiram se eleger. Uma delas é de Cristiane Brasil (DC/RJ), filha do ex-deputado federal Roberto Jefferson, que tentou retornar à Câmara dos Deputados em 2026 e teve 237 votos. A outra candidatura tem seu processo em sigilo.


Ex-prefeitos recebem milhares de votos, mesmo com investigações


Dois casos emblemáticos envolvem os Tribunais Regionais Eleitorais de São Paulo e do Rio de Janeiro, que liberaram as candidaturas dos ex-prefeitos de Embu das Artes (SP), Ney Santos (Republicanos), e de Belford Roxo (RJ),

Márcio Canella

 (União), a deputado federal e deputado estadual, respectivamente.


Tanto Santos quanto Canella foram eleitos com centenas de milhares de votos e a Procuradoria Geral Eleitoral contesta no TSE a validação de ambas as candidaturas para impedir que eles assumam os cargos.


Canella, inclusive, está preso preventivamente desde 15 de outubro. O deputado estadual, que busca a reeleição, foi o segundo mais votado do Rio de Janeiro este ano, e recebeu quase 200 mil votos. Ele é investigado na Operação Unha e Carne, da Polícia Federal, por suspeita de integrar uma organização criminosa armada que utilizava uma rede de postos de combustíveis na Região Metropolitana do Rio de Janeiro para esquemas de lavagem de dinheiro, que teria movimentado bilhões de reais.


Na política, ele é apontado pelo MP Eleitoral como responsável por ter aberto as portas da prefeitura de Belford Roxo para a milícia “Somos Comunidade” que teria um acordo com o Comando Vermelho. Há uma investigação sobre supostos membros do grupo armado que foram nomeados para cargos na cidade. Em julho deste ano, ele foi preso com um fuzil em seu carro e disse que a arma pertencia a um PM que fazia sua segurança. Por causa da prisão com o armamento, sua pré-candidatura ao Senado, com apoio de Flávio Bolsonaro, naufragou e o político optou pela reeleição à Assembleia Legislativa do Rio de Janeiro (Alerj). Rogéria Bolsonaro, mãe de Flávio, seria suplente de Canella.


Mesmo com esses elementos, o TRE entendeu, por 6 votos a 1, que os elementos juntados pelo MP contra a candidatura de Canella e sobre suas relações com as milícias não eram robustos o suficiente e deferiu o registro. A decisão foi proferida em 29 de setembro, duas semanas antes do ex-prefeito ser preso novamente.


Postos de combustíveis, também, seriam o principal meio empregado por

Ney Santos

, segundo o MP Estadual e o MP Eleitoral de São Paulo, para lavar dinheiro de crimes do PCC. Santos, que já esteve preso por roubo a carro forte, foi prefeito de Embu das Artes por dois mandatos entre 2017 e 2024. Há anos suas atividades são investigadas pelo Ministério Público.


No julgamento de seu caso no Tribunal Regional Federal de São Paulo, Santos teve a candidatura deferida por 3 votos a 2. O MP …

author: Unknown
title: Pera Müzesi’nde ekranlara ara: Sanat eserleri arasında kitap okuma buluşması
content:
Suna ve İnan Kıraç Vakfı Pera Müzesi, ekranlara ara vererek insanların kendileriyle ve birbirleriyle bağ kurmasını amaçlayan The Offline Club’ın İstanbul topluluğuyla birlikte “Çevrimdışı Okuma Buluşması” düzenliyor.

19 Kasım 2026 Perşembe günü saat 19.00’da gerçekleştirilecek ücretsiz etkinlik, katılımcıları müzenin sergi salonunda kitap okumaya ve okuma deneyimlerini paylaşmaya davet ediyor. Buluşma, müzenin ikinci katında yer alan Kesişen Dünyalar: Elçiler ve Ressamlar koleksiyon sergisinde yapılacak.

Günlük yaşamın ekranlarla çevrili akışına ara vermek isteyenlere yönelik etkinlikte katılımcılar, canlı akustik gitar eşliğinde bir saat boyunca yanlarında getirdikleri kitapları okuyacak. Müzenin sergi salonu, bu buluşmayla kitapların, müziğin ve sanat eserlerinin bir araya geldiği ortak bir okuma alanına dönüşecek.

Okuma saatinin ardından kitap temalı sohbet kartları aracılığıyla katılımcılar tanışacak, okudukları kitaplar üzerine konuşacak ve düşüncelerini paylaşacak.

Yer: Pera Müzesi, ikinci kat, Kesişen Dünyalar: Elçiler ve Ressamlar sergisi

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Administrador
title: Auf was wir aus sind. Was ja und was nein.
content:
Obacht – Familien Sucherinnen, mit oder ohne Kollektiv.

Obacht – diejenigen, die Familien Sucherinnen begleiten.

Schwestern, Compañeras [Familien Sucherinnen]:

Dies ist der erste von verschiedenen Texten, in denen wir einige Zweifel und Fragen klären werden, die uns erreichten. Wir werden darin antworten auf einige Kränkungen und Beleidigungen und Euch nach und nach den Zeitplan der Delegation bekanntgeben. Wir bitten Euch, diesem Schreiben sowie den folgenden gegenüber aufmerksam zu sein.

A.- Wir haben eine Reihe von Verwirrungen, Unverschämtheiten und Manipulationsversuche über Ziele, Daten, Orte und Aktivitäten der Delegation der Comisión Sexta Zapatista für diesen Dezember und die erste Januar-Woche 2027 entdeckt.

Es wird von einem angeblichen mexikoweiten Treffen zwischen Familien Sucherinnen und der zapatistischen Delegation am 6. Dezember an der sogenannten »Glorieta de los Desaparecidos« (*1) gesprochen und fehl informiert, sowie von anderen öffentlichen Aktivitäten der Comisión Sexta Zapatista zu anderen Daten und an anderen Orten.

Dies ist falsch, Schwestern und Compañeras Sucherinnen. Vielleicht werden einige, die dazu aufrufen, ihre Versammlung an diesem Ort halten oder anderen Orten, welche in Bezug stehen zu Eurem gerechten Kampf; wir werden dort jedoch nicht teilnehmen.

Nicht nur weil die »Einladung«, die wir von dort erhielten, Ignoranz, Unredlichkeit und Grobheiten widerspiegelt. Keine*r wird eingeladen, indem er*sie beleidigt wird. Bei passender Gelegenheit werden wir darüber mehr erklären. [Wir werden nicht teilnehmen] auch weil wir nicht auf Massenversammlungen mit den Familien Sucherinnen aus sind.

Die Gruppen, Kollektive* und Familien Sucherinnen, welche sich an den Glorietas oder wo auch immer versammeln, können sich mit uns persönlich treffen, Gruppe für Gruppe – an dem Aufenthaltsort der Delegation in Mexiko-Stadt und an Orten, die öffentlich gemacht werden – indem sie sich via des [Menschenrechtszentrums] Frayba registrieren, zu den ihnen passenden Tagen und Uhrzeiten – wenn sie es derart möchten.

B.- Schaut, Ihr und wir, die zapatistischen Pueblos, wissen, dass Ihr nicht nur Differenzen habt sondern offene Rivalitäten und Dispute – zwischen Kollektiven der Sucherinnen, zwischen Netzwerken und Bewegungen. Sogar einschließlich dass versucht wird, gegen gewisse Kollektive Einspruch zu erheben und zu bestimmen, wer sich mit der zapatistischen Delegation trifft oder nicht. Vielleicht wächst deshalb die Anzahl der Familien Sucherinnen, die in keiner Gruppe oder keinem Kollektiv sind und die uns direkt kontaktieren.

Wir werden keine*n beurteilen, verurteilen. Wir werden nicht sagen, welche die korrekte und welche die falsche Strategie ist, welche legitim ist oder nicht, welche gut ist oder schlecht.

Wir denken, dass der*diejenige – die*der Wahrheit und Gerechtigkeit sucht und zum Ziel hat, den*diejenige*n zu finden, der*die ihm*ihr auf Grund eines gewaltsamen Verschwundenmachens fehlt – kann und soll all die Wege durchlaufen und an all die Türen klopfen, die seinem*ihrem Schmerz Erleichterung bringt:

Ob sie draußen mit Spitzhacke und Schaufel die Suche umsetzen; auf lokale, bundesstaatliche oder staatliche Justiz-Instanzen zurückgreifen; sich mit der Präsidentin und ihrer Funktionärspyramide treffen; internationale und mexikoweite Kampagnen machen; oder es lediglich schaffen, die Fotos ihrer Vermissten in ihren Straßen und Stadtteilen zu plakatieren; sich an Menschenrechts-NGOs wenden; die Unterstützung von Spezialist*innen in der Verschwundenen-Suche und der Analyse von menschlichen Überresten anfordern; auf Demos, Kundgebungen, Mahnwachen, Besetzung von Gebäuden sowie Straßen- und Autobahnblockaden zurückgreifen; beten; verfluchen; all das zuvor Gesagte.

Und immerzu mit der Erinnerung, dem Eingedenken als Antrieb.

Was auch immer Ihr entscheidet und macht, es ist eine Entscheidung von Euch, von denjenigen, die diesen Schmerz tragen und diese Angst erleiden – und von sonst niemanden.

Somit werden wir Euch nicht sagen, was zu tun ist, noch für/ statt Euch tun. Wir werden Euch kennenlernen, Euch zuhören, Euch umarmen.

Wir werden nicht sagen, welches Netzwerk oder Kollektiv besser als die anderen ist.

C.- Deshalb bevorzugt unsere Reise weder Massenaktionen noch Medienspektakel, weder Vollversammlungen noch das Schaffen von Bündnissen, Zusammenschlüssen oder Ähnlichem, auch keine neue Organisation, die alle Kollektive und Familien Sucherinnen umfasst, oder außerhalb von ihnen.

Auch …

title: 6emîn Festîvala Fîlman a Rojava a Navneteweyî dest pê dike
content:
Bernameya 6emîn Festîvala Fîlman a Navneteweyî ya Rojava ya ku dê bi dirûşma “Çîrokên Hevpar, Sînemaya Azad” diyar bû.  Festîval roja 13ê Mijdarê li Navenda Mihemed Şêxo bi fîlma “Heval Kekê Min” dest pê dike.


Festîval dê di navbera 13 û 20ê Mijdarê de sînemager û sînemahezan bîne ba hev. Di nîşandana li Navenda Mihemed Şêxo de, li gel pênc fîlmên di beşa “Ji Rojava” de, kurtefîlmên bi kurdî, belgefîlm û fîlmên navneteweyî jî dê werin nîşandan. Panel û atolye jî dê li TEV-ÇAND, Sîne Jîn û Hunergeha Welat werin lidarxistin.


Bernameya Festîvalê wiha ye:


13ê Mijdarê


17.00 – Di vekirina festîvalê de MA Music dê konserekê bide û Narin Dance jî dê nîşandana dansê pêşkêş bike.


19.00 – Fîlmê vekirinê “Heval Kekê Min” ê ku derhêneriya wê Haşim Aydemir kiriye dê bi sînemahizan re werin ba hev.


14ê Mijdarê


10.00-12.00 – Belgeselçêker û karkerê kûrguyê Sasha Ayoub, dê li Sîne Jînê behsa xebatên Stories Film Labê bike ku sînemagerên serbixwe yên li Sûriyeyê projeyên xwe tê de pêş dixin. Di rûniştinê de fîlmên ku di çarçoveya bernameyê de hatine hilbijartin dê werin nîşandan.


11.00 – Nîşandanên rojê dê bi fîlmê “The Country Judge” dest pê bikin. Di bernameyê de fîlmên kurt ên kurdî “House of The Moon” û “Dorpêç” û belgesela “The Wedding of the Pirs” jî cih digirin.


15.00-17.00 – Derhênerê dîmenê Cemil Kızıldag, dê li TEV-ÇANDê li ser zimanê dîtbarî yê sînemayê perwerdehiyê bide.


15ê Mijdarê


09.00-13.00 – Atolyeya sê rojî ya li ser bikaranîna ronahiyê ya di sînemayê de ya derhênerê dîmen û ronahiyê Jafar Amin Al-Betar, dê li Hunergeha Welat dest pê bike. Atolye dê di 16 û 17ê Mijdarê de jî di heman saetan de berdewam bike.


09.00-13.00 – Belgeselçêker Guevara Namer, dê li Sîne Jînê pêvajoya çêkirina belgeselê û ezmûnên xebatê yên di qada navneteweyî de binirxîne. Rûniştina duyem a atolyeyê dê di 16ê Mijdarê de were lidarxistin.


11.00 û 11.50 – Du fîlmên yekem ên beşa “Ji Rojava” yên bi navên “Rêwiyên Ser Riya Agir” û “Keziyên Berxwedanê” dê werin nîşandan.


15.00 – Derhênera fîlma “Berbû” Sêvînaz Evdikê, dê li TEV-ÇANDê behsa Festîvala Fîlman a Jinan a Nûjîyan bike. Di heman saetê de li Navenda Mihemed Şêxo belgesela “Kî me ez?” dê were nîşandan.


18.00 û 19.10 – Bi rêzê ve belgeselên “04.17 Adiyaman” û “Pêlên Kurdan” dê bi sînemahizan re werin ba hev. Piştî her du nîşandanan jî dê rûniştina pirs û bersivan were lidarxistin.


16ê Mijdarê


11.00 – Fîlmê “To Fetch a Pail of Water” dê were nîşandan. Di saet 15.00an de jî belgesela “Under the Flags the Sun” dê bi sînemahizan re were ba hev.


15.00-17.00 – Di panela li TEV-ÇANDê de çêkirina fîlman a kolektîf a ku Komîna Fîlm a Rojava ji sala 2015an û vir ve berdewam dike dê were nirxandin. Di panela ku dê ji aliyê Mirzan Bekir ve wre birêvebirin de, ji damezrînerên komînê Diyar Hesso û Şêro Hindê û sêwirînerê deng Coni Docolomansky ê ku di fîlmên “Kobanê” û “Berbû” de xebitiye dê wekî axaftvan beşdar bibin.


17ê Mijdarê


10.00-13.00 – Senarîst Onder Çakar, dê li Sîne Jînê atolyeyekî li ser mijara, ‘Karakterê sereke yê fîlmekî ji qonaxa ramanê çawa derbasî senaryoyê dibe’ pêk bîne.


12.00 û 12.30 – Di beşa “Ji Rojava” de fîlmên “Youthful Wrinkle” û “Nameya Dawî” dê werin nîşandan.

12.25 – Fîlmê 5emîn ê bijareya “Ji Rojava” ê bi navê “Decision” dê were nîşandan.

author: John Mullen
title: France: The brass band and the revolution
content:
For the third time in a week, there were major strikes in education and mass demonstrations across France, on November 10.

More than a million people took to the streets in more than 200 towns and cities, on November 5, in support of school students and to demand wage rises, more jobs and an end to cuts in public service budgets. Health workers, dockers, teachers, journalists, municipal staff, train drivers, bank workers and many others joined the one-day strike.

Two days later, hundreds of thousands marched again.

Student assemblies attracted more than a thousand participants at many universities, including Marseille, Rennes, Bordeaux and Paris-Cité.

In some towns, notably Rennes and Bordeaux, and in sectors such as university staff and healthcare, general assemblies of workers (known as interpros or coordinations) are taking the lead in organising the struggle, hoping to overcome the horrific inertia of the national union leaderships.

High school student representatives walked out of a government consultation session on university admissions policy, held in Paris on Monday November 9, when they discovered that ministers had invited fascist MPs to take part.

There are three strands to the present revolt.

First, highschool and university students are in their sixth week of blockades, and are not giving up despite the police beating thousands and mutilating dozens.

Secondly, the Yellow Vest networks are back, and they worry the government because they seem leaderless and prefer wildcat demos.

Most importantly, there is the workers’ movement, which holds, in strike action, our most powerful weapon, but which is held back by catastrophic national leadership from a band of professional “Bordeaux and sandwiches” negotiators.

On the demonstrations, people wave thousands upon thousands of home-made cardboard placards, with slogans from the bawdy to the philosophical, quoting poets, rappers or constitutional documents.

My favourites include: “Let’s do a poo on the fascists!”, “You thirst for power, we thirst for beauty!”, “Class struggle begins in high school!”, “Looters in hoodies make you angry? Looters in suits are your government !”, “Plan A: protest in a dignified manner. Plan B: smash everything up.”, “Have you forgotten how we became a democracy?” and “This is getting expensive in cardboard!”.

The now traditional demo song rings out across the country: “For the honour of the workers, and to build a better world! Although Macron doesn’t like it, here we are!”

Brass bands and orchestras are present everywhere, following a call from the New World Orchestra, who were tear-gassed while playing in mid-October. They have popularised a new demo song: “I’ve two great loves: the brass band and the revolution! Long live blockades and sabotage, occupations and wildcat demos!” Groups of thousands were filmed singing this and dancing.

Last week, a new opinion poll found that 57% of the population approves of the movement, and 88% consider the demands concerning purchasing power and the cost of living legitimate, while 75% approve of the students’ demands. This is impressive, given the massive government propaganda campaign against the revolt.

With such support, even the mainstream media feel obliged to feature interviews with inspiring high schoolers, explaining their demands in detail, even if the channels rapidly return to their preferred fare — interviews with headmasters, police and shopkeepers upset by the movement, and political experts who want to discuss supposed personality clashes between left politicians.

This crisis is not going to go away. Emmanuel Macron’s minority government must push its national budget through before Christmas. Massive tax cuts for the rich mean they are short of money, so their initial proposal is for €50 billion in budget cuts. The international bankers are breathing down their necks, already charging France more than neighbouring countries to borrow money.

The situation is extremely fluid. The government met with unions and bosses on November 9, and then declared that the national minimum monthly wage would be raised — by €24. The CGT union demand is for a €150 rise. Later this week a decision will be announced about public sector wages. Public servants have lost 20% of their purchasing power since 2010, and nearly a million are on the minimum wage.

The national union leaders are following their habitual hymn sheet of “days of action”. The dynamism of Thursday’s social …

author: Kerry Smith
title: Students organise nationwide rallies against artificial intelligence
content:
A student-led national day of action against artificial intelligence (AI) and mega data centres was held on November 10. The rallies were called by Students for AI Regulation (SAR), a group of high school and university students, and supported by the Tomorrow Movement.

SAR said students are “terrified of the impact AI is going to have on our future”. “It’s easy to wallow in AI news and climate disasters but … we must act now!”

Speakers at the Gadigal Country/Sydney rally highlighted successful campaigns against AI data centres in Arncliffe, Lane Cove and the Blue Mountains, and called on people to join the December 5 statewide rally against data centres.

Paddy Gibson from Stop the Cooks River AI Project said defeating the project was an important win for people power. He said the fight is not over, as the community wants to stop the developer Stockland’s other plans for the former Kogarah Golf Club site.

Gibson said students and staff at universities and schools are raising important anti-AI demands and cited the National Tertiary Education Union’s push to include AI protection clauses in enterprise agreements.

Robin, a student at the University of New South Wales, high school teacher and campaigner with Students Hate AI, said it was being forced on teachers and students.

Isaac Nellist from Sydney Students for Climate detailed the climate impacts of mega data centres, including their use of vast amounts of electricity and water, and thereby helping the continued expansion of coal and gas mining projects.

“The huge amount of money being invested into AI and AI infrastructure around the world is money that should be going into addressing the existential threat of climate change, and the countless other social issues that we are facing.”

He said data centres were being used to “accelerate militarism and war, drive down wages and workers rights and replace artists and steal their work”, while driving inflation and pushing up the cost-of-living.

“AI is a key part of the AUKUS pillar two agreement, which further ties Australia to the US military … and we are seeing the devastating impacts of AI-enabled warfare in Gaza and Iran.

“The good news is that communities are fighting back, we know data centres are massively unpopular and when communities organise and fight back, they win.”

About 80 people joined the Naarm/Melbourne rally at the State Library of Victoria. Jacob Andrewartha, childcare worker and Socialist Alliance candidate for Pascoe Vale, said AI is a “technology that represents the destruction of the environment and an attack on our democratic rights”.

He said AI was being used in surveillance and by government agencies. “There isn’t a convincing case for why we should use AI … What does it have to offer? Worse artistic works? Polluting social media?

“Young people are rejecting this technology, despite the massive investment from big tech capitalists.”

Rallies were also held in Garamilla/Darwin, Nipaluna/Hobart, Kaurna Yerta/Adelaide, Kanamaluka/Launceston, Magan-djin/Brisbane and Kabi Kabi Country/Sunshine Coast.

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Artists, Ayta sing vs Pax Silica
content:
Photo by Shannia Angel Cabuello

Artists and other advocates amplified their opposition against a US-led initiative through song.

On November 6, an artist group launched the anti-Pax Silica anthem “Get Off Our Lands” in a solidarity night filled with protest songs.

Produced by the Concerned Artists of the Philippines (CAP), the song was accompanied by a documentary music video featuring the Ayta community in Sitio Kalangitan, whose ancestral lands and natural resources are threatened by displacement and plunder.

Through the song, CAP aimed to expose the false promises behind the Pax Silica and to condemn those in power who allowed it.

Cultural performances and solidarity messages completed the program as part of the Trump Out campaign and the ‘12 Days of Protests’, building up the major protest actions on November 16 and 17.

Ayta elders also attended the solidarity night and expressed their strong rejection of Pax Silica, chanting “Ako Labay Ya Pax Silica!” (I don’t like Pax Silica!).

They led a community dance ritual to drive away “bad spirits,” which they associate with the Pax Silica Initiative and the impending visit of US President Donald Trump for the ASEAN Summit.

Ayta Chieftain Nelson De Guzman countered the statement of Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) President Joshua Bingcang that no Indigenous community would be affected by the Pax Silica Initiative. He said that no proper consultation was conducted within their community.

“They learned that they were being driven away from their land even before they knew about the project,” said Sandiwa Network project coordinator Gina Cambronero.

“The Pax Silica will kill our future. We nurtured our lands. We cannot allow foreigners to claim it,” said Ayta Indigenous woman Tessie Sanchez.

Sanchez told Bulatlat that planting rice, taro, and sweet potato helped support her seven children. She feared that the signing of the agreement could dry their water sources and take away their farmlands.

“The ruling class used the term pax which meant peace. But is there peace in it? They use it as instruments for deception,” Cambronero said.

“We just want peace in our tribe and in our land,” De Guzman said in the song’s documentary music video.

Around 20,000 peasants and 15,000 Ayta could be reportedly displaced once its Artificial Intelligence hub was established on the 1,620 hectares of land in Tarlac.

author: labor4pal
title: The U.S. government is escalating its attack on Palestine activism in Michigan (Mondoweiss)
content:
Four more pro-Palestine activists have been indicted on “conspiracy” charges stemming from protests at the University of Michigan, bringing the total to 12. The defendants now face sentences ranging from five years to several decades.

By Yarden Azoulay Katz and Adi Saleem November 10, 2026

FBI agent stopping and searching a vehicle in Ann Arbor, MI as part of the crackdown on new defendants, October 29, 2026.

The U.S. government is expanding its assault on Palestine solidarity activism in Michigan. Last summer, the FBI conducted raids against pro-Palestine activists connected to the University of Michigan. The defendants, known as the Michigan 8, were indicted by the Department of Justice on “conspiracy” charges, specifically “conspiracy to transmit threats in interstate and foreign commerce” and “conspiracy to intimidate a witness.” On Thursday, October 29, the FBI raided the home of activists in the same circle. The next day, the government unsealed a superseding indictment that adds four more defendants to the case, turning the Michigan 8 into the Michigan 12.

The four new defendants are all recent graduates of the University of Michigan with ties to campus Palestine activism. Like the initial eight defendants, they are charged with conspiracy and potentially face long prison sentences, from five years to several decades.

The federal government’s new indictment doubles down on previous allegations of “antisemitism.” In a press release announcing the indictment, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan Jerome F. Gorgon, Jr. claims the defendants aimed “to terrorize our Jewish community” and even compares them to Hitler and the biblical Pharaoh. The government again portrays the defendants as “terrorists” because of their alleged support for Palestinian resistance groups, despite never charging any defendant with “terrorism,” “hate crimes,” or even “vandalism.”

As part of this attack, the government filed an emergency motion to detain one of the initial eight defendants (who had been released on bond) all the way until trial. In recent months, FBI agents have also made visits to the homes of several Palestine activists in southeast Michigan.

This new wave of repression and propaganda is intended to send chills through the Palestine solidarity movement and sway public opinion against the defendants. But community supporters, family, and friends of the Michigan 12 are continuing to fight back.

On October 29, Henry David Mackeen-Shapiro (who goes by Drin Shapiro) was heading home from the Detroit public school where he teaches. Shapiro was stopped by FBI agents who had their guns pointed at him, with about six police vehicles present. They arrested him and seized his car and phone.

Around an hour later, about fifteen FBI agents arrived at Shapiro’s home. They knocked on the door, announcing they had a search warrant but refusing to show it, according to one person who was present for the entire raid. Those inside the house decided to open the door to avoid having the agents break through it (as they have done in the June 2026 and April 2025 raids on local Palestine activists). As the search began, two agents were stationed outside, pointing their rifles at the house windows, while another agent with a rifle guarded the door.

The agents conducting the search made clear to those present that if they stay in the house, they must remain put and not follow the agents. The agents soon received a message on their radio devices asking them to turn off their body cameras; they later confirmed to the residents that they have done so. The agents refused additional requests to show a warrant, only leaving it on the kitchen table when the search was over. The warrant instructs the agents to seize devices that may contain communications with several other Michigan 12 defendants (the agents took Shapiro’s computer).https://archive.org/embed/fbiagents-seizing-materials-drin-shapiro-home-oct-29-2026

FBI agents exiting defendants’ Detroit home after the raid, carrying a box with seized materials, October 29, 2026. Video by the Michigan 12 defense effort.

“It was a really unjust process,” a person present during the raid said. “I was not told what was happening, I was not told my rights, and I was not shown a warrant.” That the agents turned off their body cameras made it obvious the government is acting with “a total lack of transparency,” they added.

Shapiro spent the night in jail and was arraigned the next day …

author: Kodao Productions
title: Angry farmers dump rotten vegetables at DA
content:
Vegetable farmers from the Cordillera dumped rotten vegetables at Department of Agriculture’s (DA) main office in Quezon City on Tuesday, protesting the agency’s failure to solve the worsening crisis faced by local food producers.


The protesters said plummeting farm gate prices and continuously rising costs of agricultural inputs have forced many farmers in the upland region to refuse farming or selling their produce at bottom level prices.


Farmers led by the Kanatengan Network, Apit Tako, the Cordillera Peoples Alliance (CPA), and KATRIBU are demanding fair floor prices, affordable agricultural inputs, sufficient subsidies, improved farm-to-market roads, measures against vegetable importation and smuggling, and an end to usurious lending and excessive land rental costs.


“The rotten vegetables thrown at the agency were the very same produce that farmers could no longer sell amid intensifying competition with imported vegetables, plummeting farm gate prices, and continuously rising costs of agricultural inputs,” KATRIBU in a statement said.


The Indigenous Peoples’ group said the agriculture department allowed local farmers struggling to recover production costs and earn a decent livelihood.


“Instead of strengthening domestic agricultural production through genuine agrarian reform, adequate government support, and the development of local industries, the Marcos Jr. administration continues to allow agricultural importation and smuggling to undermine Filipino farmers. Local producers are left competing with cheaper imported vegetables while receiving inadequate support to sustain their own production,” the group said.


On Tuesday, the Bureau of Customs announced a planned investigation of a P524.27 million worth of reportedly smuggled agricultural products found in a warehouse in Valenzuela City last October 17. Tons of red onions, beans and legumes, ginger and carrots, as well as peanut products were allowed to pass through customs inspection and were seized outside port premises.


While Cordillera farmers complain of diving farm gate prices, meanwhile, retail prices for their produce have risen in lowland wet markets.


The Philippine Statistics Authority reported the following selling prices in Mimaropa region this week:


Carrots: ₱140.00 per kg

(Bantay Presyo, Nov 1, 2026)


Baguio Beans (Habichuelas): ₱100.00 per kg

(Bantay Presyo, Nov 1, 2026)


White Potato: ₱160.00 per kg

(Bantay Presyo, Nov 1, 2026)


Pechay (Baguio): ₱80.00 per kg

(Bantay Presyo, Nov 1, 2026)


Cabbage: Varies around ₱120.00 – ₱180.00 per kg depending on the market source.


Sayote: Varies around ₱125.00 – ₱130.00 per kg.


(Raymund B. Villanueva)

Kiñe: El día sábado 07 de noviembre del presente año, llevamos a cabo un txawun Palin, dónde asistieron diferentes comunidades de wallmapu, logrando así una jornada familiar llena de nutxam hacia nuestros ppm y nuestros lamgen caídos en el weichan, cómo también un gran palikantun en honor a ellos.

Hoy a casi 6 meses de su partida queremos reivindicar la figura de nuestro weichafe como una persona profundamente humana que brindó su vida para cuidar y aportar al proyecto de reconstrucción nacional tanto desde su rol como weichafe así como en su vida personal donde pudimos dar fé de su integridad, su feyentun y apego a los valores del mapuche gen. author: none
title: Why Alex Contompasis deserves Executive Clemency
content:
More than five years have passed since January 6, 2021, a date forever linked with one of the most divisive moments in modern American history.

by Don Ritter (The Saratogian)


While the nation’s attention focused on the attack on the United States Capitol in Washington, D.C., another violent confrontation unfolded hundreds of miles away outside the New York State Capitol in Albany during a “Stop the Steal” rally. It was there that Albany resident Alex Contompasis became involved in a violent altercation that ultimately resulted in his conviction and a lengthy prison sentence.


Today, a striking contradiction exists. Nearly all of the individuals convicted of federal crimes arising from the January 6 events at the U.S. Capitol have been released after President Donald Trump issued sweeping pardons and commutations in January 2025. Yet Alex Contompasis remains incarcerated in New York State. 


Whether one agrees with his politics is not the issue. The real question is whether justice has been served and whether executive clemency is appropriate. Supporters argue that Contompasis believed he was defending himself and others during a rapidly escalating confrontation involving members of the Proud Boys and counter-protesters. They contend that the circumstances were chaotic, emotions were high, and decisions had to be made in seconds rather than after hours of legal analysis. Advocates have continued to campaign for clemency, arguing that his sentence is disproportionate and that his case raises broader questions about New York’s self-defense laws.


The courts, however, viewed the evidence differently. An Albany County jury convicted Contompasis, and in 2025, the Appellate Division unanimously upheld his conviction, concluding that the evidence supported the verdict and rejecting his self-defense arguments. Still, executive clemency exists precisely because the legal system recognizes that mercy may sometimes be appropriate even after a lawful conviction.One of the strongest arguments for clemency is consistency. The federal government chose to extend extraordinary mercy to those convicted of offenses connected to the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, including individuals convicted of assaulting police officers and other serious crimes. Whether one


supported or opposed those pardons, they fundamentally changed the landscape of January 6 justice. Against that backdrop, Contompasis’ continued imprisonment appears, to many observers, increasingly difficult to reconcile. Executive clemency is not a declaration that someone was legally innocent. It is an acknowledgment that mercy, fairness, rehabilitation, or broader public interests justify reducing or ending a sentence. Governors and presidents have exercised this authority throughout American history.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul has granted numerous pardons and commutations during her administration after reviewing evidence of rehabilitation and other equitable considerations. If executive clemency is intended to recognize cases deserving individualized consideration, then supporters argue that


Alex Contompasis deserves that consideration as well.Reasonable people can disagree about what happened outside the State Capitol that day. They can disagree about whether Contompasis acted reasonably, whether he overreacted, or whether the jury reached the correct verdict. Those debates will likely continue for years. But clemency is not about retrying a criminal


case. Instead, it asks whether continued imprisonment still serves the interests of justice.If New York believes in redemption, proportionality, and individualized review, then Contompasis’ petition deserves careful consideration. His supporters argue that enough time has passed, that he no longer presents a danger to society, and that continued incarceration accomplishes little beyond extending punishment.


Others will disagree and believe the seriousness of the assault warrants completion of the sentence.


Ultimately, clemency is an act of executive judgment, not judicial review. It allows elected leaders to balance justice with mercy when extraordinary circumstances warrant. Whether Governor Hochul ultimately agrees is her decision alone. Under New York law, she has constitutional authority to grant pardons and commutations after reviewing the facts of each individual case.As New York continues to reflect on the divisions exposed on January 6, it may also be time to ask whether mercy has been …

title: Sara’s clown show at the Senate
content:
The Nov. 9 and 10 impeachment trial sessions of Sara Zimmerman Duterte Carpio turned out to be poorly choreographed, with the defense witnesses apparently unprepared to handle questions from the prosecution, with two of them suffering from instant amnesia and can’t recall joining an all-expenses paid excursion to China the previous year. One, Davao City assessor Jaime Adalin, even tried to be funny by tagging a question “irrelevant,” and drew guffaws from the gallery.


However, he could determine a property of Sara’s husband, Manases Carpio, is listed in Sara’s SALNs even without seeing the coordinates, or the meters and bounds, of the asset. His testimony runs afoul of the testimony of two property registrars who said Carpio’s landholdings were not reflected in Duterte’s SALN. Davao City Register of Deeds IV Kathy Florence Baldonado testified that Carpio had acquired a 379-sq-m lot in Juna Subdivision, Matina Crossing, Talomo, Davao City, which was not declared in her SALN.


Samal Deputy Register of Deeds III Marco Pineda testified that Carpio bought a 751-sq-m lot in Matanos for P3,453,849 on March 15, 2018. Pineda said no entry in Duterte’s SALN matched the deed of absolute sale for that property. However, when shown images of a building from Google Maps with the sign “Prime Bistro,” Adalin admitted he wasn’t sure. He can’t remember the China journey and couldn’t be certain that it was the property which he said was included in Sara’s SALNs. On Nov. 10, the defense presented its second witness, Samal City Assessor Engr. John Kenneth Enumerables, who will testify on property records linked to Atty. Manases Carpio.


Presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero said senators might be confused with the location of the Carpio property in the deed of sale since it says the property is located in Barangay San Isidro but the TCT shows the lot is in Barangay Matanos. Enumerables says it is a small matter, a mere technical description. Sen. Panfilo Lacson said Matanos is actually located in Barangay Pangubatan, which Enumerables confirmed. Prosecutor Prosecutor Benjamon Tolosa Jr. noted that the deed of Absolute Sale for the property was executed on March 2018, while Duterte’s 2025 SALN showed the property was acquired in 2013. Enumerables acknowledged the discrepancy and said he is not certain if the property in the TCT is the same property in the SALN.


If Adalin performed badly for the defense, Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan snatched the bragging rights for the day’s worst dodger. Bajan claimed she wasn’t friends with Sara Zimmerman Suterte Carpio when she was appointed city accountant in 2026. Apparently, prosecutor Mae Divinagracia argued, Sara trusted Bajan so much that she appointed her chairperson of the City Audit and Transition Teams for Barangays in 2018, and as member of the Investigating Committee of Davao City in 2020.


Divinagracia asked Bajan if the accounting firm she worked for was registered in 2023 with the Securities and Exchange Commission in (SEC). Bajan could not answer at first, but later said “yes” after getting some signal from the defense, prompting the prosecutor to ask the court to stop her from getting coached. Bajan also hesitated when asked by Divinagracia to confirm if the signature appearing in the original Articles of Partnership of the accounting firm she worked with was hers, and she dithered and said she cannot remember the 2003 documents of Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., causing uproar among the senators who told her pointblank that it was unacceptable that she could not answer such a simple question. Still, Bajan said the signature was similar as hers but insisted she cannot recall signing the document that contains her tax account number. Sensing that she is not being truthful, Escudero, Sens. Bam Aquino and Francis Pangilinan warned her that she is in “danger zone,” which could lead to a contempt citation or even a case of perjury.


Divinagracia noted that the firm Elises and Ciudadano is the same Elises and Ciudadano which is the external auditor of GenCorp Industries Inc., Metro City Chow Foods, and Great Jolly Times, all of which are businesses in which Sara and her hubby own shares of stock. Pangilinan points out that the address of Bajan’s former accounting firm – Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co. – in Davao City is the same address of the auditing firm of GenCorp and Metro City Chow. Bajan also denied knowing anything about GenCorp, Pikimong Pikimong and other companies …

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: First Nations Bank CEO says federal budget is a ‘generational’ opportunity for First Nations
content:
First Nations Bank of Canada (FNBC) president and CEO Bill Lomax says the federal budget offers a rare opening for First Nations to move from consultation into genuine ownership of the infrastructure and energy projects that will define Canada’s economy for decades.


Lomax framed the scale of planned investments in transportation, energy and electricity infrastructure as “a generational opportunity for First Nations to play a leading role in building Canada’s future.”


“When First Nations move beyond participation to become owners, we create lasting economic opportunities, build wealth for future generations and strengthen Canada’s economy as a whole. When First Nations succeed, Canada succeeds,” Lomax said in a statement following the budget. 


“But we need to think beyond consultation, employment and contracting opportunities. While these remain important, First Nations must also be recognized as business partners and owners, with the ability to build businesses, acquire equity and participate directly in the long-term economic benefits these projects generate.”


The FNBC is Canada’s only Indigenous-owned chartered bank, founded in 1996, operates 22 branches and service centres across six provinces and three territories, manages more than $1.6 billion in assets, and through its subsidiary FNB Trust, administers approximately $5.5 billion.


The federal budget, tabled Nov. 5, commits more than $50 billion over 10 years to Indigenous programs and services. The largest single piece is $32 billion over a decade for First Nations housing and on-reserve infrastructure. 


That includes the new First Nations On-Reserve Infrastructure Program, backed by $18.5 billion for infrastructure and $11 billion for housing that aims to maintain, renovate and build thousands of homes over 10 years. 


“This budget is an opportunity to invest in who we are,” Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty told APTN News in an interview Tuesday. “It’s an opportunity to better define who we are. It’s an opportunity to have a strategic approach to what our financial position is going to be, and I think the greatest opportunity of all is to demonstrate to Canadians the fiscal impact that Indigenous people have on the Canadian economy.”


Indigenous Services Canada Minister Mandy Gull Masty at a news conference on Parliament Hill in May. Photo: APTN.


The budget also introduces the new Canada Growth Incentive (CGI) for Canadian entrepreneurs, investors and employees, which is also open to Indigenous business people. The goal of the CGI is to keep investment money in Canada. 


It offers a new capital gains tax exemption for “Canadian builders” of up to $15 million earned from the Canadian businesses they invested in. 

To benefit, Canadians will have to reinvest and keep their money in Canada and Canadian businesses.  


“The Canada Growth Incentive (CGI) will be one of the most significant incentives to attract and retain builders here in Canada by creating the path for entrepreneurs, investors, and employees to reinvest in Canada,” the budget said. “This represents a level shift in the attractiveness of firms, large and small, to invest-and reinvest-in Canada, and deliver lasting prosperity for all Canadians.”  


The budget is also promising money for education, health, child welfare, policing and emergency management. 


The budget also outlines the government’s support for the Indigenous Loan Program that loans money to First Nations for projects. 


“I hope everybody listening or reading our interviews about the budget understands that I’m here to spend money; come to me with your proposals. I’m going to do everything I can to meet the needs, so work with me,” said Gull Masty. 


 Where’s the money?


Aaron Pete, chief of Chawathil First Nation in British Columbia, told APTN that he’s taking a cautious approach to the budget because the money “rarely finds its way to First Nation communities in a constructive way.” 


Chief of Chawathil First Nation Aaron Pete. Photo From aaronpete.com,


“It [the budget] sounds promising, but again, my concern is that it gets stuck in Ottawa and doesn’t actually reach these communities,” he said. 


Pete was a councillor in 2022 and became chief in 2025. He has a podcast where politicians of all stripes are invited to share their opinions on the state of the country and First Nations politics. 


He acknowledged that many of the government’s stated priorities — clean running water …

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: From the battlefield to barriers at home: Remembering Indigenous veterans in Yellowknife
content:
One by one, veterans, cadets, Elders and community leaders line up for a smudge to mark the beginning of Yellowknife’s

Indigenous Veterans Day ceremony

.


For the first time, the annual gathering incorporates traditional practice and offers participants a moment to ground themselves, reflect and honour First Nations, Inuit and Métis people who served in Canada’s military.


Retired chief warrant officer Richard Francoeur says the day provides Indigenous veterans recognition for their service and sacrifices.


“There are so many people from the Indigenous communities that went into wars that a lot of people weren’t aware of,” Francoeur told

APTN News.


He says Indigenous people have served in conflicts throughout Canada’s military history, including the First and Second World Wars, as well as NATO and United Nations operations.


Indigenous Veterans Day is recognized across Canada on Nov. 8.


A Métis veteran lays a wreath at the memorial in Yellowknife’s Lakeview Cemetery paying respects to those who served. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Returning home 


During the Yellowknife ceremony, attendees heard how some Indigenous veterans returned home to a country that did not recognize their service on equal terms.


Many faced racism and prejudice and were denied the same veterans benefits, land grants and reintegration support available to non-Indigenous veterans.


A reflection shared during the ceremony described the difficult choice some veterans faced between their military identities and their Indigenous identities.


“Many were forced to choose between their identities as soldiers or their identities as Indigenous peoples and often experienced barriers from receiving veterans benefits,” Framcoeur said.


Indigenous soldiers also brought skills from their communities onto the frontlines. The ceremony recognized their knowledge of tracking, marksmanship and the land, along with the use of Indigenous language such as Cree, which helped encode military communications during the Second World War.


The ceremony also recognized the 80 veterans buried at Yellowknife’s Lakeview Cemetery, many of them Indigenous.


Organizers paid tribute specifically to two Métis soldiers from the Northwest Territories who died during the First World War.


Private George McKenzie, from Fort Resolution, died on active service on Nov. 9, 1918.


Private Frank McPherson, from Fort Simpson, died three days earlier, on Nov. 6, 1918.


The ceremony included two minutes of silence, an Act of Remembrance and readings by cadets from Yellowknife.


Cadets line up to take part in Yellowknife’s Indigenous Veterans Day ceremony. For the first time, the annual ceremony incorporated the traditional practice of smudge. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Cadets help keep the stories alive


The history was not lost on the younger generation.


Blake Ohokannoak, a cadet with 2837 Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry said he hopes people continue to share the stories.


“I think more Canadians should know about the discrimination they face while serving and after serving,” he said.


Ohokannoak, who is Inuit, has been involved with cadets for four years. He says his interest in the program started with his father, who was a commanding officer with the Cambridge Bay Cadets.


Jason Meyer has been a cadet with the 825 Yellowknife Royal Canadian Elks for a year. His father was a member of the Canadian Rangers in Nunavut.


Meyer said attending the ceremony is personal for him.


“I’m Inuit, so I come every year that I can, so I can honour those who served,” he said.


The cadets also help maintain the Field of Honour and take part in the annual remembrance activities, including placing candles in honour of Indigenous veterans.

From the battlefield to barriers at home: Remembering Indigenous veterans in Yellowknife

APTN News

author: Dennis Ward
title: Australia’s inaugural Ambassador for First Nations People visits Canada
content:
Four years ago, the Australian government took a step that no other country has taken when it created the position of Ambassador for First Nations People.

The ambassador, Justin Mohamed, is a Gooreng Gooreng man from Bundaberg in Queensland.

Mohamed recently visited Canada for a series of high-level meetings with Canadian ministers, including Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty.

The ambassador also met with national Indigenous organizations and economic groups. Among the similarities between the two countries, says Mohamed, is the effort to involve Indigenous peoples in economic opportunities.

“For the first time, in my 36 years of working in Indigenous affairs, where both of our leaders are talking very positively about the uplift of economic engagement with our First peoples in our country and seeing the benefits of that,” says Mohamed on the latest episode of Face to Face.

“Obviously, here there is things that we can learn and things that Canada can learn from Australia. Our vast country, we’ve got a lot of land mass, we’ve got so many people spread across that, how to get those connections across our land and hopefully across our waters so we have more connections from country to country.”

The ambassador says Australia has strong laws and policies around consultation when it comes to mining and development on Indigenous Peoples’ lands.

However, he acknowledges that can be improved.

“With the new uptake of critical minerals, the renewable energies, that’s definitely a big conversation piece that is taking place and structures and Traditional Owner Groups as we call them in Australia are positioning themselves to be economically part of these new developments and hopefully learn from the past,” says Mohamed.

We have a long relationship with mining companies, with communities, hopefully learning from those experiences and that we can have a better relationship with the critical minerals, renewable energy space. We know this is a conversation and there’s a whole range of things that wrap around that that are taking place as we sit here,” adds Mohamed.

One of the previous roles Justin Mohamed had was chief executive officer of Reconciliation Australia.

The non-government, not-for-profit was established in January 2001 to promote a continuing national focus for reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians.

While he believes reconciliation has come a long way since he was a child, Mohamed says there are still challenges.

“I think the appetite sways back and forth when you have different governments and political leaders and also things that kind of hit us and impact us and the focus and the direction and the energy may be diverted like pandemics or global crashes in our economy these things happen,” says Mohamed.

“I think one of the things that is staying on course is ensuring there’s a path that we still got to walk and that’s part of our history. So, I think in Australia to be fair and as honest as I can be around where we are, we’ve taken steps, but the journey is still a long way in front of us to keep going on that and there’s still healing our nation needs to have collectively together,” he adds.

Dennis is Métis from southern Manitoba. After spending a decade working in TV in Alberta and Ontario, Dennis returned to Manitoba to join APTN. In 2016, he won a Canadian Association of Journalists award for his story A Soldier Scorned for APTN Investigates. In 2017, he became a host/producer for APTN National News and Face to Face.

author: Administrador
title: PREGUNTAS
content:
A las familias buscadoras sin y con colectivo:

Desde el día 3 de octubre, en horas de la tarde, personas cercanas a la glorieta de los desaparecidos, anunciaron en sus redes sociales que estaba confirmado un encuentro, el 6 de diciembre, de colectivos de familiares y el EZLN en la Glorieta de las y los Desaparecidos, mientras la Comisión Sexta mantenía una reunión con enviados de la Sexta Nacional, y a la que asistieron, sin invitación, varias buscadoras.

Días después, alguien y a nombre de las familias buscadoras de “La Glorieta de las y los Desaparecidos”, circuló en sus redes una “invitación”. Por varios medios se les hizo saber que no era el conducto. Que mandaran la invitación vía el Frayba, quien nos apoyaba y apoya en todo lo referente a registro y propuestas de familias, grupos y colectivas de buscadoras.

Entonces, después de varios días también, les mandamos mensajes por varios lados. Que retiraran la invitación porque en esos términos iba a ser rechazada. Que contenía menciones que podrían considerarse síntoma de que no conocían a quien invitaban, y cosas que podrían considerarse ofensivas para las comunidades zapatistas.

Además de que no era ese tipo de “reuniones” las que pensaba la Comisión Sexta Zapatista, y que correspondía a la delegación zapatista el definir su agenda con fechas y horas.

No sólo no nos hicieron caso, sino que aumentaron su difusión agregando que era seguro que se daría la reunión con la delegación zapatista en la glorieta, poniendo fecha, y hasta hora en algunos casos.

Insistimos mandándoles mensajes de que rehicieran la invitación por lo mismo. Mientras, seguía creciendo la confusión, y colectivas y grupos empezaban a cambiar sus fechas para estar presentes en “LA” reunión. Les advertimos que nos estaban orillando a un desmentido público. Esto es, a una respuesta severa para aclarar.

Hasta donde entendemos, el espacio de La Glorieta de las y los Desaparecidos no es una organización, sino un espacio de encuentro. Esto es, no tienen una vocería ni dirección establecida. Es un lugar donde suelen converger grupos y colectivas de familias buscadoras. Supusimos que tienen o tenían un mecanismo para hacer acuerdos y tomar decisiones. Y que, por lo tanto, someterían a ese mecanismo la pertinencia o no de esa redacción que, lo sabían con antelación, provocaba molestia en los zapatistas.

La “invitación” contiene 3 elementos fundamentales:

1.- Se ofrece a los zapatistas apoyo. Por eso “invitaron” a las comunidades zapatistas a que llevaran fotos de sus desaparecidos, y que nos iban a enseñar cómo se hace una ficha de desaparición forzada, cómo se pega en la glorieta – junto con cientos de fotos de desaparecidos-, qué trámites hay que hacer para que una ONG otorgue financiamiento, a quién dirigirse en la pirámide gubernamental, etc.

Hermanas familias buscadoras: en territorio zapatista y en las comunidades que fueron zapatistas y ahora son partidistas, NO HAY DESAPARICIONES FORZADAS desde hace 30 años.

Miren, hay grupos feministas que conocen todo lo relacionado con feminicidios. Otros con infanticidios. Otros con trata de personas. Otros con crímenes impunes. Otros en homofobia. Otros en racismo y segregación. Y así con cada uno de los horrores que se padecen en esta geografía llamada México.

Antes de ofrecernos cursos de qué hacer por estos problemas, ¿no es de esperar que al menos investiguen la tasa, ya no digan de feminicidios, sino de violencia de género en general? Porque sí, en territorios zapatistas no hay feminicidios. Ni infanticidios, ni crímenes impunes. Ni trata de personas (comercio, pues, compra venta de hombres, mujeres e infantes). Y así sea usted güero, alto y habla una lengua incomprensible, entra y sale de territorio zapatista sin ser desaparecido, humillado, burlado, esclavizado, asesinado.

Ni homofobia. Así sea usted otroa (lesbiana, homosexual, transexual y todos los nombres con los que identifica la diferencia sexual), no sólo puede dar clases a infantes heterosexuales (si se capacita antes, claro), ser milicianoa, ocupar cargos en las comunidades y en la organización, y llamarse como le dé la gana y tener la identidad de género que le plazca.

Hay hasta quien ha tratado de venir a dar clases de erotismo y autoestimulación erótica. Hermanas, tenemos la más alta tasa de natalidad comparada con la de las grandes urbes y, créanme, no son clases de erotismo lo que nos hace falta. Las músicas favoritas en la mayoría de la juventud zapatista son el rock, el ska …

author: Daron Letts
title: Offshore Western Arctic oil and gas exploration could be back on the table
content:
The days might be numbered for the federal government’s decade-long

moratorium

 on oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic — at least in its present form.


“There is a review happening,” said Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand during a news conference at Nunavut Arctic College in Iqaluit on Tuesday.


The moratorium, established in December 2016 by then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, remains in place as the Liberal government charts “the best path forward,” Chartrand said.


The moratorium agreement calls for a review every five years.

This includes ongoing meetings with Inuit organizations and territorial governments, Chartrand said.


At a news conference in Montreal at the same time, Prime Minister Mark Carney highlighted $11 million in funding to support “the governance and oversight of offshore oil and gas activities in the Arctic Ocean.”


“This is capacity funding for Inuit leadership. It is absolutely not in any way, shape, or form a decision about lifting the moratorium,” Carney said.


Chartrand’s comments came in response to questions after a media event about the federal government’s $4 billion in cultural spending outlined in Thursday’s

budget

.


In her opening address at the event, she highlighted the new Canada Creative Credit, an annual tax cut on up to $45,000 of arts-related net business income for artists.


Qikiqtani Inuit Association President Olayuk Akesuk says he and other Inuit leaders met with Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand virtually two weeks ago. They discussed lifting the decade-long moratorium on oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic. (Photo by Daron Letts)


“We are also proposing stronger support for film, television, and digital production and a new productivity mega deduction to help eligible businesses invest in equipment and technology,” she added.


Chartrand met with staff at the Inuit Broadcasting Corp. on Monday.


The budget would provide an additional $300 million in funding to the CBC and Radio-Canada. The public broadcaster got $1.46 billion in the 2025-26 fiscal year. The budget also proposes $134 million over four years for the Local Journalism Initiative, a program that supports independent local news in rural, remote, and under-served regions, including the Arctic.


She also highlighted $393 million in spending in support of francophone cultural institutions.


As for the moratorium on oil and gas exploration, Qikiqtani Inuit Association President Olayuk Akesuk and fellow Inuit leaders expressed their perspective with Chartrand during a virtual meeting two weeks ago, he said in an interview Tuesday.


“It is important to go through the regulatory process in order for us to support anything that might impact the environment,” he said. “Let’s work together to ensure that we are doing it properly.”


Nunavut Liberal MP Lori Idlout said she is confident that discussions about any return to exploration will be made in collaboration with Inuit.


— With files from Nehaa Bimal

author: Sharon Zhang
title: “The Time Is Now for Change”: Sanders Says He Won’t Back Schumer for Leader
content:
Emerging leader Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he is refusing to fund the government next month until the war is defunded.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) announced on Tuesday that he will not be supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer’s (D-New York) run for Senate majority leader in the new Congress and suggested that someone else will be running to replace him.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for 30 years, and I like Chuck — nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer,” said Sanders in a press conference. “But, in my view, the time is now for change. And I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”

This marks the first major public defection in the caucus against Schumer. There hasn’t yet been a senator to formally nominate themselves to challenge Schumer. But Sanders suggested in his remarks that Schumer won’t be running unopposed and floated the name of progressive favorite Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) for the role.

“I think one of the names out there is Chris Van Hollen. I think Chris has indicated some interest, but you’ll have to talk to him,” Sanders said. Sanders added in an interview that he would back Van Hollen if he ran.

Van Hollen is reportedly actively considering a run. On Tuesday, Van Hollen said at the Popular Mandate conference that he is “actively listening to people who are looking for” change, and called for a “bold agenda.”

“I am in the process right now of calling my colleagues,” he said. “Because at the end of the day, this is a vote in the Democratic caucus. So let’s just keep in touch.”

Further in his press conference, Sanders said that voters must be shown that the party is ready to respond to their demands after Americans entrusted them with a massive congressional majority, adding: “We need a process, we need a vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party.”

Sanders was joined by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), who agreed that lawmakers must come together to decide on their goals. Slotkin said that Democrats should withhold quorum if Schumer is the only candidate and doesn’t present a vision for the future of the party.

The two lawmakers had just come out of a meeting with Senate Democrats in which they said Schumer had not provided a clear goal for their upcoming majority.

Flanked by Senators Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York), Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) in a press conference after that same meeting on Tuesday, Schumer said that he’s “confident” he will be reelected as leader.

Polling by YouGov for Indivisible released on Tuesday found that only 10 percent of voters say that Democrats should choose Schumer to be majority leader, while 57 percent said they should choose someone else.

Van Hollen has long criticized Schumer’s leadership as ineffective, especially in times when Schumer has ceded Democrats’ power during the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term. Progressives have favored the Maryland senator’s actions on foreign policy, including on Israel and Palestinian rights. They have also pointed to Van Hollen’s visit with constituent Kilmar Abrego García after he was deported to El Salvador as a sign of his willingness to fight against the Trump administration.

Michigan Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) has said for months that he would support Van Hollen for leader, and repeated that assertion last week after winning his election.

“We have two members in that room, duly elected senators, that would not be there if Schumer and the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC)] had had their way,” Van Hollen said at Popular Mandate on Tuesday, likely referring to El-Sayed and Troy Jackson. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates.”

author: Unknown
title: Women’s vigil in Amed commemorates 14 victims of femicide and unexplained deaths
content:
Women gathered outside the courthouse in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) on Tuesday for the sixth time to protest against femicide, gender-based violence and the failure to adequately investigate suspicious deaths. The vigil, organized by the Network Against Violence, focused this week on the names and life stories of 14 women who were murdered between November 2 and 10. Numerous women joined the demonstration alongside representatives of political parties and civil society organizations.


Under a banner reading “Women Stand Vigil for Justice and Memory,” participants carried photographs of women who had been killed. Chants such as “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom), “Femicide is political” and “Bijî tekoşîna jinan” (Long live women’s struggle) echoed throughout the gathering. With the slogan “Do not protect, do not whitewash, prosecute,” they denounced impunity for violence against women.


Remembering 14 women and their life stories


Speaking on behalf of the network, Irem Ilhan of the Association for Solidarity from a Women’s Perspective (DAKAHDER) stated that women refused to allow the victims’ fates to be forgotten. She emphasized the need to insist on thorough investigations in a society where women’s deaths are frequently classified as suicides, accidents or unexplained incidents. She described the systematic threat to women’s lives as femicide.


The participants then read aloud the stories of 14 women, explicitly distinguishing between confirmed homicides and deaths whose causes have yet to be determined.


Among the victims was 33-year-old Şefika Yeşildağ, who was stabbed to death by her former husband, Osman Oruç, in Aksaray on November 2. The couple had been divorced for six years. According to her mother, the man had continued to harass Şefika. Nazmiye Özer, 56, was also killed by her former husband on November 7, six years after their divorce. Women’s organizations called for an investigation into possible previous threats and failures by state authorities responsible for providing protection.


Latife Mengüç, 50, was shot dead on November 5 by a man from whom she wanted to separate. The perpetrator subsequently took his own life.


Domestic violence


Particularly distressing was the case of Huriye Çiçek and her daughter Zeynep Demircan. The 50-year-old mother and her 25-year-old daughter were killed in an armed attack in early November, carried out by Huriye’s son, who was also Zeynep’s brother. An eleven-year-old girl was seriously injured in the attack.


Hülya Aktaş, 73, was stabbed to death by her son on November 6. Another of her sons was also killed in the same attack.


Citing these cases, women’s organizations emphasized that family ties offered no guarantee of protection against patriarchal violence and that violence within the family must not be treated as a private matter.


Other victims included 31-year-old Hilal Mete and 46-year-old Ayşe Sena Demir. Both were shot dead inside a vehicle on November 5. A suspect was arrested. Satı Aydoğmuş, 68, was also killed in an armed attack that claimed the life of another person.


Unexplained deaths must be investigated


In several of the cases presented, it has yet to be established whether the women were victims of violent crimes. Participants therefore demanded comprehensive forensic examinations and transparent investigations.


These cases include the death of 18-year-old Havva Büşra Kural, who was found dead alongside her father in an apartment on November 2. The circumstances surrounding the deaths of 44-year-old Melek Altun, Olessya Shudrina, also 44, and Melek Kaval, who were found dead in their apartments in early November, also remain unclear.


The vigil also commemorated an unidentified woman whose body was discovered on November 4 off the coast of Izmir, in the Bayraklı district. Women’s organizations called for her identity to be established and the cause of her death to be determined.


The vigil thus also drew attention to women whose deaths have not yet been confirmed as homicides but whose fates could remain unresolved without effective investigations.


“Justice is needed for all women”


After the names were read aloud, Irem Ilhan emphasized the responsibility of state institutions to protect women, saying: “When a woman is killed despite having reported violence, applied for protection or already been granted protective measures, not only the perpetrators but also any public officials who may bear responsibility must be …

author: Unknown
title: Students in Rojava protest for education in Kurdish
content:
Students in several cities across the Cizîrê region of Rojava demonstrated against restrictions on Kurdish-language education imposed by the Syrian transitional government. In Qamişlo, Girkê Legê and Rimêlan, they took to the streets to demand recognition of Kurdish as a language of instruction and guarantees for the right to education in their mother tongue. The protests were sparked by a decision made by the Syrian Ministry of Education in late August to limit Kurdish-language instruction in schools to three hours per week.


In Qamişlo, students from the Hetîn and Şehîd Jîr schools participated in a demonstration that began at the Şehîd Osman Sabrî intersection in the Hilêliyê neighborhood. From there, the protesters marched to the regional administrative headquarters in the city center. During the march, they chanted slogans demanding recognition of their mother tongue and opposing restrictions on education.


Students: Our language is our identity


Outside the regional administrative headquarters, Diyana Sonchan and Viyan Mehmûd read out a joint statement in Kurdish and Arabic on behalf of the students. In the statement, they condemned the Ministry of Education’s decision to reduce the number of hours allocated to Kurdish-language instruction.


“Kurdish is not merely another school subject, but an expression of the identity, culture, history and existence of the Kurdish people. Restricting Kurdish-language instruction therefore goes far beyond a change to the school timetable. It directly infringes upon the linguistic and cultural rights of the Kurdish population,” the statement read.


The students called on the Ministry of Education and the Syrian transitional government to recognize the linguistic and educational rights of the Kurdish people. They also demanded guarantees of equal rights for all communities in Syria.


Protests in Girkê Legê and Rimêlan


Students in Girkê Legê and Rimêlan also organized joint protests. The demonstrators marched to the school administration building in Rimêlan, chanting slogans demanding the right to education in Kurdish. Participants declared that education in one’s mother tongue was a fundamental, non-negotiable right. They announced that they would continue their protests as long as restrictions on Kurdish-language education remained in place.


The latest demonstrations mark a continuation of protests against the education policies of the Syrian transitional government. Since early September, students and families in various cities across Rojava and Northeast Syria have been protesting against the reduction of Kurdish-language instruction to three hours per week.

author: Άγγελος Χατζηνικολάου
title: 15 Νοεμβρίου: Πορεία υπεράσπισης του Πολυτεχνείου, της ιστορικής μνήμης και των κοινωνικών – ταξικών αγώνων
content:
15 Νοεμβρίου: Πορεία υπεράσπισης του Πολυτεχνείου, της ιστορικής μνήμης και των κοινωνικών – ταξικών αγώνων


53 χρόνια

 μετά, η εξέγερση του Νοέμβρη του 1973, καθώς και οι αγώνες και οι κατακτήσεις που αυτή ενέπνευσε για δεκαετίες, βρίσκονται στο στόχαστρο ενός ανελέητου ρεβανσισμού από την πλευρά του κράτους και της άρχουσας τάξης της χώρας.


 


53 χρόνια

 μετά, η υφιστάμενη κυβέρνηση, το κράτος και οι ακροδεξιές εφεδρείες του πολιτικού συστήματος, επιχειρούν να αντικαταστήσουν την ιστορική μνήμη του Πολυτεχνείου με έναν επικίνδυνο αναθεωρητισμό της κοινωνικής και ταξικής ιστορίας αυτού του τόπου. Μια επιχείρηση που δεν περιορίζεται μόνο στην αμφισβήτηση των ιστορικών γεγονότων, όπως την ύπαρξη των νεκρών του Πολυτεχνείου, αλλά επεκτείνεται στη συνολική επανανοηματοδότηση της εξέγερσης, στην αποκοπή της από τις κοινωνικές και πολιτικές συγκρούσεις που ακολούθησαν την αντικατάσταση του δικτατορικού καθεστώτος από την αστική κοινοβουλευτική δημοκρατία και, τελικά, στην απονεύρωση του ίδιου του πολιτικού της περιεχομένου. Στόχος είναι να αποσυνδεθεί το Πολυτεχνείο από τα αντικρατικά – αντικαπιταλιστικά του συνθήματα, αλλά και από τους κοινωνικούς αγώνες και τις διεκδικήσεις που ακολούθησαν, ώστε να απομείνει ένα ακίνδυνο ιστορικό σύμβολο, με τις παρακαταθήκες και τις επιδράσεις του στο παρόν και το μέλλον να αποψιλώνονται.


53 χρόνια

 το πολιτικό σύστημα επιχειρεί την ενσωμάτωση της εξέγερσης στην κυρίαρχη αφήγηση περί αποκατάστασης της δημοκρατίας, με την μετατροπή της σε μια θεσμική επέτειο συμφιλίωσης και εθνικής ομοψυχίας. Σύμμαχος και εγγυητής αυτής της προσπάθειας υπήρξε επί δεκαετίες η σοσιαλδημοκρατική και ένα μεγάλο μέρος της κομμουνιστικής αριστεράς, η ιστορική συνέχεια δηλαδή αυτών που τις μέρες του Νοέμβρη μιλούσαν για «εξέγερση προβοκατόρων» και προσδοκούσαν στην φιλελευθεροποίηση της χούντας και την παλινόρθωση της αστικής δημοκρατίας χωρίς την καθοριστική συμβολή του ταξικού-λαϊκού παράγοντα.


53 χρόνια

 μετά επιχειρείται ένα ακόμη πιο επιθετικό βήμα: η πολιτική και ιστορική απονομιμοποίηση της εξέγερσης του 1973. Η εξέγερση προβάλλεται ως ένα παρωχημένο γεγονός, λίγο ή πολύ ασήμαντο στην πορεία της πτώσης της χούντας των συνταγματαρχών, οι πολιτικές της προεκτάσεις αντιμετωπίζονται ως αναχρονιστικές, ενώ οι αγώνες που εμπνεύστηκαν από αυτήν επιχειρείται να αποσυσχετιστούν από την αιματοβαμμένη ιστορική τους προέλευση. Ακόμη περισσότερο, σκοπός της αστικής προπαγάνδας και των κρατικών σχεδιασμών, είναι να στιγματιστούν τα υλικά κεκτημένα που πέτυχαν οι αγώνες που ενέπνευσε η εξέγερση του Πολυτεχνείου, όπως το πανεπιστημιακό άσυλο, οι καταλήψεις στις σχολές και οι νικηφόρες διεκδικήσεις του φοιτητικού κινήματος που σήμερα διασύρονται ως μια «ελληνική εκτροπή» από το ευρωπαϊκό καπιταλιστικό υπόδειγμα. Πρόκειται για μια συστηματική απόπειρα ανατροπής της ιστορικής μνήμης, με σκοπό να πληγεί όχι μόνο η υλική και συμβολική κληρονομιά του Νοέμβρη, αλλά και η δυνατότητα των σύγχρονων κοινωνικών και ταξικών αγώνων να αντλούν από αυτόν παραδείγματα αντίστασης και συλλογικής δράσης.


53 χρόνια

 μετά το κατεχόμενο κτήριο του Πολυτεχνείου με τα σφραγισμένα αμφιθέατρα, την αστυνομοκρατία, τις κλειδαμπαρωμένες πύλες, τις κάμερες και τις απειλές για ανατροπή, ακόμη και του θεσμικού πλαισίου του τριήμερου εορτασμού «χωρίς έκτροπα» που επί χρόνια φρουρούν οι δυνάμεις της αριστεράς και του οπορτουνισμού, αποτελούν τα απότοκα της αφρενάριστης εδώ και χρόνια κινηματικής υποχώρησης που έχουμε καθήκον να ανακόψουμε. author: Chris Walker
title: Outgoing GOP Texas Lt. Gov. Wants to Limit His Democratic Successor’s Powers
content:
Texas Republicans could convene a special session, voting to limit Democrats’ executive powers before they are sworn in.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Texas Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick has called for GOP lawmakers in the state legislature to pass new limits on his Democratic successor, Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin, who won in the state’s “blue wave” last week.

Patrick issued the call to alter the powers of his own office during an appearance on a conservative radio show on Monday.

The office of lieutenant governor has far more powers in Texas than it does in other states. Amending such powers would impose significant limitations on the incoming Democratic-controlled executive branch.

“I support the Republicans standing up for their voters,” Patrick said in his call to limit Goodwin’s future powers, adding that Republicans should make the changes to “protect the conservative majority.”

Patrick’s remarks disregard that Texas voters overwhelmingly rejected the GOP’s agenda in the midterm elections. Democratic candidate for governor Gina Hinojosa, for example, ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott by more than seven points in last week’s elections. Meanwhile, Goodwin won her race by over six points, and Democrats also won control of the state House of Representatives.

Yet, because Republicans retained control of the state Senate, any changes state lawmakers make to the powers of the office of lieutenant governor during the interim period would be difficult to undo once Democrats assume office. Indeed, Democratic lawmakers would likely have to pursue a lawsuit to challenge any such changes, which would put the matter into the hands of the state’s still conservative judicial system.

Texas Republican lawmakers indicated they were considering changes to the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s powers shortly after Hinojosa’s and Goodwin’s victories.

“We still have total power in Texas, and we must act like it by using the remaining ten weeks to restore separation of powers and limit the emergency powers that Governor-Elect Hinojosa is set to inherit,” read a social media post from state Rep. Brian Harrison (R), who called on Abbott to convene a special session of the legislature to implement the changes.

Hinojosa warned against lawmakers taking such actions.

“The people of Texas have spoken,” she said in response to the proposed plan.

Goodwin similarly argued against Republicans stripping her and the governor-elect of their executive branch powers, stating that they would be doing so “at their peril because we will have elections again in 2028.”
